explanation: Section 7(7) empowers the Tribunal (NCLT), on an application made to it, to pass orders such as directing the regulation of the management, winding up of the company, or declaring that the liability of the members shall be unlimited, when incorporation has been obtained by fraud or false information.

subject: Law
prompt: Can a charitable company registered under Section 8 alter the objects clause in its Memorandum of Association?
optionA: Yes, by ordinary resolution and Central Government approval
optionB: Yes, by special resolution and prior approval of the Central Government
optionC: No, Section 8 companies can never alter their objects
optionD: Yes, simply by filing an e-form with the ROC without any special resolution
answerText: Yes, by special resolution and prior approval of the Central Government
explanation: Under Section 8(4)(i), a Section 8 company cannot alter the provisions of its memorandum or articles except with the previous approval of the Central Government, and such alteration must also comply with provisions regarding special resolutions.
conceptTags: Section 8 Company | Alteration of Memorandum | Central Government Approval

subject: Law
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a permissible form of pre-incorporation contract liability ratification by a company under Indian company law?
optionA: Express novation of contract
optionB: Adoption of the contract by the company after incorporation
optionC: Automatic statutory ratification upon obtaining the Certificate of Incorporation
optionD: Entering into a new contract on the same terms after incorporation
answerText: Automatic statutory ratification upon obtaining the Certificate of Incorporation
explanation: Pre-incorporation contracts cannot be ratified automatically upon incorporation because a company does not exist prior to its incorporation. Valid legal options include novation, fresh contract, or specific adoption as per Indian Contract Act principles.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the designated web-based service introduced by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) for simplified proforma for incorporating a company electronically?
optionA: SPICe+
optionB: RUN-MCA
optionC: DIR-3 KYC
optionD: MGT-7A
answerText: SPICe+
explanation: SPICe+ (Simplified Proforma for Incorporating Company Electronically Plus) is an integrated web form offering multiple services like name reservation, incorporation, DIN allotment, PAN/TAN application, etc.

subject: Law
prompt: In the case of a One Person Company, if the sole member becomes a member in another OPC due to being a nominee in that other OPC, within how many days must the limit be complied with?
optionA: 30 days
optionB: 90 days
optionC: 180 days
optionD: 365 days
answerText: 180 days
explanation: Rule 3(7) of the Companies (Incorporation) Rules specifies that where a person is a member in one OPC and becomes a nominee in another such company, such person shall meet the eligibility criteria within a period of 180 days.
conceptTags: One Person Company | Rule 3 | Eligibility Compliance

subject: Law
prompt: Which of the following particulars is NOT required to be stated in the Memorandum of Association of a limited company?
optionA: Name clause
optionB: Registered office state clause
optionC: First directors appointment clause
optionD: Liability clause
answerText: First directors appointment clause
explanation: Section 4 lists the mandatory clauses of the Memorandum: Name, State, Objects, Liability, and Capital. The appointment of first directors is typically dealt with in the Articles or separate board resolutions/regulatory filings, not as a mandatory clause of the MoA.
conceptTags: Memorandum of Association | Mandatory Clauses | Section 4

subject: Law
prompt: Under Section 10 of the Companies Act, 2013, what is the legal effect of the registered Memorandum and Articles of Association once they are bound?
optionA: They bind the company and its members as if signed by each member
optionB: They are merely recommendatory guidelines
optionC: They are binding only on the promoters
optionD: They have no legal standing until a court order is passed
answerText: They bind the company and its members as if signed by each member
explanation: Section 10 states that when the memorandum and articles are registered, they bind the company and the members thereof to the same extent as if they respectively had been signed by each member and contained covenants on the part of each member to observe all provisions.
conceptTags: Section 10 | Binding Effect | MoA and AoA

subject: Law
prompt: Which type of company is prohibited from accepting any deposits from the public under the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013?
optionA: Public company with a net worth of over 500 crores
optionB: Private company
optionC: Banking company
optionD: Non-banking financial company registered with RBI
answerText: Private company
explanation: While public companies can accept deposits under strict regulations, private companies are generally restricted from accepting deposits from the general public (though they can accept from members/directors as per exemptions). However, looking strictly at the chapter on incorporation and basic rules, private companies cannot invite deposits from the public.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the maximum time limit specified for a company to notify the Registrar of any change in its registered office address from the date of such change?
optionA: 15 days
optionB: 30 days
optionC: 60 days
optionD: 90 days
answerText: 30 days
explanation: Section 12(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that notice of every change of the situation of the registered office, verified in the prescribed manner, shall be given to the Registrar within 30 days of the change.
conceptTags: Registered Office | Section 12 | Change of Address

subject: Law
prompt: If an existing company wants to alter its Articles of Association, which resolution must be passed by the shareholders?
optionA: Ordinary Resolution
optionB: Special Resolution
optionC: Board Resolution only
optionD: Unanimous Resolution
answerText: Special Resolution
explanation: Section 14 of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates that subject to the provisions of this Act and the conditions contained in its memorandum, a company may alter its articles by passing a special resolution.

subject: Law
prompt: Which of the following authorities has the power to accord sanction for the conversion of a public company into a private company?
optionA: Registrar of Companies
optionB: National Company Law Tribunal (Central Government)
optionC: Securities and Exchange Board of India
optionD: High Court
answerText: National Company Law Tribunal (Central Government)
explanation: Conversion of a public company into a private company requires approval from the Central Government (powers delegated to the Regional Director / Tribunal as per statutory amendments).
conceptTags: Conversion of Company | Public to Private | Section 13/18

subject: Law
prompt: Can a minor be a subscriber to the Memorandum of Association of a company under the Companies Act, 2013?
optionA: Yes, through a natural guardian
optionB: No, a minor's agreement is void ab initio, hence a minor cannot be a subscriber
optionC: Yes, provided the share capital is fully paid up
optionD: Yes, if approved by the Board of Directors
answerText: No, a minor's agreement is void ab initio, hence a minor cannot be a subscriber
explanation: Since a minor lacks the capacity to contract under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a minor cannot be a subscriber to the memorandum of association. Shares cannot be allotted to a minor except if they are fully paid and acquired by way of transfer/transmission.
conceptTags: Subscriber to Memorandum | Minor | Capacity to Contract

subject: Law
prompt: What is the status of the doctrine of indoor management in relation to the Memorandum and Articles of Association?
optionA: It protects the company from outsiders
optionB: It protects outsiders dealing with the company from internal irregularities
optionC: It allows directors to bypass the Articles
optionD: It overrides statutory provisions of the Companies Act
answerText: It protects outsiders dealing with the company from internal irregularities
explanation: The doctrine of indoor management (Turquand's Rule) protects outsiders who deal with a company in good faith from being affected by internal irregularities or procedural non-compliance within the company.
conceptTags: Doctrine of Indoor Management | Turquand Rule | Articles of Association

subject: Law
prompt: Under Section 3A of the Companies Act, 2013, if the number of members of a public company falls below seven and it continues to carry on business for more than how many months, every such member shall be severally liable?
optionA: 3 months
optionB: 6 months
optionC: 9 months
optionD: 12 months
answerText: 6 months
explanation: Section 3A provides that if the number of members is reduced below the statutory minimum (7 for public, 2 for private) and business is carried on for more than 6 months, every person who is a member during that time with knowledge shall be severally liable for the payment of debts contracted during that time.
conceptTags: Reduction of Members | Section 3A | Liability of Members

subject: Law
prompt: Which of the following cannot be included in the name of a company unless previous approval of the Central Government is obtained?
optionA: Industrial
optionB: Cooperative
optionC: Federal
optionD: Limited
answerText: Federal
explanation: Rule 8 of the Companies (Incorporation) Rules specifies words which require prior approval of the Central Government, such as 'Federal', 'Republic', 'State', 'Bank', 'Union', etc., as they might imply government patronage.
conceptTags: Company Name | Rule 8 | Central Government Approval

subject: Law
prompt: What does the 'Doctrine of Ultra Vires' signify in company law?
optionA: Acts done by directors beyond their authority but within company powers
optionB: Acts done beyond the powers of the company as defined in its Memorandum
optionC: Acts done by members without board approval
optionD: Internal management procedures
answerText: Acts done beyond the powers of the company as defined in its Memorandum
explanation: An act is ultra vires the company if it is beyond the powers conferred upon the company by its Memorandum of Association. Such acts are void and cannot be ratified even by all members.
conceptTags: Doctrine of Ultra Vires | Memorandum of Association | Company Powers

subject: Law
prompt: Which form is used for filing the application for incorporation of a company electronically under the SPICe+ framework?
optionA: INC-32
optionB: SPICe+ (INC-32)
optionC: INC-7
optionD: INC-22
answerText: SPICe+ (INC-32)
explanation: SPICe+ has replaced the old INC-32 form as the integrated web form for company incorporation under the Companies Act, 2013.

subject: Law
prompt: In the case of a Section 8 company, what is the minimum capital requirement prescribed under the Act?
optionA: 1 Lakh rupees
optionB: 5 Lakhs rupees
optionC: 10 Lakhs rupees
optionD: No minimum capital requirement
answerText: No minimum capital requirement
explanation: Section 8 companies do not have any prescribed minimum paid-up share capital requirement under the Companies Act, 2013, unlike private or public companies which historically had minimum capital thresholds.

subject: Law
prompt: Can a foreign company establish a place of business in India without registering with the Registrar of Companies?
optionA: Yes, if it operates for less than 90 days
optionB: No, it must deliver required documents to the ROC within 30 days of establishment
optionC: Yes, if it has a local agent
optionD: No, but it has 180 days to register
answerText: No, it must deliver required documents to the ROC within 30 days of establishment
explanation: Section 380 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires every foreign company to deliver specified documents and particulars to the Registrar of Companies within 30 days of establishing a place of business in India.
conceptTags: Foreign Company | Section 380 | Place of Business

subject: Law
prompt: What is the effect of registration of a company under Section 9 of the Companies Act, 2013?
optionA: It creates a partnership between subscribers
optionB: It creates a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal (optional)
optionC: It makes directors personally liable for all future debts
optionD: It requires annual renewal of incorporation
answerText: It creates a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal (optional)
explanation: Section 9 provides that from the date of incorporation, the subscribers to the memorandum and other persons shall be a body corporate capable of exercising all functions, having perpetual succession and a common seal.

subject: Law
prompt: When can a company commence its business or exercise borrowing powers after incorporation?
optionA: Immediately upon getting the Certificate of Incorporation
optionB: Only after filing a declaration under Section 10A regarding receipt of subscription money
optionC: After holding its first Annual General Meeting
optionD: After obtaining a separate trading license from the High Court
answerText: Only after filing a declaration under Section 10A regarding receipt of subscription money
explanation: Section 10A of the Companies Act, 2013 stipulates that a company having a share capital cannot commence any business or exercise borrowing powers unless a director files a verification declaration within 180 days that every subscriber has paid the value of shares agreed.
conceptTags: Section 10A | Commencement of Business | Subscription Money

subject: Law
prompt: If a promoter makes a secret profit from a transaction entered into on behalf of a prospective company, what is the legal remedy available to the company?
optionA: The company can only reprimand the promoter
optionB: The company can rescind the contract and recover the secret profit
optionC: The company must pay an additional bonus to the promoter
optionD: The contract becomes automatically binding with no remedies
answerText: The company can rescind the contract and recover the secret profit
explanation: Promoters stand in a fiduciary position towards the company they promote. They cannot make any secret profits, and if they do, the company can compel them to account for such profits or rescind the contract.

subject: Law
prompt: Which of the following documents is NOT required to be filed along with SPICe+ for the incorporation of a company?
optionA: Subscriber sheet / Memorandum and Articles
optionB: Proof of registered office address
optionC: Audited balance sheet of promoters for the last 3 years
optionD: Declaration by professionals and subscribers in INC-9
answerText: Audited balance sheet of promoters for the last 3 years
explanation: Promoters' historical audited balance sheets are not required for company incorporation. The required documents include MoA, AoA, registered office proof, declarations (INC-9), and identity proofs of subscribers/directors.

subject: Law
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Mr. Rohan, an enthusiastic entrepreneur, decides to start a software development business in Pune. He plans to register a private limited company named 'TechInnovate Solutions Private Limited' with five initial subscribers. He prepares the Memorandum of Association and Articles of Association. During the incorporation process, Rohan acts quickly to secure a commercial property as the registered office, but due to delays in final paperwork, the registered office address is registered 45 days after the date of incorporation.

subject: Law
prompt: Is the registration of the registered office address within 45 days compliant with Section 12 of the Companies Act, 2013?
optionA: Yes, because private companies get a grace period of 60 days
optionB: No, Section 12 requires the company to have a registered office within 30 days of incorporation
optionC: Yes, if approved by the Regional Director
optionD: No, but it attracts only a minor fee without legal consequences
answerText: No, Section 12 requires the company to have a registered office within 30 days of incorporation
explanation: Section 12(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates that a company must have a registered office capable of receiving communications within 30 days of its incorporation. Registering it after 45 days is a non-compliance.

subject: Law
prompt: With five subscribers, does 'TechInnovate Solutions Private Limited' satisfy the minimum subscriber requirement for a private company?
optionA: No, a private company requires at least seven subscribers
optionB: Yes, a private company requires a minimum of two subscribers, and five is compliant
optionC: No, it must have exactly ten subscribers
optionD: Yes, but only if all subscribers are corporate bodies
answerText: Yes, a private company requires a minimum of two subscribers, and five is compliant
explanation: Under Section 3 of the Companies Act, 2013, a private company requires a minimum of two persons to form it. Having five subscribers fully satisfies this legal requirement.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the legal nature of the Memorandum and Articles prepared by Rohan once the company is successfully incorporated?
optionA: They are bilateral agreements between Rohan and the Registrar
optionB: They constitute a contract between the company and its members as per Section 10
optionC: They are internal guidelines that do not bind the members
optionD: They have no legal force until approved by NCLT
answerText: They constitute a contract between the company and its members as per Section 10
explanation: Under Section 10, once registered, the MoA and AoA bind the company and its members to the same extent as if they had been signed by each member, establishing a statutory contract.
conceptTags: Section 10 | Binding Nature | MoA and AoA

subject: Law
prompt: If Rohan had instead decided to form a One Person Company (OPC) for the same business, what would have been the mandatory requirement regarding a nominee?
optionA: No nominee is required for software businesses
optionB: A nominee must be appointed whose prior written consent is filed with the Registrar at incorporation
optionC: A nominee must be a public financial institution
optionD: The nominee must hold 51% of the shares
answerText: A nominee must be appointed whose prior written consent is filed with the Registrar at incorporation
explanation: For an OPC, Rule 3 requires the memorandum to indicate the name of a nominee who shall become the member in case of death or incapacity, and their prior written consent must be filed at incorporation.

subject: Law
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: A group of six philanthropic individuals intend to incorporate a company under Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013, named 'GreenEarth Foundation', with the object of promoting environmental awareness and wildlife conservation. They intend to apply all their profits towards promoting their objects and prohibit the payment of any dividend to their members. They submit their application for a license to the Central Government / Registrar.

subject: Law
prompt: Is 'GreenEarth Foundation' eligible for a Section 8 license with six initial subscribers?
optionA: No, Section 8 requires a minimum of 50 subscribers
optionB: Yes, Section 8 companies can be formed by individuals or associations for charitable objects without any special high subscriber minimums beyond standard private/public rules
optionC: No, charitable companies must be registered as public companies with at least 7 subscribers
optionD: Yes, but they must have a minimum capital of 50 lakhs
answerText: Yes, Section 8 companies can be formed by individuals or associations for charitable objects without any special high subscriber minimums beyond standard private/public rules
explanation: Section 8 allows persons or associations of persons to form a company for charitable objects with restricted profit distribution. They can be registered as private or public companies complying with basic member requirements.

subject: Law
prompt: Can 'GreenEarth Foundation' alter the objects clause in its Memorandum of Association after incorporation?
optionA: No, Section 8 company objects can never be altered
optionB: Yes, but only with the previous approval of the Central Government and via special resolution
optionC: Yes, by passing a simple board resolution
optionD: Yes, by notifying the local municipal authority
answerText: Yes, but only with the previous approval of the Central Government and via special resolution
explanation: Section 8(4) stipulates that a Section 8 company cannot alter the provisions of its memorandum or articles except with the previous approval of the Central Government.
conceptTags: Section 8 Company | Alteration of Memorandum | Central Government Approval

subject: Law
prompt: What happens to the restriction on payment of dividends for members of 'GreenEarth Foundation'?
optionA: Dividends can be paid up to 10% per annum
optionB: Dividends are strictly prohibited, and profits must be applied solely to the promotion of its objects
optionC: Dividends can be distributed if approved by ordinary resolution
optionD: Dividends are permitted only after 5 years of operation
answerText: Dividends are strictly prohibited, and profits must be applied solely to the promotion of its objects
explanation: A Section 8 company is prohibited from paying any dividend to its members; its profits and income must be applied solely for the promotion of the objects for which it is established.
conceptTags: Section 8 Company | Prohibition of Dividend | Charitable Purpose

subject: Law
prompt: If at any time the Central Government revokes the Section 8 license of 'GreenEarth Foundation' due to violation of conditions, what action can the Government take?
optionA: Only impose a monetary penalty on the founders
optionB: Direct the company to wind up or amalgamate with another Section 8 company having similar objects
optionC: Automatically convert the company into an unlimited partnership
optionD: Dissolve the company and forfeit all its assets to the promoters
answerText: Direct the company to wind up or amalgamate with another Section 8 company having similar objects
explanation: Under Section 8(6), upon revocation of the license, the Central Government may order the company to be wound up, or amalgamated with another Section 8 company, after giving an opportunity of being heard.
conceptTags: Section 8 Company | Revocation of License | Winding Up / Amalgamation

subject: Law
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Apex Infrastructure Limited is an existing public company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013. The Board of Directors wishes to alter the Articles of Association to include restrictive clauses on share transfers and wants to convert the company into Apex Infrastructure Private Limited. The company has 80 members on its register. The management calls an extraordinary general meeting to pass the necessary resolutions.

subject: Law
prompt: What type of resolution is required for altering the Articles of Association under Section 14 of the Companies Act, 2013?
optionA: Ordinary Resolution
optionB: Special Resolution
optionC: Unanimous Board Resolution
optionD: Resolution requiring 100% consent
answerText: Special Resolution
explanation: Section 14 of the Companies Act, 2013 explicitly states that a company may alter its articles by passing a special resolution.

subject: Law
prompt: To convert Apex Infrastructure Limited into a private company, whose approval is mandatory under the Companies Act, 2013?
optionA: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
optionB: Central Government (Regional Director / Tribunal)
optionC: Reserve Bank of India
optionD: Registrar of Companies only via e-form without sanction
answerText: Central Government (Regional Director / Tribunal)
explanation: Conversion of a public company into a private company requires the sanction/approval of the Central Government (powers delegated to Regional Director/Tribunal) in accordance with Section 13 and 18 read with rules.
conceptTags: Conversion of Company | Public to Private | Central Government Approval

subject: Law
prompt: Does the number of members (80 members) comply with the maximum limit prescribed for a private company under the Companies Act, 2013?
optionA: No, the maximum limit for a private company is 50 members
optionB: Yes, the maximum limit for a private company is 200 members
optionC: No, private companies cannot have more than 20 members
optionD: Yes, because public companies converting to private have no member limits
answerText: Yes, the maximum limit for a private company is 200 members
explanation: Section 2(68) defines a private company as one which has a minimum of 2 members and restricts the maximum number of its members to 200 (excluding employee-members and past employee-members). 80 members is well within this limit.
conceptTags: Private Company Definition | Maximum Members | Section 2(68)

subject: Law
prompt: If a dissenting minority shareholder challenges the conversion in court, what is the primary consideration the Tribunal evaluates?
optionA: Whether the conversion prejudices the interests of shareholders or creditors
optionB: Whether the company has paid dividends for the last 10 years
optionC: Whether the company's registered office is in a metropolitan city
optionD: Whether the promoters are Indian citizens
answerText: Whether the conversion prejudices the interests of shareholders or creditors
explanation: When evaluating conversion of a public company to a private company, the Tribunal/Central Government ensures that adequate provision is made for safeguarding the interests of creditors and dissenting shareholders.
conceptTags: Conversion Sanction | Shareholder Interests | Tribunal Powers

subject: Law
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Mr. Vikram starts a trading business and promotes 'Vikram Agro-Products Private Limited'. During the promoter stage, before obtaining the Certificate of Incorporation, Vikram enters into a lease agreement on behalf of the prospective company with a landlord for a warehouse. After the company is incorporated, the board of directors continues to use the warehouse and pays rent, but never formally executes a new contract or novates the old agreement.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the legal status of the lease agreement entered into by Vikram prior to incorporation?
optionA: It is automatically binding on the company from day one
optionB: It is a pre-incorporation contract which is not automatically binding on the company unless adopted/novated
optionC: It is completely illegal and void under criminal law
optionD: It binds the landlord personally with no recourse
answerText: It is a pre-incorporation contract which is not automatically binding on the company unless adopted/novated
explanation: Pre-incorporation contracts entered into by promoters on behalf of a yet-to-be-formed company are not automatically binding on the company upon incorporation unless the company adopts the contract or enters into a fresh novation.

subject: Law
prompt: Can the company adopt or ratify the pre-incorporation contract expressly after its incorporation?
optionA: Yes, by adopting it or entering into a new contract on the same terms (novation)
optionB: No, a company can never adopt a pre-incorporation contract under any circumstance
optionC: Yes, automatically after 6 months of use
optionD: Only if approved by the National Company Law Tribunal
answerText: Yes, by adopting it or entering into a new contract on the same terms (novation)
explanation: While ratification in the strict agency sense is not possible because the principal (company) did not exist when the contract was made, the company can become bound by entering into a new contract (novation) or specific adoption.

subject: Law
prompt: What position do Vikram and the other promoters hold in relation to the prospective company during the promotion phase?
optionA: They are mere employees with no fiduciary duties
optionB: They stand in a fiduciary relationship towards the company
optionC: They are statutory directors automatically
optionD: They act as legal guardians of the company
answerText: They stand in a fiduciary relationship towards the company
explanation: Promoters stand in a fiduciary (position of trust) relationship with the company they promote, meaning they must not make secret profits and must act in good faith.

subject: Law
prompt: If Vikram had made a secret profit from the lease transaction without disclosing it to the subscribers, what remedy is available to the company?
optionA: The company can recover the secret profit or rescind the transaction
optionB: The company must reward Vikram with additional shares
optionC: The contract becomes voidable only at the option of the landlord
optionD: No remedy, as promoters are immune from profits
answerText: The company can recover the secret profit or rescind the transaction
explanation: If a promoter makes a secret profit in a transaction on behalf of the company, the company can compel the promoter to disgorge the secret profit or rescind the transaction for breach of fiduciary duty.
conceptTags: Secret Profits | Promoter Liability | Fiduciary Duty

subject: Law
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Zenith Global Limited is incorporated with an authorized share capital of 50 lakhs divided into equity shares. The Certificate of Incorporation is issued by the Registrar of Companies on 1st October. The directors are eager to commence business operations and issue a large supply order on 10th October without filing the statutory declaration required under Section 10A of the Companies Act, 2013.

subject: Law
prompt: Is Zenith Global Limited legally permitted to commence business operations or exercise borrowing powers on 10th October?
optionA: Yes, because incorporation gives immediate commencement rights
optionB: No, a company having share capital cannot commence business without filing the Section 10A declaration regarding subscription money
optionC: Yes, if the board passes an ordinary resolution
optionD: No, unless approved by SEBI
answerText: No, a company having share capital cannot commence business without filing the Section 10A declaration regarding subscription money
explanation: Section 10A explicitly prohibits a company having a share capital from commencing business or exercising borrowing powers unless a director files a declaration verifying that every subscriber has paid the value of shares.
conceptTags: Section 10A | Commencement of Business | Subscription Money

subject: Law
prompt: Within what maximum time frame from the date of incorporation must the Section 10A declaration be filed by a director?
optionA: 30 days
optionB: 60 days
optionC: 180 days
optionD: 365 days
answerText: 180 days
explanation: Section 10A(1)(a) requires that the declaration by a director must be filed with the Registrar within a period of 180 days of the date of incorporation of the company.

subject: Law
prompt: What are the penal consequences for the company and defaulting officers if business is commenced in violation of Section 10A?
optionA: Only a warning letter from the ROC
optionB: Penalty of fifty thousand rupees for the company and one thousand rupees per day for defaulting officers, plus potential removal of name
optionC: Immediate imprisonment of all shareholders for 7 years
optionD: Mandatory dissolution by High Court order only
answerText: Penalty of fifty thousand rupees for the company and one thousand rupees per day for defaulting officers, plus potential removal of name
explanation: Section 10A prescribes a penalty of fifty thousand rupees for the company and one thousand rupees for each day during which the default continues for every officer in default, along with Registrar action for striking off if no business is commenced.
conceptTags: Section 10A Penalties | Default Consequences | Officer Liability

subject: Law
prompt: From which date does Zenith Global Limited acquire its corporate personality and perpetual succession?
optionA: From the date of filing the SPICe+ form
optionB: From the date mentioned in the Certificate of Incorporation
optionC: From the date of the first board meeting
optionD: From the date Section 10A declaration is filed
answerText: From the date mentioned in the Certificate of Incorporation
explanation: Under Section 9, from the date of incorporation mentioned in the Certificate of Incorporation issued by the Registrar, the subscribers become a body corporate with perpetual succession.
conceptTags: Section 9 | Certificate of Incorporation | Corporate Personality

subject: Law
prompt: Which of the following documents is specifically defined under Section 2(70) of the Companies Act, 2013 as including any notice, circular, advertisement, or other document inviting offers from the public for the subscription or purchase of any securities of a body corporate?
optionA: Abridged Prospectus
optionB: Prospectus
optionC: Shelf Prospectus
optionD: Red Herring Prospectus
answerText: Prospectus
explanation: Section 2(70) of the Companies Act, 2013 defines a prospectus as any document described or issued as a prospectus including a red herring prospectus or shelf prospectus or any notice, circular, advertisement or other document inviting offers from the public for the subscription or purchase of any securities of a body corporate.

subject: Law
prompt: When a company issues an Abridged Prospectus along with a form of application for purchase of any of its securities, what is the legal position regarding the inclusion of the abridged prospectus?
optionA: It is optional for private companies but mandatory for public companies.
optionB: Every application form for securities must be accompanied by an abridged prospectus.
optionC: It is required only if the applicant specifically requests it in writing.
optionD: It is required only for rights issues and bonus issues.
answerText: Every application form for securities must be accompanied by an abridged prospectus.
explanation: According to Section 33(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, no form of application for the purchase of any of the securities of a company shall be issued unless such form is accompanied by an abridged prospectus containing all necessary disclosures.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the maximum period for which a Shelf Prospectus can be stated to be valid by a company issuing a class or classes of securities under Section 31 of the Companies Act, 2013?
optionA: Six months
optionB: One year
optionC: Two years
optionD: Three years
answerText: One year
explanation: Under Section 31 of the Companies Act, 2013, a shelf prospectus issued by any class or classes of companies shall be valid for a period not exceeding one year from the date of opening of the first issue of securities under that prospectus.

subject: Law
prompt: A company issues a Red Herring Prospectus (RHP) prior to the issue of securities. Which of the following details is typically *not* included in an RHP?
optionA: Quantum of securities
optionB: Price of the securities
optionC: General nature of business
optionD: Financial background of promoters
answerText: Price of the securities
explanation: Section 32 defines a red herring prospectus as one which lacks complete particulars about the quantum or price of the securities being offered, as these are determined after the book-building process concludes.
conceptTags: Red Herring Prospectus | Section 32 | Book Building

subject: Law
prompt: When does a Red Herring Prospectus need to be filed with the Registrar of Companies (RoC)?
optionA: At least 3 days prior to the opening of the issue
optionB: At least 7 days prior to the opening of the issue
optionC: At least 15 days prior to the opening of the issue
optionD: At least 30 days prior to the opening of the issue
answerText: At least 3 days prior to the opening of the issue
explanation: Under Section 32(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company proposing to make an offer of securities may issue a red herring prospectus prior to the issue of securities and must file it with the Registrar at least 3 days prior to the opening of the subscription list and the issue.

subject: Law
prompt: What must a company do upon the closing of the offer under a Red Herring Prospectus regarding the final details of the issue?
optionA: File a fresh prospectus with SEBI only
optionB: State the final price and quantum of securities and file it with the Registrar and SEBI
optionC: Obtain a court order confirming the price
optionD: Issue a notice in a local newspaper without filing with RoC
answerText: State the final price and quantum of securities and file it with the Registrar and SEBI
explanation: Section 32(4) specifies that upon the closing of the offer, the red herring prospectus shall be filed with the Registrar and SEBI, stating the total capital raised, closing price of securities, and other details not included earlier.

subject: Law
prompt: Which section of the Companies Act, 2013 deals with criminal liability for misstatements in a prospectus?
optionA: Section 34
optionB: Section 35
optionC: Section 38
optionD: Section 40
answerText: Section 34
explanation: Section 34 of the Companies Act, 2013 imposes criminal liability on any person who authorizes the issue of a prospectus containing untrue or misleading statements, attracting punishment under Section 447.

subject: Law
prompt: Under Section 35 of the Companies Act, 2013, who among the following is *not* typically held liable to pay compensation for loss or damage sustained by any person who subscribed for securities acting on a misleading prospectus?
optionA: Every person who is a director of the company at the time of the issue
optionB: Every person who has authorized themselves to be named as a director in the prospectus
optionC: An ordinary employee of the company who had no role in drafting the prospectus
optionD: Every promoter of the company
answerText: An ordinary employee of the company who had no role in drafting the prospectus
explanation: Section 35 specifies civil liability for directors, promoters, and persons named as directors with their consent. Ordinary employees without management/drafting responsibilities are not categorized among those strictly liable under Section 35.
conceptTags: Civil Liability | Section 35 | Directors and Promoters

subject: Law
prompt: What is the penalty range for fraud under Section 447, which is triggered when Section 34 (criminal liability for misstatement in prospectus) is invoked?
optionA: Imprisonment from 6 months up to 3 years
optionB: Imprisonment from 6 months up to 10 years and fine up to the amount involved
optionC: Only monetary fine without imprisonment
optionD: Imprisonment for a fixed term of 5 years
answerText: Imprisonment from 6 months up to 10 years and fine up to the amount involved
explanation: Section 34 attracts punishment under Section 447, which mandates imprisonment for a term not less than 6 months extending up to 10 years, and a fine not less than the amount involved in the fraud, extending up to 3 times the amount involved.

subject: Law
prompt: Under Section 38 of the Companies Act, 2013, what penalty is prescribed for any person who makes or abets making of an application in a fictitious name for acquiring securities in a company?
optionA: Imprisonment up to 1 year or fine up to Rs. 50,000
optionB: Imprisonment for a term of 1 to 5 years and fine
optionC: Strictly a civil penalty equal to twice the application money
optionD: No criminal penalty, only cancellation of application
answerText: Imprisonment for a term of 1 to 5 years and fine
explanation: Section 38 prescribes punishment for personation in acquisitions, stating that any person who makes an application in a fictitious name shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term of 1 to 5 years.

subject: Law
prompt: When a company makes a public offer, every company must make an application to one or more recognized stock exchange(s) for permission for the securities to be dealt with on such stock exchange, as mandated by which section?
optionA: Section 39
optionB: Section 40
optionC: Section 26
optionD: Section 42
answerText: Section 40
explanation: Section 40 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires every company making a public offer to make an application before issuing prospectus to one or more recognized stock exchange or exchanges and obtain permission thereof.

subject: Law
prompt: Under Section 39(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, if a company fails to repay application money within the prescribed time after the minimum subscription is not received, what is the rate of interest payable by the company and its officers in default?
optionA: 6% per annum
optionB: 12% per annum
optionC: 15% per annum
optionD: 18% per annum
answerText: 15% per annum
explanation: Section 39(3) dictates that if the stated minimum subscription is not received and application money is not repaid within 15 days from the closure of the issue, the company and every officer in default shall be liable to repay application money with interest at the rate of 15% per annum.
conceptTags: Minimum Subscription | Section 39 | Interest on Refund

subject: Law
prompt: What is the maximum number of persons to whom a private placement of securities can be made in a financial year, as per the rules prescribed under Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013, excluding qualified institutional buyers and employees under ESOP?
optionA: 50 persons
optionB: 100 persons
optionC: 200 persons
optionD: 499 persons
answerText: 200 persons
explanation: Section 42 read with relevant rules specifies that an offer or invitation through private placement can be made to not more than 200 persons in the aggregate in a financial year, excluding QIBs and employees given securities under ESOP.

subject: Law
prompt: Moneys received under a private placement offer must be paid through which of the following modes?
optionA: Cash only
optionB: Cheque or demand draft or other banking channels only, but not cash
optionC: Either cash up to Rs. 10,000 or cheque
optionD: Cryptocurrency or bank transfer
answerText: Cheque or demand draft or other banking channels only, but not cash
explanation: Rule 14 of the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014 mandates that monies payable on subscription to private placement shall be paid through cheque or demand draft or other banking channels, and not by cash.

subject: Law
prompt: Within how many days from the date of allotment of securities under a private placement must a company file a return of allotment with the Registrar in Form PAS-3?
optionA: 15 days
optionB: 30 days
optionC: 60 days
optionD: 90 days
answerText: 30 days
explanation: Section 42(9) and Rule 14 require a company making any allotment of securities under private placement to file with the Registrar a return of allotment in Form PAS-3 within 30 days from the date of the allotment.
conceptTags: Return of Allotment | Form PAS-3 | Private Placement

subject: Law
prompt: Which of the following is an exception where a civil liability defense under Section 35 is available to a director who otherwise consented to be named in the prospectus?
optionA: The director did not read the prospectus before signing.
optionB: The director withdrew consent publicly before the issue of the prospectus and gave reasonable public notice.
optionC: The director relied entirely on the company secretary's advice.
optionD: The prospectus was approved by the Board of Directors unanimously.
answerText: The director withdrew consent publicly before the issue of the prospectus and gave reasonable public notice.
explanation: Section 35(2) provides a defense from civil liability if a director proves that, having consented to become a director of the company, they withdrew their consent before the issue of the prospectus, and that it was issued without their authority or consent.

subject: Law
prompt: Can a company utilize any monies raised through private placement before making the relevant allotment of securities and filing the return of allotment?
optionA: Yes, immediately upon receiving the application money.
optionB: Yes, up to 50% of the money received.
optionC: No, monies received must be kept in a separate bank account and cannot be utilized until allotment is made.
optionD: Yes, if approved by an ordinary resolution.
answerText: No, monies received must be kept in a separate bank account and cannot be utilized until allotment is made.
explanation: Section 42(6) states that monies received on application under private placement shall be kept in a separate bank account in a scheduled bank and shall not be utilized for any purpose other than for adjustment against allotment or repayment for failure to allot.
conceptTags: Private Placement | Separate Bank Account | Section 42

subject: Law
prompt: What constitutes a 'Global Depository Receipt' (GDR) under Section 2(44) of the Companies Act, 2013?
optionA: Any instrument issued outside India by a company, foreign or domestic, for local deposits.
optionB: Any instrument in the form of a depository receipt, created by a foreign depository outside India, authorizing acquisition of securities issued by an Indian company.
optionC: A receipt issued by the Reserve Bank of India for holding foreign exchange.
optionD: A bond issued by the Central Government in global markets.
answerText: Any instrument in the form of a depository receipt, created by a foreign depository outside India, authorizing acquisition of securities issued by an Indian company.
explanation: Section 2(44) defines Global Depository Receipt as any instrument in the form of a depository receipt, created by a foreign depository outside India and authorized by a company, making an issue of depository receipts.

subject: Law
prompt: If a company defaults in filing the return of allotment in Form PAS-3 within the prescribed 30 days under private placement provisions, what is the penalty structure for the company and officers in default?
optionA: Rs. 1,000 per day up to a maximum of Rs. 1,00,000
optionB: A penalty of one thousand rupees for each day during which such default continues but not exceeding twenty-five lakh rupees for the company and officer in default
optionC: Immediate winding up of the company
optionD: Strict criminal imprisonment without fine options
answerText: A penalty of one thousand rupees for each day during which such default continues but not exceeding twenty-five lakh rupees for the company and officer in default
explanation: Section 42(10) prescribes that if a company defaults in filing the return of allotment within the specified period, the company, promoters and directors shall be liable to a penalty of Rs. 1,000 for each day during which default continues, up to a maximum of Rs. 25 lakhs.

subject: Law
prompt: Under Section 26 of the Companies Act, 2013, every prospectus issued by or on behalf of a public company must be dated and signed by whom?
optionA: The Chief Executive Officer alone
optionB: All the directors or proposed directors of the company or their duly authorized attorneys
optionC: The Registrar of Companies
optionD: The statutory auditor of the company
answerText: All the directors or proposed directors of the company or their duly authorized attorneys
explanation: Section 26(4) states that every prospectus shall be dated and signed by every director or proposed director named in the prospectus or by his duly authorized attorney.

subject: Law
prompt: Which of the following matters must be explicitly reported upon by the statutory auditors in a prospectus as required under Section 26?
optionA: Profits and losses of the company for each of the 5 financial years immediately preceding the issue of prospectus
optionB: Projected future market share for the next 10 years
optionC: Personal tax returns of all individual promoters
optionD: Daily attendance records of employees
answerText: Profits and losses of the company for each of the 5 financial years immediately preceding the issue of prospectus
explanation: Section 26(1) requires the prospectus to set out reports by the auditors of the company with respect to profits and losses of the company for each of the 5 financial years immediately preceding the financial year of the issue.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the primary objective of requiring a company to issue a 'Shelf Prospectus'?
optionA: To bypass SEBI approvals entirely for equity shares
optionB: To allow a company to issue one or more issues of securities over a certain period without the need of issuing a fresh prospectus for each offer
optionC: To permanently avoid publishing annual financial statements
optionD: To raise funds exclusively from foreign institutional investors
answerText: To allow a company to issue one or more issues of securities over a certain period without the need of issuing a fresh prospectus for each offer
explanation: A shelf prospectus allows a class or classes of companies (like public financial institutions or banks) to issue securities in one or more tranches over a period of up to one year without issuing a full prospectus every single time.

subject: Law
prompt: Which of the following entities is permitted to issue a 'Shelf Prospectus' under the rules and provisions of the Companies Act, 2013?
optionA: Any newly incorporated private company
optionB: Any company engaged in retail trade
optionC: Public Financial Institutions, Banks or Public Sector Companies as specified by SEBI
optionD: Foreign companies operating without an Indian branch
answerText: Public Financial Institutions, Banks or Public Sector Companies as specified by SEBI
explanation: Section 31 restricts the issuance of a shelf prospectus to such classes of companies as the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) may specify in this behalf, primarily Public Financial Institutions, banks, and large public sector issuers.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the consequence if an invitation to subscribe for securities is made to 250 persons without complying with the private placement provisions under Section 42?
optionA: It is treated as a valid private placement.
optionB: It is deemed to be a public offer, attracting all public offer regulations and severe penalties.
optionC: It is automatically converted into a bonus issue.
optionD: The company is dissolved without judicial intervention.
answerText: It is deemed to be a public offer, attracting all public offer regulations and severe penalties.
explanation: Section 42(2) stipulates that if an offer or invitation is made to more than the prescribed number of persons (200), it shall be deemed to be a public offer and shall require compliance with all provisions of public offers, besides attracting monetary penalties.
conceptTags: Private Placement | Deemed Public Offer | Section 42

subject: Law
prompt: What is the maximum time limit within which a company making a public offer must allot securities after the closure of the subscription list?
optionA: 30 days
optionB: 60 days
optionC: 90 days
optionD: 120 days
answerText: 30 days
explanation: Under Section 39(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, no allotment of any securities of a company shall be made unless the amount stated in the prospectus as the minimum amount has been subscribed, and within 30 days of the closure of the issue (or such other period as SEBI may specify).
conceptTags: Allotment of Securities | Time Limit | Section 39

subject: Law
prompt: If a prospectus includes any statement which is misleading, fraudulent, or untrue, which section provides for civil liability for misstatement?
optionA: Section 34
optionB: Section 35
optionC: Section 36
optionD: Section 37
answerText: Section 35
explanation: Section 35 of the Companies Act, 2013 provides for civil liability for misstatements in a prospectus, rendering persons responsible liable to pay compensation to every person who subscribed for securities acting on such prospectus.

subject: Law
prompt: What does Section 36 of the Companies Act, 2013 specifically penalize?
optionA: Failure to issue a shelf prospectus
optionB: Fraudulently inducing persons to invest money through misleading statements, promises, or forecasts
optionC: Delay in listing shares on a foreign stock exchange
optionD: Non-payment of interim dividends
answerText: Fraudulently inducing persons to invest money through misleading statements, promises, or forecasts
explanation: Section 36 punishes any person who either knowingly or recklessly makes any statement, promise or forecast which is false, deceptive or misleading, or deliberately conceals any material facts, to induce another person to enter into an agreement for acquiring securities.
conceptTags: Fraudulently Inducing Persons | Section 36 | Punishment for Fraud

subject: Law
prompt: When a company issues a Red Herring Prospectus, what information must accompany it when filing with the Registrar before the opening of the issue?
optionA: Information memorandum containing updates on financial position and changes since the shelf prospectus
optionB: Board resolution approving exact allotment prices
optionC: Details of every individual retail investor
optionD: Foreign exchange reserve clearance
answerText: Information memorandum containing updates on financial position and changes since the shelf prospectus
explanation: Under Section 31(2), a company filing a shelf prospectus is required to file an Information Memorandum containing material facts such as financial position changes and charges created, prior to the issue of a second or subsequent tranche of securities.

subject: Law
prompt: Can a public company allot securities before the beginning of the subscription list?
optionA: Yes, if the board approves it.
optionB: No allotment can be made until the beginning of the 5th day after the prospectus is issued or such time specified in the prospectus (the minimum waiting period).
optionC: Yes, through private placement rules.
optionD: No, public companies cannot allot securities at all.
answerText: No allotment can be made until the beginning of the 5th day after the prospectus is issued or such time specified in the prospectus (the minimum waiting period).
explanation: As per general regulations and SEBI ICDR guidelines, no allotment can be made until the time specified in the prospectus, ensuring investors get adequate time to study the prospectus.
conceptTags: Allotment | Minimum Waiting Period | Public Offer

subject: Law
prompt: What is the effect if a company fails to obtain permission from a recognized stock exchange under Section 40?
optionA: The allotment becomes void.
optionB: The company is given a 1-year extension to comply.
optionC: The securities are automatically converted into debt instruments.
optionD: The penalty applies only to the auditors.
answerText: The allotment becomes void.
explanation: Section 40(5) provides that if permission from stock exchanges has not been applied for or granted, any allotment made shall be void, and the application money must be refunded.

subject: Law
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Zenith Pharma Limited, an unlisted public company, decided to raise capital by issuing equity shares to the public. The company drafted a prospectus, but due to an oversight by the finance team, certain material financial disclosures regarding contingent liabilities were omitted. Mr. A, a retail investor, relied on this prospectus and subscribed for 5,000 shares. Shortly after listing, the omitted contingent liabilities materialized, causing the share price to crash, resulting in substantial financial loss to Mr. A.

subject: Law
prompt: Which section of the Companies Act, 2013 governs the criminal liability of Zenith Pharma Limited and persons authorizing the issue of this defective prospectus?
optionA: Section 33
optionB: Section 34
optionC: Section 38
optionD: Section 42
answerText: Section 34
explanation: Section 34 of the Companies Act, 2013 deals with criminal liability for misstatements in a prospectus, making every person who authorized the issue liable under Section 447.

subject: Law
prompt: What kind of civil liability can Mr. A invoke against the directors and promoters under Section 35 of the Act?
optionA: Liability to pay compensation for the loss or damage sustained by him due to the misleading statement.
optionB: Mandatory imprisonment of directors for 7 years without trial.
optionC: Automatic transfer of promoter shares to Mr. A.
optionD: No civil liability exists if the omission was unintentional.
answerText: Liability to pay compensation for the loss or damage sustained by him due to the misleading statement.
explanation: Section 35 establishes civil liability, making directors, promoters, and experts liable to pay compensation to every person who sustained loss or damage by subscribing to securities on the faith of a misleading prospectus.

subject: Law
prompt: If a director of Zenith Pharma Limited wishes to claim a defense against civil liability under Section 35, which of the following grounds would be valid?
optionA: The director proves that they never attended board meetings.
optionB: The director proves that the prospectus was issued without their knowledge or consent, and that they gave reasonable public notice of such fact upon becoming aware of it.
optionC: The director relies on the excuse that they relied entirely on the chief financial officer.
optionD: The director resigned two years after the issue.
answerText: The director proves that the prospectus was issued without their knowledge or consent, and that they gave reasonable public notice of such fact upon becoming aware of it.
explanation: Section 35(2) provides specific statutory defenses, including proving that the prospectus was issued without the director's knowledge or consent, and that reasonable public notice was given upon becoming aware of it.

subject: Law
prompt: If the omission in the prospectus is proved to be an act of fraud with an intent to deceive investors, which penal provision is attracted for criminal liability?
optionA: Section 447
optionB: Section 149
optionC: Section 92
optionD: Section 134
answerText: Section 447
explanation: When criminal liability is invoked under Section 34 for a fraudulent misstatement or omission in a prospectus, the punishment is governed by Section 447 for fraud.

subject: Law
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Omega Infrastructure Bank Limited decided to issue non-convertible debentures to the public. Because it intended to make multiple tranches of issues over the financial year without drafting a fresh prospectus each time, it chose to issue a Shelf Prospectus under Section 31 of the Companies Act, 2013, valid for a period of one year. Before issuing the second tranche of debentures, a significant change in the financial position of the bank occurred due to a major asset acquisition.

subject: Law
prompt: What document must Omega Infrastructure Bank Limited file prior to the issue of the second tranche of debentures under the shelf prospectus?
optionA: A completely new prospectus approved by the court
optionB: An Information Memorandum containing material facts and changes in financial position
optionC: A winding-up petition
optionD: A memorandum of association amendment
answerText: An Information Memorandum containing material facts and changes in financial position
explanation: Section 31(2) mandates that a company filing a shelf prospectus shall file an Information Memorandum containing details of material facts, financial position changes, and other prescribed particulars prior to the second or subsequent offer.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the maximum validity period allowed for the Shelf Prospectus issued by Omega Infrastructure Bank Limited?
optionA: 3 months
optionB: 6 months
optionC: 1 year
optionD: 3 years
answerText: 1 year
explanation: Under Section 31(1), a shelf prospectus is valid for a period not exceeding one year from the date of opening of the first issue of securities under that prospectus.

subject: Law
prompt: If an investor who subscribed to the first tranche wishes to review the abridged information regarding the debenture issue, what must accompany the application form?
optionA: An abridged prospectus
optionB: The full incorporation certificate only
optionC: A copy of the annual tax audit report
optionD: No document is required if the investor is institutional
answerText: An abridged prospectus
explanation: Section 33 mandates that no form of application for the purchase of securities shall be issued unless accompanied by an abridged prospectus containing key disclosures.

subject: Law
prompt: Which regulatory authority specifies the classes of companies eligible to issue a Shelf Prospectus?
optionA: Reserve Bank of India alone
optionB: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
optionC: Registrar of Companies directly without SEBI
optionD: National Company Law Tribunal
answerText: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
explanation: Section 31 explicitly states that a shelf prospectus may be issued by such class or classes of companies as the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) may specify.

subject: Law
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Solaris Tech Solutions Private Limited wanted to raise funds urgently. The Board of Directors resolved to make a private placement of equity shares to 220 identified persons, including retail friends and family, without restricting it to Qualified Institutional Buyers or employees under ESOP. The application money collected was deposited directly into the company's operational current account and utilized immediately to pay off a short-term bank loan before filing the return of allotment.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the legal consequence of Solaris Tech Solutions Private Limited making a private placement offer to 220 persons in a financial year?
optionA: It is completely valid since private companies have no investor limits.
optionB: It is deemed to be a public offer because it exceeds the limit of 200 persons, violating Section 42.
optionC: It converts the company into a partnership firm automatically.
optionD: It is permitted if approved by an ordinary resolution.
answerText: It is deemed to be a public offer because it exceeds the limit of 200 persons, violating Section 42.
explanation: Section 42(2) provides that any offer or invitation made to more than 200 persons in the aggregate in a financial year is deemed to be a public offer, attracting all public offer regulations and penalties.
conceptTags: Private Placement | Deemed Public Offer | Section 42

subject: Law
prompt: Was it legally permissible for Solaris Tech Solutions Private Limited to utilize the application money before making the allotment?
optionA: Yes, private companies can use application money immediately.
optionB: No, application monies received under private placement must be kept in a separate bank account and cannot be utilized until allotment is made.
optionC: Yes, if utilized for debt repayment.
optionD: Yes, with 75% shareholder approval.
answerText: No, application monies received under private placement must be kept in a separate bank account and cannot be utilized until allotment is made.
explanation: Section 42(6) mandates that monies received on application under private placement shall be kept in a separate bank account in a scheduled bank and shall not be utilized for any purpose other than for adjustment against allotment or repayment.
conceptTags: Private Placement | Separate Bank Account | Section 42

subject: Law
prompt: Within what timeframe must Solaris Tech Solutions Private Limited file the return of allotment in Form PAS-3 with the Registrar after making an allotment?
optionA: 15 days
optionB: 30 days
optionC: 60 days
optionD: 90 days
answerText: 30 days
explanation: Rule 14 and Section 42(9) require the company to file a return of allotment with the Registrar in Form PAS-3 within 30 days from the date of the allotment.
conceptTags: Return of Allotment | Form PAS-3 | Rule 14

subject: Law
prompt: Through which mode must the subscription money for private placement be paid by the investors?
optionA: Cash up to Rs. 2,00,000
optionB: Cheque, demand draft, or other banking channels only, but never by cash
optionC: Barter or exchange of physical assets
optionD: Promissory notes
answerText: Cheque, demand draft, or other banking channels only, but never by cash
explanation: Rule 14 of the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014 expressly mandates that subscription monies payable on private placement must be paid through banking channels (cheque/DD/bank transfer) and not in cash.

subject: Law
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Beta Power Corporation opened a public issue of equity shares worth Rs. 50 crores, specifying a minimum subscription of 90% of the issue size in its prospectus. When the subscription list closed, the company received valid applications amounting to only 75% of the issue size. Failing to secure the minimum subscription, the company delayed refunding the application money beyond the statutory timeline of 15 days from the closure of the issue.

subject: Law
prompt: Within how many days from the closure of the issue must Beta Power Corporation refund the application money when minimum subscription is not received?
optionA: 10 days
optionB: 15 days
optionC: 30 days
optionD: 60 days
answerText: 15 days
explanation: Section 39(3) stipulates that if the stated minimum subscription is not received, the application money shall be repaid within 15 days from the closure of the issue.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the rate of interest payable by Beta Power Corporation and its officers in default for failing to refund application money within the statutory period?
optionA: 6% per annum
optionB: 10% per annum
optionC: 12% per annum
optionD: 15% per annum
answerText: 15% per annum
explanation: Section 39(3) prescribes that failure to repay application money within 15 days makes the company and officers in default liable to repay it with interest at the rate of 15% per annum.

subject: Law
prompt: Can Beta Power Corporation legally proceed with the allotment of shares when only 75% subscription is received?
optionA: Yes, if approved by the Board of Directors.
optionB: No allotment can be made unless minimum subscription is received.
optionC: Yes, if the shortfall is less than 20%.
optionD: Yes, with NCLT permission.
answerText: No allotment can be made unless minimum subscription is received.
explanation: Section 39(1) expressly prohibits any allotment of securities unless the amount stated in the prospectus as the minimum amount has been subscribed.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the maximum time limit prescribed under Section 39(1) for making allotment of securities in a normal successful public issue from the closure of the subscription list?
optionA: 30 days
optionB: 60 days
optionC: 90 days
optionD: 120 days
answerText: 30 days
explanation: Section 39(1) states that no allotment shall be made unless minimum subscription is received and within 30 days of the closure of the issue (or such other period as specified by SEBI).
conceptTags: Allotment Time Limit | Section 39 | Public Issue

subject: Law
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Delta Dynamics Limited proposed to make a public offer of equity shares. Prior to launching the issue, the company failed to make an application to any recognized stock exchange for permission for the shares to be dealt with on the exchange. Furthermore, during the marketing campaign, an individual named Mr. X deliberately made false and deceptive promises and forecasts about future dividend payouts to induce several retail investors to apply for shares.

subject: Law
prompt: Which section of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates that a company making a public offer must apply to one or more recognized stock exchanges for listing permission?
optionA: Section 38
optionB: Section 40
optionC: Section 42
optionD: Section 26
answerText: Section 40
explanation: Section 40(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires every company making a public offer to make an application before issuing a prospectus to one or more recognized stock exchanges and obtain permission.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the legal status of any allotment made by Delta Dynamics Limited if it fails to comply with the stock exchange permission requirement under Section 40?
optionA: The allotment is fully valid.
optionB: The allotment is void.
optionC: The allotment is subject to regularizing by the Board.
optionD: The allotment converts into debentures.
answerText: The allotment is void.
explanation: Section 40(5) provides that if permission from stock exchanges has not been applied for or granted, any allotment made pursuant to the prospectus shall be void.

subject: Law
prompt: Which section of the Act specifically penalizes Mr. X for fraudulently inducing persons to invest money through deceptive promises and forecasts?
optionA: Section 34
optionB: Section 35
optionC: Section 36
optionD: Section 39
answerText: Section 36
explanation: Section 36 of the Companies Act, 2013 penalizes any person who knowingly or recklessly makes false, deceptive, or misleading statements, promises, or forecasts to induce another person to enter into an agreement for acquiring securities.
conceptTags: Fraudulently Inducing Persons | Section 36 | Deceptive Statements

subject: Law
prompt: If application monies are required to be refunded due to void allotment resulting from lack of stock exchange permission, where must such monies be kept pending refund?
optionA: In a separate bank account in a scheduled bank
optionB: In the company's general operational ledger
optionC: With the Registrar of Companies directly
optionD: With the stock exchange clearing house
answerText: In a separate bank account in a scheduled bank
explanation: Section 40(3) requires that all monies received on application from the public be kept in a separate bank account in a scheduled bank, to be repaid if permission is not granted or allotment becomes void.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the maximum period within which a company limited by shares must issue share certificates to its subscribers to the memorandum after incorporation under the Companies Act, 2013?
optionA: 1 month
optionB: 2 months
optionC: 60 days
optionD: 6 months
answerText: 2 months
explanation: According to Section 56(4)(a) of the Companies Act, 2013, every company must deliver the certificates of all shares allotted, transferred, or transmitted within two months from the date of incorporation to the subscribers to the memorandum. Hence, 2 months is the correct statutory timeline.
conceptTags: Share Certificate | Time limit for delivery | Section 56

subject: Law
prompt: Under Section 53 of the Companies Act, 2013, a company is prohibited from issuing shares at a discount, except in the case of which type of shares?
optionA: Preference shares
optionB: Sweat equity shares
optionC: Bonus shares
optionD: Redeemable preference shares
answerText: Sweat equity shares
explanation: Section 53 explicitly prohibits the issue of shares at a discount, except under Section 54 which permits a company to issue sweat equity shares to its directors or employees at a discount or for consideration other than cash.
conceptTags: Prohibition of discount | Sweat Equity | Section 53

subject: Law
prompt: Which of the following is a mandatory condition for a company to issue sweat equity shares under Section 54 of the Companies Act, 2013?
optionA: The issue must be authorized by a Board Resolution.
optionB: The resolution must specify the number of shares, current market price, and consideration.
optionC: The company must have completed at least 3 years since commencement of business.
optionD: The sweat equity shares of a class must be locked in for a maximum period of 1 year.
answerText: The company must have completed at least 3 years since commencement of business.
explanation: Section 54 requires that the sweat equity shares of a class of shares already issued are authorized by a special resolution passed in a general meeting and the company has been in business for at least one year since the date it was entitled to commence business. The lock-in period is 3 years.
conceptTags: Sweat Equity Shares | Section 54 | Special Resolution

subject: Law
prompt: What is the maximum limit on the issue of sweat equity shares in any financial year as a percentage of the paid-up equity share capital of the company, unless prescribed otherwise for startup companies?
explanation: As per the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, a company shall not issue sweat equity shares for more than 15% of the existing paid-up equity share capital in a financial year, or shares of the issue value of Rs. 5 crores, whichever is higher, subject to a maximum of 25% of the paid-up equity share capital at any time.
conceptTags: Sweat Equity Limits | Share Capital Rules | Percentage Limit

subject: Law
prompt: In the case of a public company, what is the maximum permissible discount or commission that can be paid to any person for subscribing or agreeing to subscribe to its debentures?
optionA: 2.5% of the issue price
optionB: 5% of the issue price
optionC: 10% of the issue price
optionD: No statutory percentage limit is prescribed under the Act for debentures
answerText: No statutory percentage limit is prescribed under the Act for debentures
explanation: Section 40 regulates underwriting commission for shares and debentures, but the Companies (Specification of definitions details) Rules and Section 40 rules set the maximum commission for shares at 5% and debentures at 2.5%, BUT wait - under Section 40 read with Rule 13, underwriting commission for shares is 5% and for debentures is 2.5%. Let's check the options. Underwriting commission for shares is 5% and for debentures is 2.5% as per Rule 13 of Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014.

subject: Law
prompt: Can a company limited by shares issue fully paid-up bonus shares out of its Securities Premium Account?
optionA: No, securities premium can only be used for writing off preliminary expenses.
optionB: Yes, under Section 52(2), securities premium can be applied for issuing fully paid-up bonus shares.
optionC: Yes, but only if approved by the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT).
optionD: No, bonus shares can only be issued out of Free Reserves.
answerText: Yes, under Section 52(2), securities premium can be applied for issuing fully paid-up bonus shares.
explanation: Section 52(2) explicitly permits the application of the securities premium account for the company's issue of unissued shares of the company to the members of the company as fully paid bonus shares.

subject: Law
prompt: Which of the following funds CANNOT be utilized for the redemption of preference shares by a company?
optionA: Proceeds of a fresh issue of shares made for the specific purpose of redemption
optionB: Out of the profits of the company which would otherwise be available for dividend
optionC: Out of the proceeds of a fresh issue of debentures
optionD: Out of Capital Redemption Reserve account
answerText: Out of the proceeds of a fresh issue of debentures
explanation: Section 55 states that preference shares can be redeemed out of the proceeds of a fresh issue of shares or out of profits of the company available for dividend. Debenture proceeds cannot be used for redeeming preference shares.
conceptTags: Redemption of Preference Shares | Section 55 | Capital Redemption Reserve

subject: Law
prompt: When unredeemed preference shares are redeemed out of profits, an amount equal to the nominal amount of the shares to be redeemed must be transferred to:
optionA: General Reserve
optionB: Capital Redemption Reserve Account
optionC: Securities Premium Account
optionD: Capital Reserve
answerText: Capital Redemption Reserve Account
explanation: According to the proviso to Section 55(2), where preference shares are redeemed out of profits, an amount equal to the nominal value of the shares so redeemed shall be transferred to the Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR) account.
conceptTags: Capital Redemption Reserve | Section 55 | Preference Shares

subject: Law
prompt: What is the maximum tenure for which preference shares can be issued by a company engaged in setting up infrastructure projects, as per the proviso to Section 55(1)?
optionA: 20 years
optionB: 25 years
optionC: 30 years
optionD: No limit for infrastructure projects
answerText: 25 years
explanation: As per the proviso to Section 55(1), a company engaged in setting up infrastructure projects may issue preference shares for a period exceeding 20 years but not exceeding 25 years, subject to redemption of a minimum percentage each year starting from the 21st year.

subject: Law
prompt: Under Section 62(1)(a) of the Companies Act, 2013, when a company having share capital proposes to increase its subscribed capital by the issue of further shares, such shares must first be offered to:
optionA: The public through a prospectus
optionB: Existing equity shareholders in proportion to their paid-up capital
optionC: Institutional investors and mutual funds
optionD: Employees under an Employee Stock Option Scheme
answerText: Existing equity shareholders in proportion to their paid-up capital
explanation: Section 62(1)(a) embodies the pre-emptive rights of existing equity shareholders, requiring further shares to be offered in proportion to the paid-up capital on those shares.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the minimum notice period required to be given to existing equity shareholders when making a rights issue under Section 62(1)(a) of the Companies Act, 2013?
optionA: Not less than 7 days and not more than 14 days
optionB: Not less than 10 days and not more than 15 days
optionC: Not less than 15 days and not more than 30 days
optionD: Not less than 21 days and not more than 45 days
answerText: Not less than 15 days and not more than 30 days
explanation: Section 62(1)(a)(i) prescribes that the notice of a rights issue shall be dispatched through registered post, speed post, or electronic mode at least 15 days before the date of opening of the issue and shall not exceed 30 days.

subject: Law
prompt: By what majority must a special resolution be passed in a general meeting to issue shares on a preferential basis to persons other than existing shareholders under Section 62(1)(c)?
optionA: Simple majority (more than 50%)
optionB: Not less than two-thirds majority
optionC: Special resolution (not less than three-fourths majority)
optionD: Unanimous resolution
answerText: Special resolution (not less than three-fourths majority)
explanation: Section 62(1)(c) permits preferential allotment of shares if it is authorized by a special resolution passed by the shareholders in a general meeting.

subject: Law
prompt: Can a company issue fully paid-up bonus shares by capitalizing its revaluation reserve?
optionA: Yes, provided the revaluation is certified by a registered valuer.
optionB: No, bonus shares cannot be issued out of capitalization of reserves created from revaluation of assets.
optionC: Yes, with the prior approval of the Central Government.
optionD: Yes, if approved by a unanimous resolution.
answerText: No, bonus shares cannot be issued out of capitalization of reserves created from revaluation of assets.
explanation: As per Rule 14 of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, bonus shares shall not be issued by capitalizing reserves created by the revaluation of assets.

subject: Law
