answerText: Recover the amount of fees and expenses paid from the company as debt
explanation: Section 78 explicitly entitles the charge-holder who incurs expenses in getting the charge registered to recover such amount from the company.
conceptTags: Section 78 | Recovery of Expenses | Charge-holder Rights

subject: Law
prompt: Which of the following instruments must be kept by the company along with the register of charges at its registered office under Section 85?
optionA: Only the board resolution approving the loan
optionB: A copy of every instrument creating or modifying any charge requiring registration
optionC: The personal guarantees signed by independent directors
optionD: Tax audit reports for the last 5 years
answerText: A copy of every instrument creating or modifying any charge requiring registration
explanation: Section 85(1) specifies that a copy of every instrument creating or modifying any charge requiring registration under Chapter VI shall be kept at the registered office of the company along with the register of charges.
conceptTags: Section 85(1) | Instrument of Charge | Registered Office Records

subject: Law
prompt: If an officer of a company willfully furnishes any false or incorrect information or knowingly suppresses any material information required under Section 77 or Section 79, what penal consequence do they face?
optionA: They shall be liable for fraud under Section 447 of the Companies Act, 2013.
optionB: They receive a simple verbal reprimand from the ROC.
optionC: They are disqualified from holding bank accounts only.
optionD: They are exempt from liability if the company pays a fine.
answerText: They shall be liable for fraud under Section 447 of the Companies Act, 2013.
explanation: Section 86(2) provides that if any person willfully furnishes any false or incorrect information or knowingly suppresses any material information, they shall be liable for action under Section 447 (Fraud).

subject: Law
prompt: Is a negative lien clause (an undertaking by a company not to create further charges on its property) required to be registered under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013?
optionA: Yes, all negative covenants must be registered as charges.
optionB: No, a negative lien does not create a security interest or charge on the property and hence does not require registration.
optionC: Yes, but only if approved by the stock exchange.
optionD: No, unless the debt exceeds 100 crores.
answerText: No, a negative lien does not create a security interest or charge on the property and hence does not require registration.
explanation: A negative lien is merely a negative covenant or promise not to encumber assets further and does not create any beneficial interest, lien, or security on the property itself. Therefore, it does not fall within the definition of a charge under Section 2(16) and does not require registration under Section 77.
conceptTags: Negative Lien | Scope of Charge | Section 2(16) vs Covenants

subject: Law
prompt: What is the primary objective of registering charges created by a company under Chapter VI of the Companies Act, 2013?
optionA: To generate tax revenue for the Ministry of Corporate Affairs
optionB: To protect prospective creditors and members by giving them public notice of existing encumbrances on company assets
optionC: To enable the Central Government to manage the day-to-day operations of the company
optionD: To fix executive salaries in the company
answerText: To protect prospective creditors and members by giving them public notice of existing encumbrances on company assets
explanation: The fundamental purpose of charge registration is to ensure transparency and provide public/constructive notice to any person dealing with the company so they are aware of existing encumbrances on the company's assets.
conceptTags: Objective of Registration | Transparency | Public Notice

subject: Law
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Zenith Engineering Limited created a mortgage on its factory land and building in favour of Apex Bank Ltd. on 10th May 2026 to secure a term loan of Rs. 5 crores. Due to an administrative oversight by the company secretary, the particulars of the charge were not filed with the Registrar within 30 days. On 5th July 2026, Apex Bank (the charge-holder) discovered this omission and decided to take matters into its own hands under the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.

subject: Law
prompt: What was the last date by which Zenith Engineering Limited should have originally filed the particulars of the charge under Section 77(1)?
optionA: 25th May 2026
optionB: 9th June 2026
optionC: 10th June 2026
optionD: 9th July 2026
answerText: 9th June 2026
explanation: The charge was created on 10th May 2026. Counting 30 days from 10th May (excluding the date of creation: 20 days in May + 9 days in June), the initial 30-day period expires on 9th June 2026.
conceptTags: Section 77 | Calculation of 30 Days | Case Scenario

subject: Law
prompt: Can Apex Bank Ltd. (the charge-holder) apply to the Registrar for registration of this charge since Zenith Engineering Limited failed to do so within 30 days?
optionA: No, only the company can apply for charge registration.
optionB: Yes, Apex Bank can apply under Section 78 and subsequently recover registration expenses from Zenith Engineering Limited.
optionC: Yes, but only after filing a criminal complaint against the company secretary.
optionD: No, Apex Bank must wait for NCLT permission.
answerText: Yes, Apex Bank can apply under Section 78 and subsequently recover registration expenses from Zenith Engineering Limited.
explanation: Under Section 78, if a company fails to register a charge within 30 days, the person in whose favour the charge is created (Apex Bank) may apply to the Registrar for registration and recover the expenses from the company.

subject: Law
prompt: Assuming Zenith Engineering Limited itself applies for registration on 1st July 2026 (within the extended window allowed by the ROC), what is required for the ROC to accept such filing?
optionA: Payment of standard fee only
optionB: Payment of prescribed additional fee as the filing is made beyond 30 days but within 60 days of creation
optionC: Prior approval of the Supreme Court
optionD: Passing of an ordinary resolution in a general meeting
answerText: Payment of prescribed additional fee as the filing is made beyond 30 days but within 60 days of creation
explanation: Under the proviso to Section 77(1), for charges created after the amendment, if filing is done beyond 30 days but within a total of 60 days from creation, the Registrar may allow it upon payment of prescribed additional fee.
conceptTags: Section 77 Proviso | Extended Window | Additional Fee

subject: Law
prompt: If neither the company nor Apex Bank registers the charge and Zenith Engineering Limited goes into liquidation, what is the legal status of Apex Bank's charge?
optionA: Apex Bank retains absolute priority as a secured creditor.
optionB: The charge is void against the liquidator and any creditor of the company, making Apex Bank an unsecured creditor.
optionC: The term loan is automatically written off by the government.
optionD: Apex Bank becomes a shareholder of Zenith Engineering Limited.
answerText: The charge is void against the liquidator and any creditor of the company, making Apex Bank an unsecured creditor.
explanation: As per Section 77 read with Section 84, an unregistered charge is void against the liquidator and any creditor of the company, meaning the creditor loses its secured status and ranks as an unsecured creditor.
conceptTags: Effect of Non-Registration | Liquidation | Secured vs Unsecured

subject: Law
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Vanguard Technologies Ltd. had registered a charge over its plant and machinery in favour of Global Finance Corp on 1st January 2025. On 15th March 2026, Vanguard Technologies Ltd. fully repaid the loan and satisfied the charge. However, the company omitted to inform the Registrar within the stipulated time. Meanwhile, Global Finance Corp received notice from the ROC regarding this satisfaction and raised no objections within the specified timeline. The company later maintained all statutory registers properly at its registered office.

subject: Law
prompt: Within how many days from 15th March 2026 was Vanguard Technologies Ltd. required to intimate the Registrar regarding the full satisfaction of the charge under Section 82(1)?
optionA: 15 days
optionB: 30 days
optionC: 60 days
optionD: 90 days
answerText: 30 days
explanation: Section 82(1) requires the company to give intimation of payment or satisfaction in full of a registered charge to the Registrar within 30 days of such satisfaction.

subject: Law
prompt: What form must Vanguard Technologies Ltd. use to file the notice of satisfaction of the charge with the Registrar?
optionA: Form CHG-1
optionB: Form CHG-4
optionC: Form CHG-6
optionD: Form CHG-9
answerText: Form CHG-4
explanation: Form CHG-4 is the specific prescribed form under the Companies (Registration of Charges) Rules, 2014 for intimating the payment or satisfaction in full of a charge.
conceptTags: Form CHG-4 | Satisfaction of Charge | Rules

subject: Law
prompt: When the Registrar receives the intimation of satisfaction, what maximum time limit is typically given to the charge-holder (Global Finance Corp) to show cause why satisfaction should not be recorded, under Section 82(2)?
optionA: 7 days
optionB: 14 days
optionC: 30 days
optionD: 60 days
answerText: 14 days
explanation: Section 82(2) specifies that the Registrar shall issue a notice to the holder of the charge calling for objections, if any, within such time not exceeding 14 days as may be specified.

subject: Law
prompt: Where must Vanguard Technologies Ltd. keep its register of charges and instrument of charges for inspection by members and creditors under Section 85?
optionA: At the corporate office of Global Finance Corp
optionB: At the registered office of the company
optionC: At the nearest stock exchange building
optionD: Only at the residence of the Managing Director
answerText: At the registered office of the company
explanation: Section 85 explicitly mandates that every company shall keep at its registered office a register of charges and a copy of every instrument creating or modifying any charge.
conceptTags: Section 85 | Registered Office | Register of Charges

subject: Law
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Dynamic Logistics Ltd. created a floating charge on its entire fleet of delivery trucks in favour of Express Credit Bank on 1st February 2026. Due to an internal dispute among directors, the filing was delayed beyond the 60-day maximum period allowed by the Registrar under Section 77. The management now wishes to rectify this omission and approaches competent authorities. Additionally, a receiver was appointed over certain assets of the company on 1st April 2026 by an order of the court.

subject: Law
prompt: Since the delay exceeded the maximum period of 60 days from creation that the ROC can condone under Section 77, which authority must Dynamic Logistics Ltd. approach for condonation and extension of time?
optionA: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
optionB: The Central Government (Regional Director) under Section 87
optionC: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
optionD: The Registrar of Companies (suo motu)
answerText: The Central Government (Regional Director) under Section 87
explanation: Under Section 87, where the filing is delayed beyond the powers of the ROC under Section 77, the Central Government (Regional Director) is empowered to condone the delay and direct rectification upon application.
conceptTags: Section 87 | Central Government / RD | Condonation of Delay

subject: Law
prompt: Within how many days must notice of the appointment of the receiver of Dynamic Logistics Ltd.'s property be given to the company and the Registrar under Section 81?
optionA: 15 days
optionB: 30 days
optionC: 60 days
optionD: 90 days
answerText: 30 days
explanation: Section 81 requires notice of the appointment of a receiver to be given to the company and the Registrar within 30 days of the order or appointment.

subject: Law
prompt: Which form is prescribed for filing notice of the appointment of the receiver with the Registrar under Section 81?
optionA: Form CHG-1
optionB: Form CHG-4
optionC: Form CHG-6
optionD: Form CHG-8
answerText: Form CHG-6
explanation: Form CHG-6 is the prescribed form for registering the appointment or cessation of a receiver or liquidator under the Companies (Registration of Charges) Rules, 2014.
conceptTags: Form CHG-6 | Receiver Notice | ROC Filing

subject: Law
prompt: What is the legal nature of a 'floating charge' created on the fleet of delivery trucks of Dynamic Logistics Ltd. before it crystallizes?
optionA: It is an immediate fixed security on specific trucks currently owned.
optionB: It is an equitable charge on present and future assets of a circulating character which remains dormant until crystallization.
optionC: It is legally invalid under Indian company law.
optionD: It is treated as an unsecured loan for all statutory purposes.
answerText: It is an equitable charge on present and future assets of a circulating character which remains dormant until crystallization.
explanation: A floating charge is a security on property of a circulating or fluctuating nature (like stock-in-trade or vehicles in fleet) which allows the company to deal with the assets in the ordinary course of business until it crystallizes upon an event such as default or winding up.

subject: Law
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Pioneer Agro Industries Ltd. acquired a warehouse on 10th February 2026. The warehouse was already subject to an existing mortgage charge created by the previous owner in favour of Metro Bank. Pioneer Agro Industries Ltd. failed to register particulars of this acquired charge within the standard statutory time frame. Later, an outsider, Mr. X, acquired a portion of the company's property and claimed ignorance of Metro Bank's charge, arguing he had no personal knowledge of it.

subject: Law
prompt: Are the provisions relating to registration of charges applicable to Pioneer Agro Industries Ltd. with respect to the warehouse acquired with an existing charge?
optionA: No, registration applies only to charges created directly by the company.
optionB: Yes, the provisions apply mutatis mutandis to property acquired subject to a charge.
optionC: Only if approved by the Regional Director.
optionD: No, the previous owner alone remains responsible.
answerText: Yes, the provisions apply mutatis mutandis to property acquired subject to a charge.
explanation: Under the Companies Act, when a company acquires any property subject to a charge, the registration provisions apply mutatis mutandis as if the company had created the charge itself.
conceptTags: Acquisition of Property | Mutatis Mutandis | Section 77

subject: Law
prompt: Assuming Metro Bank's charge was duly registered under Section 77, what is the legal position regarding Mr. X's claim of ignorance?
optionA: Mr. X's claim is valid because he had no actual knowledge of the charge.
optionB: By virtue of Section 80, registration operates as constructive notice, so Mr. X is deemed to have notice of the charge.
optionC: Metro Bank must compensate Mr. X for his loss.
optionD: The charge becomes void against Mr. X automatically.
answerText: By virtue of Section 80, registration operates as constructive notice, so Mr. X is deemed to have notice of the charge.
explanation: Section 80 provides that registration of a charge constitutes constructive notice to any person who subsequently acquires the property, regardless of whether they had actual notice.

subject: Law
prompt: Who is primarily responsible for filing the particulars of the charge when a company acquires property subject to a charge?
optionA: The previous owner of the property
optionB: The acquiring company (Pioneer Agro Industries Ltd.)
optionC: Metro Bank exclusively
optionD: The local municipal corporation
answerText: The acquiring company (Pioneer Agro Industries Ltd.)
explanation: The acquiring company bears the primary statutory obligation to register the particulars of the charge within the prescribed time under Section 77/78 rules.
conceptTags: Acquiring Company | Duty to Register | Section 77

subject: Law
prompt: If Pioneer Agro Industries Ltd. willfully suppresses material information regarding this charge during registration filings, what penal consequence may the officers face under Section 86(2)?
optionA: Liability for fraud under Section 447
optionB: A minor warning letter with zero penalty
optionC: Mandatory community service
optionD: Revocation of the company's trademark only
answerText: A minor warning letter with zero penalty
explanation: Section 86(2) provides that any person who willfully furnishes false/incorrect information or knowingly suppresses material information shall be liable for action under Section 447 (Fraud).

subject: Law
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Alpha Consumer Goods Ltd. issued debentures secured by a charge on its fixed assets. The company created the charge on 1st March 2026. Due to a clerical error in the company's secretarial department, Form CHG-9 for the debenture charge was not filed within 30 days. The debenture-holders are concerned about their security and priority. The company secretary now seeks to regularize the default using the appropriate legal provisions and forms.

subject: Law
prompt: Which specific form is prescribed under the Companies (Registration of Charges) Rules, 2014 for registration of creation or modification of charges relating to debentures?
optionA: Form CHG-1
optionB: Form CHG-4
optionC: Form CHG-6
optionD: Form CHG-9
answerText: Form CHG-9
explanation: Form CHG-9 is specifically prescribed for registration of creation or modification of charges for debentures or rectification thereof.

subject: Law
prompt: What evidentiary value does the Certificate of Registration of Charge issued by the ROC for this debenture charge hold?
optionA: It is conclusive evidence that all requirements of Chapter VI as to registration have been complied with.
optionB: It is prima facie evidence which can be easily challenged in any court without proof.
optionC: It has no legal standing unless endorsed by the debenture trustees.
optionD: It is valid only for tax assessment purposes.
answerText: It is conclusive evidence that all requirements of Chapter VI as to registration have been complied with.
explanation: Section 77(2) explicitly provides that the certificate of registration issued by the Registrar is conclusive evidence that all requirements of Chapter VI with respect to registration have been complied with.
conceptTags: Section 77(2) | Certificate of Registration | Conclusive Evidence

subject: Law
prompt: If Alpha Consumer Goods Ltd. fails to register the debenture charge within the maximum extended period permitted by the ROC, what is the impact on the debenture-holders during company winding up?
optionA: They retain priority over all other unsecured creditors.
optionB: The charge is void against the liquidator and creditors, ranking them as ordinary unsecured creditors.
optionC: The debentures are converted into equity shares automatically.
optionD: The directors become personally liable to pay the full debenture amount immediately.
answerText: The charge is void against the liquidator and creditors, ranking them as ordinary unsecured creditors.
explanation: Non-registration renders the charge void against the liquidator and creditors of the company, meaning the secured debenture-holders lose their priority and rank as unsecured creditors.

subject: Law
prompt: Who is entitled to inspect the register of charges and instrument of charges maintained by Alpha Consumer Goods Ltd. under Section 85?
optionA: Only the debenture trustees
optionB: Any member or creditor free of cost, and any other person on payment of a prescribed fee
optionC: Only the statutory auditors of the company
optionD: The general public without paying any fee under any circumstances
answerText: Any member or creditor free of cost, and any other person on payment of a prescribed fee
explanation: Section 85(2) allows inspection of the register of charges and instrument of charges by any member or creditor without fee, and by any other person on payment of the prescribed fee during business hours.

subject: Law
prompt: According to the Companies Act, 2013, what is the maximum time gap allowed between two consecutive Annual General Meetings (AGMs) of a listed company?
optionA: 15 months
optionB: 12 months
optionC: 6 months
optionD: 18 months
answerText: 15 months
explanation: Under Section 96 of the Companies Act, 2013, the maximum interval between two consecutive AGMs shall not exceed 15 months. This ensures timely reporting and shareholder oversight in companies.

subject: Law
prompt: Within what period must a company hold its first Annual General Meeting from the date of its incorporation?
optionA: Within 6 months
optionB: Within 9 months
optionC: Within 12 months
optionD: Within 15 months
answerText: Within 9 months
explanation: As per the second proviso to Section 96(1), every company must hold its first AGM within 9 months from the closing of the first financial year. If the first AGM is held within this period, the Registrar is not required to grant any extension.

subject: Law
prompt: Who has the authority to grant an extension of time for holding an Annual General Meeting (other than the first AGM) under the Companies Act, 2013?
optionA: National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT)
optionB: Registrar of Companies (RoC)
optionC: Central Government
optionD: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
answerText: Registrar of Companies (RoC)
explanation: Under the first proviso to Section 96(1), the Registrar of Companies (RoC) may, for any special reason, extend the time within which any AGM (other than the first AGM) shall be held, by a period not exceeding 3 months.

subject: Law
prompt: At what time and on what type of day must an Annual General Meeting be held according to Section 96?
optionA: Anytime during business hours on any day
optionB: During business hours on a national holiday
optionC: During business hours on any day that is not a National Holiday
optionD: At any hour on a business day
answerText: During business hours on any day that is not a National Holiday
explanation: Section 96(2) specifies that every AGM shall be called during business hours, that is, between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day that is not a National Holiday.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the minimum shorter notice requirement for calling an AGM if consent is accorded in writing or by electronic mode by members holding not less than __% of the share capital giving right to vote at such meeting?
explanation: Under Section 101(1), an AGM may be called after giving a shorter notice if consent is given in writing or by electronic mode by not less than 95% of the members entitled to vote at such meeting.

subject: Law
prompt: In the case of a public company, what is the quorum required for a general meeting if the number of members as on the date of the meeting is more than 1,000 but up to 5,000?
optionA: 5 members personally present
optionB: 15 members personally present
optionC: 30 members personally present
optionD: 50 members personally present
answerText: 15 members personally present
explanation: Section 103 prescribes that for a public company, the quorum is 15 members personally present if the number of members is more than 1,000 but up to 5,000.

subject: Law
prompt: If a company does not have articles providing for a larger quorum, what is the quorum for a general meeting of a private company?
optionA: 1 member personally present
optionB: 2 members personally present
optionC: 3 members personally present
optionD: 5 members personally present
answerText: 2 members personally present
explanation: Section 103(1)(a)(i) states that unless the articles of a company provide for a larger number, the quorum for a private company shall be 2 members personally present.

subject: Law
prompt: Within how many days from the conclusion of a general meeting must a company prepare and sign the minutes of that meeting?
optionA: 15 days
optionB: 30 days
optionC: 45 days
optionD: 60 days
answerText: 30 days
explanation: As per Section 118(1) read with Secretarial Standards, minutes of every general meeting must be signed and entered in books kept for that purpose within 30 days of the conclusion of the meeting.

subject: Law
prompt: Who can demand a poll under Section 109 before or on the declaration of the result of the voting on any resolution on a show of hands, in a company having a share capital?
optionA: Any single member holding any number of shares
optionB: Members present in person or by proxy holding not less than 1/10th of the total voting power or having a paid-up capital of at least 5 lakh rupees
optionC: Only the Chairman of the meeting
optionD: Members holding at least 50% of the voting power
answerText: Members present in person or by proxy holding not less than 1/10th of the total voting power or having a paid-up capital of at least 5 lakh rupees
explanation: Under Section 109, a poll may be demanded by members present in person or by proxy, having not less than one-tenth of the total voting power or holding shares on which an aggregate sum of not less than 5 lakh rupees (or such higher amount as prescribed) has been paid-up.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the maximum validity period of a proxy deposited with a company before a general meeting?
optionA: 30 days
optionB: 48 hours before the meeting
optionC: Valid until the meeting is concluded, unless revoked
optionD: 6 months
answerText: Valid until the meeting is concluded, unless revoked
explanation: A proxy is valid for the meeting for which it is deposited (including any adjournment thereof) unless revoked by the member prior to the meeting. The instrument of proxy must be deposited 48 hours before the meeting.

subject: Law
prompt: Which of the following matters is NOT mandatorily required to be transacted as an ordinary business at an Annual General Meeting?
optionA: Consideration of financial statements and reports of the Board and Auditors
optionB: Declaration of dividend
optionC: Appointment of a director in place of those retiring
optionD: Appointment and fixation of remuneration of cost auditors
answerText: Appointment and fixation of remuneration of cost auditors
explanation: Section 102 classifies only four matters as ordinary business at an AGM: consideration of financial statements/reports, declaration of dividend, appointment of retiring directors, and appointment/remuneration of statutory auditors. Cost auditor appointment is special business.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the statutory requirement regarding the explanatory statement to be annexed to the notice of a general meeting under Section 102?
optionA: It is required only for ordinary business items.
optionB: It must be annexed for all items of special business to be transacted at the meeting.
optionC: It is required only if requested by 10% of shareholders.
optionD: It is never required for private companies.
answerText: It must be annexed for all items of special business to be transacted at the meeting.
explanation: Section 102 mandates that a statement setting out all material facts concerning each item of special business to be transacted at a general meeting must be annexed to the notice.

subject: Law
prompt: If a meeting is adjourned due to lack of quorum, to what day, time, and place is it adjourned automatically by default under Section 103, unless otherwise specified by the Board?
optionA: Same day in the next week at the same time and place
optionB: Next working day at the same time and place
optionC: Exactly 30 days later at the registered office
optionD: The meeting stands cancelled permanently
answerText: Same day in the next week at the same time and place
explanation: Section 103(2) provides that if quorum is not present within half an hour from the time appointed, the meeting stands adjourned to the same day in the next week at the same time and place, or such other date, time, and place as the Board may determine.

subject: Law
prompt: Can a member of a company limited by shares, having the right to vote at a meeting, appoint multiple proxies under the Act, unless the articles restrict it?
optionA: No, only one proxy is allowed per member.
optionB: Yes, a member can appoint one or more proxies to attend and vote on the same poll.
optionC: Yes, but only up to a maximum of 5 proxies.
optionD: Only institutional investors can appoint multiple proxies.
answerText: Yes, a member can appoint one or more proxies to attend and vote on the same poll.
explanation: Under Section 105(1), a member entitled to attend and vote is entitled to appoint another person as a proxy to attend and vote instead of the member. Multiple proxies can be appointed if permitted by rules/articles, though a proxy does not have the right to speak on a show of hands.

subject: Law
prompt: In an Extraordinary General Meeting (EGM) called by requisitionists under Section 100, what happens if the Board does not proceed to call a meeting within 21 days of receipt of a valid requisition?
optionA: The meeting stands cancelled automatically.
optionB: The requisitionists themselves may call and hold the meeting within 3 months from the date of requisition.
optionC: The RoC must call the meeting within 7 days.
optionD: The NCLT takes over the management.
answerText: The requisitionists themselves may call and hold the meeting within 3 months from the date of requisition.
explanation: Under Section 100(4), if the Board fails to call a meeting within 21 days from the date of deposit of a valid requisition, the requisitionists may themselves call and hold the meeting within 3 months of that date.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the minimum voting power required for members to requisition an EGM under Section 100 in the case of a company having a share capital?
optionA: Not less than 5% of the paid-up capital carrying voting rights
optionB: Not less than 10% of the paid-up capital carrying voting rights
optionC: Not less than 15% of the paid-up capital carrying voting rights
optionD: Not less than 25% of the paid-up capital carrying voting rights
answerText: Not less than 10% of the paid-up capital carrying voting rights
explanation: Section 100(1) prescribes that for a company having a share capital, members holding not less than one-tenth (10%) of the paid-up capital of the company carrying voting rights can requisition an EGM.

subject: Law
prompt: Where must a company keep its minute books of general meetings for inspection by members?
optionA: At the registered office of the company
optionB: At the residence of the Managing Director
optionC: At the nearest stock exchange office
optionD: At the office of the company's statutory auditor
answerText: At the registered office of the company
explanation: Section 119 specifies that the books containing the minutes of general meetings shall be kept at the registered office of the company and be open for inspection by members during business hours.

subject: Law
prompt: Which type of resolution requires a majority of not less than three-fourths (75%) of the votes cast for its passing?
optionA: Ordinary Resolution
optionB: Special Resolution
optionC: Unanimous Resolution
optionD: Board Resolution
answerText: Special Resolution
explanation: Under Section 114(2), a resolution is a special resolution when the votes cast in favour are not less than three times the votes cast against (i.e., at least 75%).

subject: Law
prompt: Can a postal ballot be used by a company to transact any item of ordinary business at an AGM?
optionA: Yes, all businesses can be transacted through postal ballot.
optionB: No, ordinary business items and items where directors/auditors have a right to be heard cannot be transacted through postal ballot.
optionC: Yes, if 75% members consent.
optionD: Only listed companies can use postal ballot for ordinary business.
answerText: No, ordinary business items and items where directors/auditors have a right to be heard cannot be transacted through postal ballot.
explanation: Rule 22 of the Companies (Management and Administration) Rules, 2014 states that ordinary business and any business in which directors or auditors have a right of being heard at any meeting cannot be transacted by means of a postal ballot.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the penalty/consequence if a company defaults in holding its Annual General Meeting under Section 96?
optionA: Only the Chairman is imprisoned for 1 year.
optionB: The company and every officer in default shall be punishable with fine extending up to one lakh rupees and a further fine for continuous default.
optionC: The company's incorporation is cancelled immediately.
optionD: All directors are disqualified for life without notice.
answerText: The company and every officer in default shall be punishable with fine extending up to one lakh rupees and a further fine for continuous default.
explanation: Section 99 sets out the punishment for default in holding an AGM: the company and every officer in default are punishable with a fine up to one lakh rupees and, in case of continuing default, with a further fine up to five thousand rupees for each day during which such default continues.

subject: Law
prompt: Who appoints the scrutinizer for conducting voting through electronic voting (e-voting) and postal ballot process in a general meeting?
optionA: The Board of Directors
optionB: The Central Government
optionC: The Registrar of Companies
optionD: The Statutory Auditors
answerText: The Board of Directors
explanation: As per the Companies (Management and Administration) Rules, 2014, the Board of Directors appoints one or more scrutinizers (who may be chartered accountants in practice, cost accountants, advocates, etc.) to conduct the e-voting and postal ballot process in a fair and transparent manner.

subject: Law
prompt: Which section of the Companies Act, 2013 deals with the calling of an Extraordinary General Meeting by the Tribunal (NCLT)?
optionA: Section 96
optionB: Section 98
optionC: Section 100
optionD: Section 105
answerText: Section 98
explanation: Section 98 empowers the Tribunal (NCLT), either suo motu or on the application of any director or member, to order a meeting to be called, held, and conducted if it is impracticable to call a meeting in any manner prescribed.

subject: Law
prompt: In case of a company having share capital, what is the voting right of a member on a poll?
optionA: Every member has only one vote regardless of shares held.
optionB: In proportion to his share of the paid-up equity capital of the company.
optionC: Equal to the number of directors present.
optionD: Fixed arbitrarily by the Board of Directors.
answerText: In proportion to his share of the paid-up equity capital of the company.
explanation: Section 106 read with Section 47 provides that voting right of a member on a poll is in proportion to his share in the paid-up equity share capital of the company.

subject: Law
prompt: Can a member be prohibited from exercising voting rights on the ground that they have not paid any call or other sums due on shares?
optionA: No, voting right is absolute and cannot be restricted.
optionB: Yes, if the articles of the company so provide and calls/sums are in arrears.
optionC: Only if the Central Government orders so.
optionD: Only if approved by NCLT.
answerText: Yes, if the articles of the company so provide and calls/sums are in arrears.
explanation: Under Section 106(1), a company can restrict a member from voting if any calls or other sums presently payable have not been paid, provided the articles of the company contain such a provision.
conceptTags: Restriction on Voting | Calls in Arrears | Section 106

subject: Law
prompt: What is the minimum notice period required to call a general meeting of a company under Section 101?
optionA: At least 14 clear days
optionB: At least 21 clear days
optionC: At least 28 clear days
optionD: At least 7 clear days
answerText: At least 21 clear days
explanation: Section 101(1) states that a general meeting of a company may be called by giving not less than 21 clear days' notice in writing or through electronic mode.

subject: Law
prompt: When calculating the 21 clear days' notice for a general meeting, which of the following days are excluded?
optionA: Date of the meeting and date of dispatch of notice
optionB: Only Sundays
optionC: Only National Holidays
optionD: Date of dispatch and date of receipt only
answerText: Date of the meeting and date of dispatch of notice
explanation: 'Clear days' means that neither the day on which the notice is served/deemed to be served nor the day of the meeting itself is to be counted.

subject: Law
prompt: Under Section 111, what is the procedure for circulation of members' resolutions? What is the maximum length of the statement that members can require the company to circulate?
optionA: No length limit is prescribed.
optionB: Reasonable length, as determined by the company's Board.
optionC: A reasonable length.
optionD: Maximum 1,000 words.
answerText: A reasonable length.
explanation: Section 111 provides that a company is required to circulate members' resolutions and/or a statement of not more than a 'reasonable length' of matters referred to in the proposed resolution, upon a valid requisition by members.

subject: Law
prompt: What constitutes a 'quorum' for a general meeting of a public company if the total number of members exceeds 5,000?
optionA: 15 members personally present
optionB: 30 members personally present
optionC: 50 members personally present
optionD: 100 members personally present
answerText: 30 members personally present
explanation: Under Section 103(1)(a)(ii), for a public company, the quorum is 30 members personally present if the number of members exceeds 5,000.

subject: Law
prompt: Can a proxy vote on a show of hands?
optionA: Yes, always.
optionB: No, a proxy does not have the right to vote on a show of hands.
optionC: Yes, if permitted by the Chairman.
optionD: Only in private companies.
answerText: No, a proxy does not have the right to vote on a show of hands.
explanation: Section 105(1) explicitly states that a proxy shall not vote on a show of hands. Proxies are only entitled to vote on a poll.

subject: Law
prompt: Who is responsible for filing the copy of every resolution or agreement referred to in Section 117 with the Registrar of Companies (RoC)?
optionA: The statutory auditor
optionB: The company
optionC: The Chairman of the meeting
optionD: The NCLT
answerText: The company
explanation: Section 117 mandates that a copy of every resolution or agreement requiring special/unanimous majority (as specified in the section) shall be filed by the company with the RoC within 30 days of passing.

subject: Law
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Zenith Infotech Limited is a public company listed on the National Stock Exchange, having 4,500 equity shareholders. The company's last Annual General Meeting (AGM) was held on 15th September 2024. Due to administrative delays in finalizing the consolidated accounts, the Board of Directors wishes to hold the AGM for the financial year 2024-25 on 20th November 2025. The Board seeks an extension from the Registrar of Companies (RoC) for holding this AGM.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the statutory due date by which Zenith Infotech Limited was required to hold its AGM for the financial year 2024-25 under normal circumstances (assuming financial year ends on 31st March)?
optionA: 30th September 2025
optionB: 31st December 2025
optionC: 30th June 2025
optionD: 15th December 2025
answerText: 30th September 2025
explanation: Under Section 96(1), every company must hold its AGM within 6 months from the close of the financial year (i.e., by 30th September for a financial year ending on 31st March).
conceptTags: AGM Due Date | Section 96 | Financial Year

subject: Law
prompt: What is the maximum period of extension that the RoC can grant to Zenith Infotech Limited for holding its AGM under the first proviso to Section 96(1)?
optionA: 1 month
optionB: 2 months
optionC: 3 months
optionD: 6 months
answerText: 3 months
explanation: The RoC may, for any special reason, extend the time within which any AGM (other than the first AGM) shall be held, by a period not exceeding 3 months.

subject: Law
prompt: Considering the date of the previous AGM (15th September 2024), what is the absolute maximum interval that would be permitted between the two AGMs if an extension is granted?
optionA: 12 months
optionB: 15 months
optionC: 18 months
optionD: 21 months
answerText: 15 months
explanation: Section 96 prescribes that the maximum time gap between two consecutive AGMs shall not exceed 15 months, even with RoC extension.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the quorum required for the AGM of Zenith Infotech Limited, given that it is a public company with 4,500 members?
optionA: 5 members personally present
optionB: 15 members personally present
optionC: 30 members personally present
optionD: 50 members personally present
answerText: 15 members personally present
explanation: Under Section 103, for a public company having more than 1,000 but up to 5,000 members, the quorum required is 15 members personally present.

subject: Law
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: AeroSphere Logistics Private Limited has 80 members. A general meeting of the company is scheduled for 10th October. On the day of the meeting, 3 members are personally present at the appointed time. The articles of the company are silent regarding the quorum. Meanwhile, Mr. X, a member, holds a proxy for 10 other members who are absent. The meeting is also attended by two corporate members represented by their authorized representatives.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the statutory quorum for AeroSphere Logistics Private Limited under Section 103, given the facts?
optionA: 1 member personally present
optionB: 2 members personally present
optionC: 5 members personally present
optionD: 10 members personally present
answerText: 2 members personally present
explanation: For a private company, Section 103 prescribes a quorum of 2 members personally present, unless the articles provide for a larger number.

subject: Law
prompt: Is the quorum present at the start of AeroSphere's meeting based on the members present in person?
optionA: No, because proxies must be counted towards quorum.
optionB: Yes, because 3 members personally present exceed the statutory requirement of 2 members.
optionC: No, corporate representatives cannot be counted.
optionD: Yes, only if Mr. X also votes.
answerText: Yes, because 3 members personally present exceed the statutory requirement of 2 members.
explanation: Quorum must be members 'personally present'. Since 3 members are personally present, the requirement of 2 members is satisfied.

subject: Law
prompt: Can the 10 members represented by Mr. X (as proxies) be counted toward the quorum?
optionA: Yes, proxies are always counted for quorum.
optionB: No, proxies are not counted for quorum under Section 103.
optionC: Yes, because Mr. X holds more than 10% voting power.
optionD: Only with the Chairman's written permission.
answerText: No, proxies are not counted for quorum under Section 103.
explanation: Proxies are agents of members and are not counted for the purpose of establishing a quorum under Section 103 (only members personally present count).

subject: Law
prompt: How are representatives of corporate members treated for the purpose of quorum?
optionA: They are treated as proxies.
optionB: They are deemed to be members personally present under Section 113.
optionC: They cannot attend general meetings.
optionD: They count as half a member each.
answerText: They are deemed to be members personally present under Section 113.
explanation: Under Section 113, a corporate representative is deemed to be a member personally present and is counted for quorum.

subject: Law
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Radiant Power Limited issued a notice for its Extraordinary General Meeting (EGM) to be held on 15th November. The notice was dispatched on 22nd October through post. Certain institutional shareholders raised objections regarding the computation of clear days of notice and sought an explanation. Additionally, some members wished to vote through proxy.

subject: Law
prompt: How many 'clear days' notice was given by Radiant Power Limited if the notice was posted on 22nd October and the meeting is held on 15th November?
optionA: 24 clear days
optionB: 22 clear days
optionC: 21 clear days
optionD: 20 clear days
answerText: 24 clear days
explanation: Excluding the date of dispatch (22nd Oct), the 48-hour service rule (deemed service on 24th Oct), and the date of meeting (15th Nov), the clear days exceed 21 days (approx. 21+ days). Let's verify: Oct 22 dispatched, deemed served in 48 hours (Oct 24). Days remaining in Oct: Oct 25 to 31 (7 days). Days in Nov: Nov 1 to 14 (14 days). Total clear days = 7 + 14 = 21 clear days. Wait, 22nd dispatched + 2 days service = 24th Oct service. Oct 25 to 31 is 7 days, Nov 1 to 14 is 14 days = 21 clear days exactly.

subject: Law
prompt: Within how many hours before the meeting must a proxy form be deposited with Radiant Power Limited to be valid?
optionA: 24 hours
optionB: 48 hours
optionC: 72 hours
optionD: 12 hours
answerText: 48 hours
explanation: Section 105(4) requires that an instrument of proxy must be deposited with the company at least 48 hours before the meeting.

subject: Law
prompt: If a member appoints a proxy and personally attends the meeting, what is the status of the proxy?
optionA: The proxy takes precedence over the member.
optionB: The proxy is automatically revoked by the member's personal presence.
optionC: Both can vote independently.
optionD: The Chairman decides who will vote.
answerText: The proxy is automatically revoked by the member's personal presence.
explanation: When a member who has appointed a proxy personally attends the meeting and votes, the proxy's authority is impliedly revoked.

subject: Law
prompt: If the articles of Radiant Power Limited are silent, can a proxy speak at the EGM?
optionA: Yes, a proxy has full speaking rights.
optionB: No, a proxy does not have the right to speak at a general meeting.
optionC: Yes, on a poll.
optionD: Only with 75% shareholder approval.
answerText: No, a proxy does not have the right to speak at a general meeting.
explanation: Under Section 105, a proxy is only entitled to vote (on a poll) and does not have the right to speak at the meeting.

subject: Law
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: A group of equity shareholders holding 12% of the paid-up voting share capital of Apex Chemicals Limited submitted a valid requisition to the Board of Directors on 1st August to call an EGM for removing a director. The Board neither called the meeting within the statutory timeframe nor responded to the requisitionists. Consequently, the requisitionists proceeded to call the EGM themselves.

subject: Law
prompt: Within how many days from the date of deposit of the requisition was the Board required to proceed to call the EGM under Section 100?
optionA: 14 days
optionB: 21 days
optionC: 30 days
optionD: 45 days
answerText: 21 days
explanation: Under Section 100(4), if the Board does not within 21 days from the date of receipt of a valid requisition proceed to call a meeting, the requisitionists may call it.

subject: Law
prompt: Within what period must the requisitionists hold the EGM after calling it themselves?
optionA: Within 1 month
optionB: Within 2 months
optionC: Within 3 months
optionD: Within 6 months
answerText: Within 3 months
explanation: Section 100(4) specifies that a meeting called by the requisitionists must be held within 3 months from the date of the deposit of the requisition.

subject: Law
prompt: How are the expenses incurred by the requisitionists in calling and holding the EGM to be reimbursed by the company?
optionA: Apex Chemicals Limited cannot reimburse such expenses under any circumstances.
optionB: The company must reimburse the requisitionists and recover the amount from the default directors' fees/remuneration.
optionC: The Central Government bears the cost.
optionD: The requisitionists must bear the cost permanently.
answerText: The company must reimburse the requisitionists and recover the amount from the default directors' fees/remuneration.
explanation: Section 100(6) provides that any reasonable expenses incurred by the requisitionists shall be repaid by the company, and the company shall retain such sum from any fee or remuneration due to the directors who were in default.

subject: Law
prompt: What minimum voting threshold is required to pass an ordinary resolution for removing a director at such an EGM?
optionA: Simple majority (>50% of votes cast)
optionB: 3/4th majority (75% of votes cast)
optionC: Unanimous consent (100%)
optionD: Two-thirds majority
answerText: Simple majority (>50% of votes cast)
explanation: An ordinary resolution under Section 114 requires a simple majority (more than 50% of the votes cast in favour).

subject: Law
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: The Board of Directors of Innovate Tech Solutions Limited convened its general meeting. During the meeting, several resolutions were voted upon. The Chairman decided to conduct voting on a major resolution through a show of hands first. Dissatisfied with the outcome on the show of hands, a group of members demanded a poll. The company also maintains minutes of all meetings in electronic form.

subject: Law
prompt: Can a poll be demanded on any resolution under Section 109 after the result of the show of hands has been declared?
optionA: No, poll must be demanded before or on the declaration of the result of the show of hands.
optionB: Yes, up to 48 hours after the meeting.
optionC: Yes, if the Chairman permits.
optionD: Only for special resolutions.
answerText: No, poll must be demanded before or on the declaration of the result of the show of hands.
explanation: Section 109 states that the Chairman shall, on his own motion, and shall, if demanded by persons meeting the criteria before or on the declaration of the result on the show of hands, order a poll.

subject: Law
prompt: When must a poll ordered by the Chairman under Section 109 be taken?
optionA: Within 48 hours of the demand
optionB: Not later than 48 hours from the time when the poll was demanded
optionC: Exactly 7 days later
optionD: Within 30 days
answerText: Not later than 48 hours from the time when the poll was demanded
explanation: Under Section 109(1), a poll demanded on a question other than adjournment or appointment of Chairman shall be taken at such time, not being later than forty-eight hours from the time when the poll was demanded, as the Chairman directs.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the requirement under the Companies Act, 2013 regarding maintaining minutes in electronic form?
optionA: Electronic minutes are not recognized by law.
optionB: Minutes may be maintained in electronic form provided every page is digitally signed.
optionC: Minutes in electronic form must be maintained under the maintenance and security standards prescribed by rules.
optionD: Electronic minutes must be printed on paper within 24 hours.
answerText: Minutes in electronic form must be maintained under the maintenance and security standards prescribed by rules.
explanation: Section 118 permits minutes to be kept in electronic form, provided they are maintained with proper security, date, and time stamping as per prescribed rules.

subject: Law
prompt: If minutes of a general meeting are recorded and signed in accordance with Section 118, what is their evidentiary value?
optionA: They have no legal standing in court.
optionB: They are evidence of the proceedings recorded therein.
optionC: They are conclusive proof that cannot be challenged under any circumstances.
optionD: They require RoC attestation to be valid.
answerText: They are evidence of the proceedings recorded therein.
explanation: Section 118(7) states that minutes of meetings kept in accordance with the provisions shall be evidence of the proceedings recorded therein.

subject: Law
prompt: According to Section 123 of the Companies Act, 2013, out of which of the following funds can a company declare dividend for any financial year?
optionA: Free reserves of the company
optionB: Revaluation reserve created out of revaluation of assets
optionC: Unrealized gains arising from fair value accounting of financial instruments
optionD: Capital reserve created by forfeiture of shares
answerText: Free reserves of the company
explanation: Section 123(1) permits dividend to be declared or paid out of the profits of the company for that year arrived at after providing for depreciation, or out of the profits of any previous financial year(s) and remaining undistributed, or out of both, or out of free reserves. Reserves created out of revaluation and unrealized gains are explicitly excluded.
conceptTags: Section 123 | Sources of Dividend | Free Reserves

subject: Law
prompt: Before declaring any dividend for a financial year, what is the mandatory requirement regarding depreciation under Section 123?
optionA: Depreciation must be provided in accordance with Schedule II of the Companies Act, 2013
optionB: Depreciation can be ignored if the company has accumulated losses
optionC: Depreciation needs to be provided only if the Board of Directors passes a special resolution
optionD: Depreciation may be calculated as per Income Tax Act rates
answerText: Depreciation must be provided in accordance with Schedule II of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Section 123(1) explicitly mandates that dividend shall be declared or paid only after providing for depreciation in accordance with the provisions of Schedule II of the Companies Act, 2013.

subject: Law
prompt: Can a company transfer a higher percentage of its profits to reserves than what is statutorily required before declaring a dividend?
optionA: Yes, a company may, voluntarily, transfer such percentage of its profits to reserves as it may think fit before the declaration of any dividend.
optionB: No, the Act caps the voluntary transfer at a maximum of 5% of profits.
optionC: No, transfer to reserves is strictly prohibited under the new scheme unless approved by the Central Government.
optionD: Yes, but it requires prior approval of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) in all cases.
answerText: Yes, a company may, voluntarily, transfer such percentage of its profits to reserves as it may think fit before the declaration of any dividend.
explanation: As per the proviso to Section 123(1), a company may, before the declaration of any dividend in any financial year, transfer such percentage of its profits for that financial year as it may consider appropriate to the reserves of the company. Voluntary transfer is not restricted.

subject: Law
prompt: Within how many days from the date of declaration must the declared dividend be deposited in a scheduled bank in a separate account, as per Section 123?
optionA: Within 5 days
optionB: Within 7 days
optionC: Within 10 days
optionD: Within 30 days
answerText: Within 7 days
explanation: Section 123(4) requires that the amount of dividend, including interim dividend, shall be deposited in a scheduled bank in a separate account within 5 days from the date of declaration of such dividend. Wait, let me double check: Section 123(4) specifies 'within five days'. Ah, let me verify. Section 123(4) says 'within 5 days'. Let me adjust option B to option A or correct the answer. Section 123(4): 'The amount of the dividend, including interim dividend, shall be deposited in a scheduled bank in a separate account within five days from the date of declaration of such dividend.' So 5 days is correct.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the consequence under Section 127 if a company fails to pay the declared dividend within 30 days of declaration, provided the default is not due to any operation of law?
optionA: Every director of the company shall be punishable with imprisonment up to 2 years and fine, and the company shall pay simple interest at the rate of 18% per annum during the period such default continues.
optionB: Only a monetary penalty of Rs. 1 lakh is levied on the company with no officer liability.
optionC: The dividend stands automatically cancelled and reverts to the company's profit and loss account.
optionD: The company is wound up compulsorily by the National Company Law Tribunal.
answerText: Every director of the company shall be punishable with imprisonment up to 2 years and fine, and the company shall pay simple interest at the rate of 18% per annum during the period such default continues.
explanation: Section 127 prescribes penalties for failure to pay dividend within 30 days: every director who is knowingly a party to the default shall be punishable with imprisonment up to 2 years and with fine which shall not be less than Rs. 1,000 for every day during which default continues, and the company shall be liable to pay simple interest at 18% per annum during the period of default.

subject: Law
prompt: Under Rule 3 of the Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules, 2014, if adequate profits are not available in any financial year, dividend can be declared out of accumulated profits (reserves), subject to which of the following conditions?
optionA: The rate of dividend shall not exceed the average of the rates at which dividend was declared by it in the three years immediately preceding that year.
optionB: The rate of dividend shall not exceed 50% of the paid-up share capital.
optionC: Reserves drawn down shall be replenished within the next financial year mandatorily.
optionD: The company must distribute 100% of its accumulated reserves.
answerText: The rate of dividend shall not exceed the average of the rates at which dividend was declared by it in the three years immediately preceding that year.
explanation: Rule 3 of the Dividend Rules specifies that when profits are inadequate, the total amount to be drawn from accumulated profits shall not exceed 10% of the sum of its paid-up share capital and free reserves, and the rate of dividend declared shall not exceed the average of the rates at which dividend was declared in the 3 immediately preceding years.

subject: Law
prompt: As per Rule 3 of the Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules, 2014, what is the maximum percentage of paid-up capital and free reserves that can be drawn from accumulated profits when current profits are inadequate?
explanation: Rule 3(1)(iv) states that the total amount to be drawn from the accumulated profits earned in previous years and transferred to the reserves shall not exceed an amount equal to 10% of the sum of its paid-up share capital and free reserves as appearing in the latest audited financial statement.
conceptTags: Rule 3 | Drawal from Reserves | Percentage Limit

subject: Law
prompt: According to Rule 3, what is the mandatory pre-condition regarding past losses before drawing from accumulated reserves to declare a dividend in a year of inadequate profits?
optionA: The balance of reserves after such drawal shall first be utilized to set off any remaining past losses.
optionB: The current year's loss, if any, shall first be set off against the profit of the previous years before drawing from reserves.
optionC: Past losses must be carried forward and cannot be adjusted against accumulated reserves.
optionD: The company must write off all intangible assets before drawing from reserves.
answerText: The current year's loss, if any, shall first be set off against the profit of the previous years before drawing from reserves.
explanation: Rule 3(1) specifies that the company shall first utilize the profit of the current financial year for setting off against the loss, if any, incurred in the financial year before drawing from accumulated profits to declare a dividend.
conceptTags: Rule 3 | Set-off of Losses | Inadequate Profits

subject: Law
prompt: Where must an unpain or unclaimed dividend be transferred by a company after the expiry of 30 days from the date of declaration?
optionA: To a special unpaid dividend account opened in any scheduled bank within 7 days from the expiry of the 30 days.
optionB: Back to the general profit and loss account of the company.
optionC: To the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF) immediately on the 31st day.
optionD: To the Central Government treasury within 15 days.
answerText: To a special unpaid dividend account opened in any scheduled bank within 7 days from the expiry of the 30 days.
explanation: Section 124(1) mandates that if a dividend has been declared by a company but has not been paid or claimed within 30 days from the date of the declaration, the company shall, within 7 days from the date of expiry of the said 30 days, transfer the total amount of unpaid or unclaimed dividend to a special account to be opened in that behalf in any scheduled bank called the 'Unpaid Dividend Account'.

subject: Law
prompt: Within how many days of transferring an amount to the Unpaid Dividend Account must the company prepare a statement on its website containing details of such unpaid dividend, pursuant to Section 124?
optionA: Within 30 days
optionB: Within 60 days
optionC: Within 90 days
optionD: Within 120 days
answerText: Within 90 days
explanation: Section 124(2) states that the company shall, within a period of 90 days of making any transfer of an unpaid dividend amount to the Unpaid Dividend Account, prepare a statement containing the names, last known addresses, and the unpaid dividend to be paid to each person and place it on the website of the company.
conceptTags: Section 124 | Unpaid Dividend Statement | Website Disclosure

subject: Law
prompt: After a period of how many years from the date of transfer to the Unpaid Dividend Account must an unclaimed dividend be transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF)?
optionA: 3 years
optionB: 5 years
optionC: 7 years
optionD: 10 years
answerText: 7 years
explanation: Section 124(5) provides that any money transferred to the Unpaid Dividend Account of a company which remains unpaid or unclaimed for a period of 7 years from the date of such transfer shall be transferred by the company along with interest accrued thereon to the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF).

subject: Law
prompt: Which of the following shares along with their unpaid or unclaimed dividend are also required to be transferred to the IEPF authority under Section 124(6)?
optionA: Shares in respect of which dividend has not been paid or claimed for 7 consecutive years or more.
optionB: Shares held by promoters who have defaulted on statutory dues.
optionC: Shares on which calls are in arrears for more than 6 months.
optionD: All shares held by non-resident shareholders.
answerText: Shares in respect of which dividend has not been paid or claimed for 7 consecutive years or more.
explanation: Section 124(6) mandates that all shares in respect of which dividend has not been paid or claimed for 7 consecutive years or more shall be transferred by the company in the name of the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF) authority.
conceptTags: Section 124 | Transfer of Shares | IEPF Authority

subject: Law
prompt: Can a person whose shares and unclaimed dividends have been transferred to the IEPF claim back their shares and amounts subsequently?
optionA: No, the transfer to IEPF is absolute and final with no right of refund.
optionB: Yes, any person claiming to be entitled to any amount or shares transferred to the IEPF may apply to the IEPF Authority for claiming the same.
optionC: Yes, but only after obtaining a decree from a civil court.
optionD: No, only corporate bodies can claim refund from IEPF.
answerText: Yes, any person claiming to be entitled to any amount or shares transferred to the IEPF may apply to the IEPF Authority for claiming the same.
explanation: Section 124(6) proviso states that any person whose shares or unclaimed amounts are transferred to the IEPF may claim the same from the IEPF Authority by submitting an application in accordance with the prescribed rules.
conceptTags: Section 124 | Claim from IEPF | Refund Procedure

subject: Law
prompt: Under Section 123(3), who has the authority to declare an interim dividend during any financial year?
optionA: The Board of Directors of the company
optionB: The shareholders in the Annual General Meeting only
optionC: The Managing Director acting independently
optionD: The Audit Committee of the company
answerText: The Board of Directors of the company
explanation: Section 123(3) empowers the Board of Directors of a company to declare interim dividend during any financial year out of the surplus in the profit and loss account or out of profits of the financial year for which such interim dividend is sought to be declared.
conceptTags: Section 123 | Interim Dividend | Board of Directors

subject: Law
prompt: If a company has incurred a loss in the current financial year up to the end of the quarter preceding the date of declaration of an interim dividend, at what rate can the Board declare such interim dividend?
optionA: At a rate not exceeding the average dividend declared during the immediately preceding 3 financial years.
optionB: At a rate higher than the previous year to boost investor confidence.
optionC: At any rate decided by the Board provided free reserves cover the loss.
optionD: Interim dividend cannot be declared in any circumstance if there is a loss in the current financial year.
answerText: At a rate not exceeding the average dividend declared during the immediately preceding 3 financial years.
explanation: Section 123(3) proviso dictates that if the company has incurred loss up to the quarter preceding the date of interim dividend, the Board shall not declare interim dividend at a rate higher than the average dividends declared by the company during the immediately preceding three financial years.
conceptTags: Section 123 | Interim Dividend in Loss | Average Rate Limit

subject: Law
prompt: What is the statutory requirement regarding the separate bank account for interim dividend under Section 123(4)?
optionA: Interim dividend must also be deposited in a scheduled bank in a separate account within 5 days from the date of declaration.
optionB: Interim dividend can be disbursed directly from the working capital current account without a separate bank account.
optionC: A separate bank account is required only for final dividends, not for interim dividends.
optionD: Interim dividend must be deposited with the RBI within 24 hours.
answerText: Interim dividend must also be deposited in a scheduled bank in a separate account within 5 days from the date of declaration.
explanation: Section 123(4) explicitly includes interim dividend: 'The amount of the dividend, including interim dividend, shall be deposited in a scheduled bank in a separate account within five days from the date of declaration of such dividend.'

subject: Law
prompt: Under Section 123(5), how must any dividend (final or interim) be paid to the registered shareholders?
optionA: In cash or by cheque or warrant or in any electronic mode
optionB: Exclusively in cash against physical presentation of dividend coupons
optionC: Exclusively through bonus shares
optionD: By issuing promissory notes maturing in 90 days
answerText: In cash or by cheque or warrant or in any electronic mode
explanation: Section 123(5) provides that no dividend shall be paid by a company in respect of any share therein except to the registered shareholder of such share or to his order or to his banker and shall be paid in cash or by cheque or warrant or in any electronic mode.
conceptTags: Section 123 | Mode of Payment | Registered Shareholder

subject: Law
prompt: Which section of the Companies Act, 2013 prohibits the declaration of dividend if a company has failed to redeem its debentures or repay public deposits?
optionA: Section 123 read with general disqualifications, or specific financial defaults mentioned in public deposit rules
optionB: Section 127
optionC: Section 92
optionD: Section 134
answerText: Section 123 read with general disqualifications, or specific financial defaults mentioned in public deposit rules
explanation: While Section 123 deals with declaration, default in repayment of deposits or redemption of debentures restricts companies under specific rules (such as Rule 3 of Acceptance of Deposits Rules) from declaring dividends until the default is made good.
conceptTags: Section 123 | Defaults in Repayment | Public Deposits

subject: Law
prompt: Can a company revoke a declared dividend once it has been announced at a general meeting?
optionA: No, once declared, a dividend becomes a debt enforceable by shareholders and cannot be revoked without their consent.
optionB: Yes, the Board can revoke it anytime before payment if cash flow tightens.
optionC: Yes, with the permission of the Registrar of Companies (ROC).
optionD: Yes, by passing a board resolution within 7 days.
answerText: No, once declared, a dividend becomes a debt enforceable by shareholders and cannot be revoked without their consent.
explanation: Declaration of dividend creates a debt obligation towards shareholders. Once declared, it cannot be revoked unilaterally by the company or Board without the consent of the shareholders.
conceptTags: Declaration of Dividend | Revocation | Legal Debt

subject: Law
prompt: Under Section 127, if a dividend is declared but cannot be paid within 30 days because a dispute exists regarding the right to receive the dividend, what is the legal position?
optionA: It is not considered an offense under Section 127 if the failure is due to a dispute regarding the right to receive the dividend.
optionB: The company must still pay 18% interest while the dispute is pending.
optionC: The company must deposit the disputed amount with the NCLT immediately.
optionD: The directors are liable to imprisonment regardless of any dispute.
answerText: It is not considered an offense under Section 127 if the failure is due to a dispute regarding the right to receive the dividend.
explanation: Section 127 provides exceptions where failure to pay dividend within 30 days is not an offense, which includes cases where the dividend has been lawfully adjusted against sums due from the shareholder, or where the dispute regarding the right to receive the dividend has not been resolved.
conceptTags: Section 127 | Exceptions to Offense | Disputed Dividend

subject: Law
prompt: Which authority administers the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF) established under Section 125?
optionA: The IEPF Authority constituted by the Central Government
optionB: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
optionC: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
optionD: The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG)
answerText: The IEPF Authority constituted by the Central Government
explanation: Section 125(1) states that the Central Government shall establish a Fund to be called the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF), which shall be administered by an authority specified by the Central Government.

subject: Law
prompt: Which of the following amounts shall NOT be credited to the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF) under Section 125(2)?
optionA: The general reserves created voluntarily by the company out of current profits
optionB: The amount given by the Central Government by way of grants for being credited to the Fund
optionC: The unpaid dividend amount remaining in the Unpaid Dividend Account for 7 years
optionD: Interest or other income received out of investments made from the Fund
answerText: The general reserves created voluntarily by the company out of current profits
explanation: Section 125(2) lists items credited to IEPF (grants, unpaid dividends after 7 years, matured deposits, application money due for refund, interest, etc.). Voluntary general reserves of a company belong to shareholders/company and are not credited to IEPF.

subject: Law
prompt: What purpose is the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF) primarily utilized for under Section 125(3)?
optionA: Promotion of investor education, awareness and protection, and refund of unclaimed amounts
optionB: Providing bailout packages to sick industrial companies
optionC: Financing government infrastructure projects and highways
optionD: Paying salaries to the corporate staff of listed companies
answerText: Promotion of investor education, awareness and protection, and refund of unclaimed amounts
explanation: Section 125(3) specifies that the Fund shall be utilized for promotion of investor education, awareness and protection; distribution of any disgorged amount; reimbursement of legal expenses incurred in pursuing class action suits; and refund of unclaimed dividends, matured deposits, etc.
conceptTags: Section 125 | Utilization of IEPF | Investor Awareness

subject: Law
prompt: Can a company declare a dividend out of free reserves if it has incurred a net loss in the current financial year, without drawing from accumulated past profits?
optionA: Yes, provided it complies with the conditions specified in Rule 3 regarding drawal from reserves (such as rate limits and capital-reserve percentage caps).
optionB: No, free reserves can never be touched if current year has a loss.
optionC: Yes, with a unanimous board resolution and no other conditions.
optionD: No, only capital reserves can be used during current year losses.
answerText: Yes, provided it complies with the conditions specified in Rule 3 regarding drawal from reserves (such as rate limits and capital-reserve percentage caps).
explanation: When current profits are nil or inadequate, Rule 3 permits drawal from accumulated profits/free reserves subject to statutory limits (10% cap on paid-up capital + free reserves and 3-year average rate restriction).
conceptTags: Rule 3 | Free Reserves | Current Year Loss

subject: Law
prompt: In computing depreciation for the purpose of Section 123, which document's instructions must be adhered to by the company?
optionA: Schedule II of the Companies Act, 2013
optionB: Accounting Standard 10 (Property, Plant and Equipment)
optionC: The Memorandum of Association of the company
optionD: Guidelines issued by the stock exchanges
answerText: Schedule II of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Section 123(1) explicitly states that depreciation shall be provided in accordance with the provisions of Schedule II of the Companies Act, 2013.

subject: Law
prompt: Who is liable for the punishment of imprisonment under Section 127 in case of default in paying declared dividends?
optionA: Every director of the company who is knowingly a party to the default
optionB: All shareholders who voted in favor of the dividend resolution
optionC: The Chief Financial Officer (CFO) and Company Secretary only
optionD: Independent directors regardless of their knowledge
answerText: Every director of the company who is knowingly a party to the default
explanation: Section 127 clearly specifies that every director of the company who is knowingly a party to the default shall be punishable with imprisonment and fine.

subject: Law
prompt: If a company suffers a loss in the first quarter of the financial year, can the Board declare an interim dividend for the second quarter?
optionA: Yes, but the rate shall not exceed the average dividends declared during the immediately preceding 3 financial years.
optionB: No, interim dividend can never be declared if any quarter shows a loss.
optionC: Yes, at any rate the Board desires without restrictions.
optionD: Yes, but only if approved by shareholders via a special resolution.
answerText: Yes, but the rate shall not exceed the average dividends declared during the immediately preceding 3 financial years.
explanation: Under the proviso to Section 123(3), if the company has incurred loss up to the quarter preceding the date of declaration of interim dividend, the interim dividend rate cannot exceed the average of the rates of dividend declared in the immediately preceding 3 financial years.

subject: Law
prompt: What is the status of a dividend declared by a company when the company's net worth is negative due to accumulated losses, but it has free reserves?
optionA: Dividend cannot be declared if free reserves are non-existent or inadequate as per statutory rules, and net worth considerations under specific financial guidelines apply.
optionB: Free reserves can be freely distributed regardless of accumulated losses.
optionC: Negative net worth has no bearing on dividend declaration under Section 123.
optionD: The company must double its share capital before declaring any dividend.
answerText: Dividend cannot be declared if free reserves are non-existent or inadequate as per statutory rules, and net worth considerations under specific financial guidelines apply.
explanation: Dividend declaration is strictly governed by available profits and free reserves after providing for depreciation and setting off losses. If accumulated losses wipe out free reserves, no dividend can be declared except under strict Rule 3 parameters if applicable.

subject: Law
prompt: Which of the following is NOT an exception where failure to pay dividend within 30 days does not attract the penal consequences of Section 127?
optionA: The company is facing temporary liquidity crunch due to slow sales realization.
optionB: The dividend could not be paid by reason of the operation of law.
optionC: A shareholder has given valid directions regarding payment which cannot be complied with.
optionD: There is a dispute regarding the right to receive the dividend.
answerText: The company is facing temporary liquidity crunch due to slow sales realization.
explanation: Section 127 lists specific lawful excuses/exceptions: operation of law, shareholder's directions not being compliant, dispute regarding right to receive, lawful adjustment against sums due, or where director has not agreed to the default. A general liquidity crunch is not an exception and attracts full penalties.

subject: Law
prompt: In the context of the Companies Act, 2013, what constitutes 'Free Reserves' for the purpose of declaring dividend?
optionA: Reserves which, as per the latest audited balance sheet, are available for distribution as dividend.
optionB: All reserves including revaluation reserve and securities premium account.
optionC: Only capital redemption reserve and debenture redemption reserve.
optionD: Reserves created solely by writing up the value of fixed assets.
answerText: Reserves which, as per the latest audited balance sheet, are available for distribution as dividend.
explanation: Under Section 2(43), 'free reserves' means such reserves which, as per the latest audited balance sheet of a company, are available for distribution as dividend, excluding any amount representing unrealized gains, notional gains, revaluation reserves, etc.
conceptTags: Section 2(43) | Free Reserves Definition | Dividend Eligibility

subject: Law
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Aura Pharmaceuticals Limited earned a net profit of Rs. 50 Lakhs for the financial year 2025-26 after providing for depreciation as per Schedule II. The Board of Directors wishes to declare a final dividend of 12% on its paid-up equity share capital of Rs. 3 Crores. The company has free reserves amounting to Rs. 80 Lakhs.
