conceptTags: Indexed Cost of Construction | CII | Building

subject: Taxation
prompt:
CASE SCENARIO: Mr. Rajesh receives the following gifts during the previous year 2023-24:
1. Cash gift of Rs. 40,000 from his close friend on his birthday.
2. Cash gift of Rs. 75,000 from his sister on her wedding anniversary.
3. A gold ring valued at Rs. 60,000 from his maternal uncle on Diwali.
4. A plot of land received from a non-relative for a consideration of Rs. 3,00,000, while its stamp duty value is Rs. 4,00,000.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the taxability of the cash gift of Rs. 40,000 received from his friend?
optionA: Fully taxable under IFOS
optionB: Exempt because it is below Rs. 50,000
optionC: Exempt because it is from a friend
optionD: Taxable only to the extent it exceeds Rs. 25,000
answerText: Exempt because it is below Rs. 50,000
explanation: Under Section 56(2)(x), gifts from non-relatives (friends) in cash are taxable only if the aggregate value of such gifts during the previous year exceeds Rs. 50,000. Since this individual gift is Rs. 40,000, and assuming no other gifts from non-relatives, it is exempt.

subject: Taxation
prompt: How is the cash gift of Rs. 75,000 received from his sister treated under the Income-tax Act?
optionA: Taxable under IFOS as it exceeds Rs. 50,000
optionB: Exempt because sister falls within the definition of 'relative' under Section 56(2)(x)
optionC: Taxable only if received on the occasion of marriage
optionD: Exempt up to Rs. 1,00,000
answerText: Exempt because sister falls within the definition of 'relative' under Section 56(2)(x)
explanation: A sister is a 'relative' as defined under Section 56(2)(x). Any sum of money or property received from a relative is fully exempt from tax, regardless of the amount.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Is the gold ring valued at Rs. 60,000 received from his maternal uncle taxable?
optionA: Yes, because jewelry is a movable property and its value exceeds Rs. 50,000
optionB: No, because maternal uncle is included in the definition of 'relative'
optionC: Yes, because gifts from uncles are always taxable
optionD: No, because it is received on a festival
answerText: No, because maternal uncle is included in the definition of 'relative'
explanation: Under Section 56(2)(x), 'relative' includes brother or sister of either parent of the individual (which includes maternal uncle / mother's brother). Hence, any gift received from a maternal uncle is exempt.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the tax implication of the plot of land received from the non-relative for Rs. 3,00,000 (stamp duty value Rs. 4,00,000)?
optionA: Rs. 4,00,000 is taxable as IFOS
optionB: Rs. 1,00,000 is taxable as IFOS
optionC: Not taxable because the difference is less than Rs. 50,000 and 10% of stamp duty value
optionD: Rs. 3,00,000 is taxable as business income
answerText: Rs. 1,00,000 is taxable as IFOS
explanation: Under Section 56(2)(x), for immovable property received for inadequate consideration, if stamp duty value exceeds consideration by more than the higher of Rs. 50,000 and 10% of consideration (Rs. 30,000), the entire difference (Rs. 4,00,000 - Rs. 3,00,000 = Rs. 1,00,000) is taxable as IFOS.

subject: Taxation
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Mr. Suresh is a salaried employee. During the previous year, his minor son Master Amit earns interest income of Rs. 35,000 from a fixed deposit made out of a gift given by his grandfather. Furthermore, minor daughter Ms. Priya earns Rs. 20,000 by participating in a reality singing show (utilizing her special talent). Mr. Suresh's total income (excluding minor children's income) is Rs. 12,00,000, while Mrs. Suresh's total income is Rs. 14,00,000.

subject: Taxation
prompt: How is the income of minor daughter Ms. Priya (Rs. 20,000 from the reality show) treated for tax purposes?
optionA: Clubbed in the total income of Mr. Suresh
optionB: Clubbed in the total income of Mrs. Suresh
optionC: Taxable in the hands of Ms. Priya separately (not clubbed)
optionD: Fully exempt from income tax
answerText: Taxable in the hands of Ms. Priya separately (not clubbed)
explanation: Under the proviso to Section 64(1A), income of a minor child suffering from any disability specified under section 80U or income earned by a minor child from manual work or activity involving application of his/her skill, talent, or specialized knowledge is NOT clubbed with the parent's income. It is assessed in the hands of the minor.
conceptTags: Clubbing of Income | Minor Child | Special Talent

subject: Taxation
prompt: How is the interest income of Master Amit (Rs. 35,000) treated under the Income-tax Act?
optionA: Taxable in the hands of Master Amit
optionB: Clubbed in the total income of the parent whose total income is higher
optionC: Exempt under Section 10(32)
optionD: Clubbed only in the father's income
answerText: Clubbed in the total income of the parent whose total income is higher
explanation: Income of a minor child from investment is clubbed under Section 64(1A) in the total income of the parent whose total income (excluding minor's income) is higher (Mrs. Suresh, whose income is Rs. 14,00,000).
conceptTags: Clubbing of Income | Minor Child | Higher Income Parent

subject: Taxation
prompt: Is any exemption available under Section 10(32) in respect of the minor son's clubbed income?
optionA: No exemption is available
optionB: Exemption of Rs. 1,500 per minor child
optionC: Exemption of Rs. 35,000
optionD: Exemption of Rs. 10,000
answerText: Exemption of Rs. 1,500 per minor child
explanation: Section 10(32) provides an exemption of up to Rs. 1,500 per minor child in respect of income clubbed under Section 64(1A).

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the taxable amount of minor son Amit's income to be included in the parent's total income?
optionD: Nil
explanation: Master Amit's income is Rs. 35,000. Less exemption under Section 10(32) of Rs. 1,500 results in Rs. 33,500 to be clubbed in the total income of Mrs. Suresh.
conceptTags: Clubbing Computation | Section 10(32) | Net Clubbed Income

subject: Taxation
prompt: Under section 60 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, if a person transfers the income from any asset without transferring the asset itself, such income shall be included in the total income of:
optionA: The transferee
optionB: The transferor
optionC: Both jointly in the ratio of their taxable income
optionD: Neither; it is exempt from tax
answerText: The transferor
explanation: Section 60 deals with transfer of income without transfer of asset. It explicitly mandates that where a person transfers income from any asset without transferring the ownership of the asset, such income shall be included in the total income of the transferor.
conceptTags: Transfer of Income | Section 60 | Clubbing of Income

subject: Taxation
prompt: Mr. A revokes a revocable transfer of a house property after 4 years in favor of his son. The income from the property before revocation will be taxed in the hands of:
optionA: Mr. A
optionB: The son
optionC: Equally between Mr. A and the son
optionD: The HUF of Mr. A
answerText: Mr. A
explanation: Under section 61, all income arising to any person by virtue of a revocable transfer of assets is taxable in the hands of the transferor (Mr. A).

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following transfers is considered an 'irrevocable transfer' for the purposes of income inclusion under sections 61 to 63?
optionA: A transfer which contains any provision for the re-transfer of the asset to the transferor at any time.
optionB: A transfer which gives the transferor a right to reassume power over the asset.
optionC: A transfer which is not revocable during the lifetime of the transferee.
optionD: A transfer where the transferor can claim any income or asset back.
answerText: A transfer which is not revocable during the lifetime of the transferee.
explanation: Section 63 defines a revocable transfer as one containing any provision for re-transfer or right to reassume power. Conversely, a transfer not revocable during the lifetime of the beneficiary/transferee is treated as irrevocable (provided certain conditions are met).

subject: Taxation
prompt: As per section 64(1)(iv), when an individual transfers an asset (other than house property) to their spouse for inadequate consideration, the income from such asset is included in the total income of:
optionA: The spouse
optionB: The individual transferor
optionC: Both equally
optionD: The person who utilizes the asset
answerText: The individual transferor
explanation: Section 64(1)(iv) provides that income from assets transferred directly or indirectly to the spouse otherwise than for adequate consideration or in connection with an agreement to live apart is clubbed in the total income of the individual transferor.
conceptTags: Transfer to Spouse | Section 64(1)(iv) | Inadequate Consideration

subject: Taxation
prompt: Mr. X transfers 10,000 shares of a company to his wife Mrs. X as a gift. Mrs. X receives a dividend of Rs. 50,000. Mrs. X invests this dividend and earns interest of Rs. 5,000. How much amount will be clubbed in the income of Mr. X?
optionD: Nil
explanation: Under section 64(1)(iv), only the direct income from the transferred asset (dividend of Rs. 50,000) is clubbed. Income from accretion or reinvestment of such income (interest of Rs. 5,000) is not clubbed in the hands of the transferor.

subject: Taxation
prompt: If an individual transfers a house property to their spouse for inadequate consideration, who is deemed to be the owner of the house property for tax purposes under section 27, and how is the income taxed?
optionA: Spouse is owner; income is taxed in hands of spouse.
optionB: Transferor is deemed owner; income is taxed in hands of transferor under clubbing provisions.
optionC: Both are co-owners in 50:50 ratio.
optionD: The income is exempt under section 10.
answerText: Transferor is deemed owner; income is taxed in hands of transferor under clubbing provisions.
explanation: Section 27(i) deems the transferor to be the owner of house property transferred to a spouse for inadequate consideration. Consequently, the income is computed in the hands of the transferor and clubbed under section 64.
conceptTags: Deemed Owner | House Property | Section 27 | Section 64

subject: Taxation
prompt: Mr. B transfers cash to his son’s wife (daughter-in-law) for inadequate consideration. The income earned by the daughter-in-law from such cash will be clubbed in the total income of:
optionA: Mr. B
optionB: Mr. B’s son
optionC: The daughter-in-law herself
optionD: Mr. B’s HUF
answerText: Mr. B
explanation: Section 64(1)(vi) states that income from assets transferred directly or indirectly to a daughter-in-law otherwise than for adequate consideration is included in the total income of the transferor (Mr. B).

subject: Taxation
prompt: Mr. C transfers securities to a trust, and the income from the trust is applied for the immediate benefit of his son’s wife for inadequate consideration. Such income shall be clubbed with the income of:
optionA: The trust
optionB: Mr. C
optionC: The son
optionD: The son's wife
answerText: Mr. C
explanation: Under section 64(1)(viii), income arising directly or indirectly from assets transferred directly or indirectly to any person or association of persons for the immediate or deferred benefit of the transferor's son's wife, otherwise than for adequate consideration, is clubbed in the hands of the transferor.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following incomes of a minor child is NOT included in the total income of the parent under section 64(1A)?
optionA: Income earned from manual work.
optionB: Income earned from fixed deposits made out of gift from grandfather.
optionC: Interest income from a savings bank account opened with gift money from mother.
optionD: Capital gains arising from sale of shares gifted by father.
answerText: Income earned from manual work.
explanation: Section 64(1A) excludes income earned by a minor child from any manual work or from any activity involving application of their specialized skill, talent, or specialized knowledge and experience.

subject: Taxation
prompt: If both parents are alive, in whose total income shall the income of a minor child be included under section 64(1A)?
optionA: Always the mother
optionB: Always the father
optionC: The parent whose total income (excluding the minor's income) is higher
optionD: Equally divided between both parents
answerText: The parent whose total income (excluding the minor's income) is higher
explanation: Section 64(1A) prescribes that the income of a minor child shall be included in the total income of the parent whose total income (excluding the minor's income) is higher.
conceptTags: Minor Child | Higher Income Parent | Section 64(1A)

subject: Taxation
prompt: Once the income of a minor child is clubbed in the total income of a parent, what exemption is available to the parent under section 10(32)?
optionA: Full exemption of the minor's income
optionB: Exemption up to Rs. 1,500 per minor child
optionC: Exemption up to Rs. 5,000 per minor child
optionD: No exemption is available
answerText: Exemption up to Rs. 1,500 per minor child
explanation: Section 10(32) provides an exemption of up to Rs. 1,500 per minor child whose income is clubbed under section 64(1A), or the actual income clubbed, whichever is less.

subject: Taxation
prompt: How is the income of a minor child who suffers from any disability specified under section 80U treated for clubbing purposes?
optionA: It is clubbed in the parent's income as normal.
optionB: It is completely exempt from tax under section 10.
optionC: It is assessed directly in the hands of the minor child and is not clubbed in the parent's income.
optionD: It is taxed at a flat rate of 10% in the hands of the guardian.
answerText: It is assessed directly in the hands of the minor child and is not clubbed in the parent's income.
explanation: As per the proviso to section 64(1A), the income of a minor child suffering from any disability of the nature specified in section 80U shall not be clubbed in the income of the parent, but shall be taxable in the hands of the minor child.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Mr. D is a partner in a firm. His wife is employed in the same firm without any professional qualifications, and she draws a salary of Rs. 6,00,000. How will this salary be taxed?
optionA: Taxed entirely in the hands of the wife.
optionB: Included in the total income of Mr. D because he has a substantial interest in the firm.
optionC: Divided equally between Mr. D and his wife.
optionD: Disallowed as an expense to the firm and tax-free for the wife.
answerText: Included in the total income of Mr. D because he has a substantial interest in the firm.
explanation: Under section 64(1)(ii), if a spouse of an individual having a substantial interest in a concern receives salary, commission, etc., from that concern without possessing technical or professional qualifications, such income is clubbed in the total income of the individual.

subject: Taxation
prompt: For the purpose of section 64(1)(ii) relating to remuneration of a spouse, what constitutes a 'substantial interest' in a company?
optionA: Beneficial ownership of shares carrying at least 10% of the voting power at any time during the previous year.
optionB: Beneficial ownership of shares carrying at least 20% of the voting power at any time during the previous year.
optionC: Ownership of at least 50% of the equity shares.
optionD: Holding a managerial position with 5% voting power.
answerText: Beneficial ownership of shares carrying at least 10% of the voting power at any time during the previous year.
explanation: Section 64(2) Explanation defines 'substantial interest' as holding (beneficially) shares carrying not less than 10% voting power at any time during the previous year.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Both Mr. X and his wife Mrs. X have substantial interest in M/s ABC Enterprises. Mrs. X is employed in the firm without professional qualifications and receives salary. In whose hands will this salary be clubbed?
optionA: In the hands of Mrs. X herself.
optionB: In the hands of Mr. X.
optionC: In the hands of the parent whose total income is higher.
optionD: Equally in the hands of both Mr. X and Mrs. X.
answerText: In the hands of the parent whose total income is higher.
explanation: Where both husband and wife have substantial interest in a concern and receive remuneration without technical/professional qualifications, the income is included in the total income of the spouse whose total income (excluding such remuneration) is higher.
conceptTags: Both Spouses Substantial Interest | Section 64(1)(ii) | Higher Income

subject: Taxation
prompt: If an individual converts their self-acquired property into property of a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) without adequate consideration, how is the income from such property treated?
optionA: Taxed solely in the hands of the individual.
optionB: Taxed in the hands of the HUF.
optionC: Deemed to be income of the individual and clubbed in their total income under section 64(2).
optionD: Exempt from tax.
answerText: Deemed to be income of the individual and clubbed in their total income under section 64(2).
explanation: Under section 64(2), if a member of an HUF converts or transfers their separate property into HUF property without adequate consideration, the income derived from such property is deemed to be the income of the individual member, not the HUF.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Subsequent to the partition of an HUF where property converted under section 64(2) was distributed, how is the income derived by the spouse of the individual from such distributed property taxed?
optionA: Taxed in the hands of the spouse.
optionB: Deemed to be the income of the individual member and clubbed under section 64(2).
optionC: Exempt from taxation.
optionD: Taxed in the hands of the HUF.
answerText: Deemed to be the income of the individual member and clubbed under section 64(2).
explanation: Section 64(2) specifies that where the converted property is partitioned (total or partial), the income derived by the spouse of the individual from the portion received on partition is deemed to arise to the individual and is clubbed in their total income.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Can cross-transfers of assets (e.g., Mr. A gifts to Mrs. B and Mr. B gifts to Mrs. A) be arranged to avoid clubbing provisions under section 64?
optionA: Yes, clubbing provisions apply only to direct transfers.
optionB: No, the Supreme Court held that in case of cross-transfers, the transferors will be treated as indirect transferors and income will be clubbed.
optionC: Yes, provided the gifts are of equal value.
optionD: No, but only if the gifts are made in different financial years.
answerText: No, the Supreme Court held that in case of cross-transfers, the transferors will be treated as indirect transferors and income will be clubbed.
explanation: Under the doctrine of cross-transfers (established by judicial precedents like CIT v. Keshavji Morarji), if transfers are interconnected and form part of a single transaction, the indirect transferor concept applies, and income is clubbed in the respective spouse's hands.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Mr. P gifted Rs. 5,00,000 to his minor daughter. The daughter deposited the amount in a bank earning 8% interest per annum. The interest is clubbed with Mr. P’s income. Next year, the daughter becomes a major. Will the interest earned post-majority be clubbed?
optionA: Yes, because the initial asset was gifted by the father.
optionB: No, clubbing of minor's income ceases once the child attains majority.
optionC: Yes, until the daughter withdraws the principal.
optionD: No, but only if the daughter files a separate return.
answerText: No, clubbing of minor's income ceases once the child attains majority.
explanation: Clubbing under section 64(1A) applies strictly during minority. Once the child attains majority, any income earned thereafter is assessed directly in the hands of the child and is not clubbed with the parent's income.
conceptTags: Minor to Major | Section 64(1A) | Cessation of Clubbing

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following is correct regarding the computation of total income when clubbing provisions apply?
optionA: The income to be clubbed is computed after allowing all deductions and losses pertaining to that income.
optionB: Gross income is clubbed without deducting any expenses.
optionC: Only net profit without any deductions is clubbed.
optionD: Clubbing applies only to capital gains and not to other heads of income.
answerText: The income to be clubbed is computed after allowing all deductions and losses pertaining to that income.
explanation: When income is clubbed under sections 60 to 64, it is computed in accordance with the provisions of the Act, meaning all permissible deductions, expenses, and losses relating to that specific income are accounted for before clubbing the net amount.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Mr. E transfers his house property to his minor son for inadequate consideration. The property is let out. Under whose income tax return will the rental income be computed and clubbed?
optionA: The minor son
optionB: The father (Mr. E) as deemed owner under section 27 and clubbing under section 64(1A)
optionC: The mother
optionD: Exempt under section 10
answerText: The father (Mr. E) as deemed owner under section 27 and clubbing under section 64(1A)
explanation: Mr. E is the deemed owner under section 27(i) due to transfer to a minor child for inadequate consideration. Further, minor's income is clubbed with the parent under section 64(1A). Thus, the rental income (computed under House Property) is included in the father's total income.
conceptTags: Deemed Owner | Minor | House Property | Clubbing

subject: Taxation
prompt: Can a loss under a particular head of income earned by a minor child be clubbed with the income of the parent?
optionA: No, losses of a minor can never be clubbed.
optionB: Yes, losses can be clubbed and set off against the parent's income subject to normal set-off rules.
optionC: Only capital losses can be clubbed, not business losses.
optionD: Losses are carried forward only by the minor upon attaining majority.
answerText: Yes, losses can be clubbed and set off against the parent's income subject to normal set-off rules.
explanation: Just as income of a minor is clubbed, any loss incurred by the minor (e.g., under capital gains or business) is also clubbed with the parent's income and can be set off against the parent's income as per normal provisions of the Act.

subject: Taxation
prompt: An individual transfers shares to his spouse pursuant to an agreement to live apart (divorce/separation agreement). Is the dividend income from such shares clubbed in the hands of the individual?
optionA: Yes, because the transfer was to the spouse.
optionB: No, transfers in connection with an agreement to live apart are specifically excluded from clubbing under section 64(1)(iv).
optionC: Yes, unless judicial separation is finalized.
optionD: No, but only if the transfer is for adequate consideration.
answerText: No, transfers in connection with an agreement to live apart are specifically excluded from clubbing under section 64(1)(iv).
explanation: Section 64(1)(iv) contains an explicit exception: income from assets transferred to a spouse in connection with an agreement to live apart is not clubbed in the transferor's hands.
conceptTags: Agreement to Live Apart | Section 64(1)(iv) | Exception

subject: Taxation
prompt: Mr. F gifted Rs. 2,00,000 to his sister-in-law (wife's sister). The sister-in-law invested in shares and earned dividend income. How is this dividend income taxed?
optionA: Clubbed in the income of Mr. F.
optionB: Clubbed in the income of Mr. F's wife.
optionC: Taxed in the hands of the sister-in-law; no clubbing applies.
optionD: Exempt from tax.
answerText: Taxed in the hands of the sister-in-law; no clubbing applies.
explanation: Clubbing provisions under section 64 apply only to transfers to spouse, minor child, son's wife, or specified trust beneficiaries. A sister-in-law is not covered under section 64, so the income is taxed in her own hands.

subject: Taxation
prompt: If an asset is transferred for adequate consideration, do the clubbing provisions under section 64 apply?
optionA: Yes, always.
optionB: No, clubbing provisions apply strictly to transfers made otherwise than for adequate consideration (except in specific cases like section 60).
optionC: Yes, if the transfer is between relatives.
optionD: No, unless approved by the Assessing Officer.
answerText: No, clubbing provisions apply strictly to transfers made otherwise than for adequate consideration (except in specific cases like section 60).
explanation: Most clauses of section 64 (such as transfers to spouse, daughter-in-law) apply only when the transfer is made 'otherwise than for adequate consideration'. If adequate consideration is paid, clubbing does not apply.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following describes the nature of tax liability when income is clubbed under section 64?
optionA: The recipient of income pays the tax.
optionB: The assessee in whose total income the income is clubbed is liable to pay tax on such clubbed income.
optionC: Tax is paid jointly by the transferor and transferee.
optionD: The income is taxed at a flat rate of 30%.
answerText: The assessee in whose total income the income is clubbed is liable to pay tax on such clubbed income.
explanation: When income is clubbed, it is included in the total income of the assessee (parent/transferor) and forms part of their total taxable income, making them liable to pay tax thereon according to their applicable slab rates.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Mr. G gifted a commercial building to his major son. The rental income from the building is received by the son. How is this income assessed?
optionA: Clubbed in the total income of Mr. G.
optionB: Assessed directly in the hands of the major son.
optionC: Divided equally between father and son.
optionD: Taxed in the hands of Mr. G's HUF.
answerText: Assessed directly in the hands of the major son.
explanation: Clubbing provisions for gifts to children apply exclusively to minor children under section 64(1A). Gifts to major children are not clubbed; the major son is taxed directly on the rental income.
conceptTags: Major Child | Gift | Exclusion from Clubbing

subject: Taxation
prompt: Under section 64(1)(iv), if an asset is transferred to a spouse for inadequate consideration, and the spouse subsequently sells the asset at a capital gain, how is the capital gain treated?
optionA: The capital gain is taxable in the hands of the spouse.
optionB: The capital gain is clubbed in the total income of the transferor spouse.
optionC: Exempt from capital gains tax.
optionD: Shared equally between husband and wife.
answerText: The capital gain is clubbed in the total income of the transferor spouse.
explanation: Capital gains arising from the sale of an asset transferred to a spouse for inadequate consideration are also clubbed in the total income of the transferor spouse under section 64(1)(iv).
conceptTags: Capital Gains | Section 64(1)(iv) | Transfer to Spouse

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the primary objective of enacting the clubbing of income provisions (Sections 60 to 64) under the Income-tax Act, 1961?
optionA: To increase government revenue through double taxation.
optionB: To prevent tax avoidance and tax evasion through splitting of income among family members.
optionC: To simplify the filing of tax returns for HUFs.
optionD: To encourage gifts within families.
answerText: To prevent tax avoidance and tax evasion through splitting of income among family members.
explanation: Clubbing provisions are anti-tax-avoidance measures designed to curb the practice of taxpayers reducing their tax burden by transferring income or assets to family members (spouse, minor children) in lower tax brackets.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Mr. H settles an irrevocable trust where the income is accumulated for the benefit of his minor daughter, to be handed over to her when she turns 25. When is this accumulated income taxed?
optionA: Taxed in the hands of the trust when accumulated.
optionB: Clubbed in the total income of Mr. H in the year it arises.
optionC: Taxed when the daughter turns 25.
optionD: Exempt until distribution.
answerText: Clubbed in the total income of Mr. H in the year it arises.
explanation: Even if income is accumulated or deferred for the minor child's future benefit under a trust or otherwise, section 64(1A) requires it to be clubbed in the income of the parent in the year the income arises.
conceptTags: Deferred Income | Trust | Minor Child | Section 64(1A)

subject: Taxation
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Mr. Rajesh, a resident individual, owns a bungalow and 5,000 shares in X Ltd. On 1st May 2025, he transfers the bungalow to his wife, Mrs. Priya, without adequate consideration. Priya lets out the bungalow for a monthly rent of Rs. 40,000. On 1st June 2025, Rajesh gifts 2,000 shares of X Ltd. to his minor daughter, Riya. Riya receives a dividend of Rs. 20,000 from X Ltd. during the previous year 2025-26. Riya also earns Rs. 15,000 from participating in a national-level dance reality show based on her specialized dancing skills. Rajesh's total income before clubbing is Rs. 12,00,000, while Priya's total income before clubbing is Rs. 5,00,000.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Who is deemed to be the owner of the bungalow transferred by Mr. Rajesh to Mrs. Priya under the Income-tax Act, 1961?
optionA: Mrs. Priya
optionB: Mr. Rajesh
optionC: Both Rajesh and Priya as co-owners
optionD: The tenant occupying the bungalow
answerText: Mr. Rajesh
explanation: As per section 27(i), an individual who transfers a house property to their spouse otherwise than for adequate consideration is deemed to be the owner of the house property.

subject: Taxation
prompt: How will the rental income from the bungalow be computed and taxed for the previous year 2025-26?
optionA: Taxed in the hands of Mrs. Priya after standard deduction.
optionB: Computed in the hands of Mr. Rajesh as deemed owner and clubbed under section 64.
optionC: Divided equally between Rajesh and Priya.
optionD: Exempt from tax under section 10.
answerText: Computed in the hands of Mr. Rajesh as deemed owner and clubbed under section 64.
explanation: Since Mr. Rajesh is the deemed owner under section 27, the income from house property is computed in his hands and included in his total income.
conceptTags: House Property Computation | Clubbing | Deemed Owner

subject: Taxation
prompt: How will the dividend income of Rs. 20,000 received by minor daughter Riya be treated for tax purposes?
optionA: Taxed directly in Riya's hands.
optionB: Clubbed in the total income of Mrs. Priya since Priya's income is lower.
optionC: Clubbed in the total income of Mr. Rajesh since Rajesh's total income is higher.
optionD: Exempt up to Rs. 20,000.
answerText: Clubbed in the total income of Mr. Rajesh since Rajesh's total income is higher.
explanation: Minor child's income is clubbed in the income of the parent whose total income is higher. Rajesh's income (Rs. 12L) is higher than Priya's (Rs. 5L), so the dividend is clubbed with Rajesh's income, eligible for section 10(32) exemption.
conceptTags: Minor Income | Higher Income Parent | Section 10(32)

subject: Taxation
prompt: How will the income of Rs. 15,000 earned by Riya from the dance reality show be taxed?
optionA: Clubbed in Mr. Rajesh's total income.
optionB: Clubbed in Mrs. Priya's total income.
optionC: Taxed directly in the hands of minor Riya and not clubbed.
optionD: Exempt from income tax entirely.
answerText: Taxed directly in the hands of minor Riya and not clubbed.
explanation: Income earned by a minor child from an activity involving the application of specialized skills or talent (like dance reality show) is exempt from clubbing under section 64(1A) and is taxed directly in the minor's hands.

subject: Taxation
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Mr. Vikram holds a 15% equity stake (substantial interest) in Apex Ltd. His wife, Mrs. Sunita, is appointed as a receptionist in Apex Ltd. with a monthly salary of Rs. 50,000. Sunita does not possess any professional or technical qualifications relevant to the job. Additionally, Vikram gifts Rs. 3,00,000 in cash to his son’s wife, Anita, on 10th August 2025. Anita invests this cash in fixed deposits earning an interest of Rs. 24,000 during the financial year 2025-26. Vikram’s total income before clubbing is Rs. 15,00,000 and Sunita's total income before salary is Rs. 4,00,000.

subject: Taxation
prompt: How will the salary received by Mrs. Sunita from Apex Ltd. be taxed for the previous year 2025-26?
optionA: Taxed in the hands of Mrs. Sunita under salaries.
optionB: Clubbed in the total income of Mr. Vikram under section 64(1)(ii).
optionC: Disallowed as company expenditure and tax-free for Sunita.
optionD: Divided equally between Vikram and Sunita.
answerText: Clubbed in the total income of Mr. Vikram under section 64(1)(ii).
explanation: Since Mr. Vikram has a substantial interest in Apex Ltd. (15% voting power) and Sunita receives remuneration without possessing technical or professional qualifications, the salary is clubbed in Vikram's total income under section 64(1)(ii).

subject: Taxation
prompt: How will the interest income of Rs. 24,000 earned by daughter-in-law Anita be treated under the Income-tax Act?
optionA: Taxed in the hands of Anita.
optionB: Clubbed in the total income of Mr. Vikram.
optionC: Clubbed in the total income of Vikram's son.
optionD: Exempt under section 10(15).
answerText: Clubbed in the total income of Mr. Vikram.
explanation: Section 64(1)(vi) mandates that income from assets transferred to a daughter-in-law otherwise than for adequate consideration is clubbed in the total income of the transferor (Mr. Vikram).

subject: Taxation
prompt: What would be the tax treatment of Sunita's salary if she possessed a recognized professional degree and was employed based on her professional qualifications?
optionA: It would still be clubbed in Mr. Vikram's income.
optionB: It would be taxable directly in the hands of Mrs. Sunita and NOT clubbed.
optionC: It would be taxed in the hands of Apex Ltd.
optionD: It would be exempt from income tax.
answerText: It would be taxable directly in the hands of Mrs. Sunita and NOT clubbed.
explanation: The clubbing provision under section 64(1)(ii) does not apply if the spouse possesses technical or professional qualifications and the income is solely attributable to the application of such qualifications.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Suppose Anita reinvests the interest of Rs. 24,000 earned from the fixed deposit into mutual funds and earns a further return of Rs. 3,000. What amount is clubbed in Mr. Vikram's hands with respect to Anita?
optionD: Nil
explanation: Only the direct income from the transferred asset (interest of Rs. 24,000) is clubbed. Income from the accretion or reinvestment of such income (Rs. 3,000) is not clubbed.
conceptTags: Accretion of Income | Daughter-in-law | Clubbing Limit

subject: Taxation
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Mr. Kuber, an individual, converts his self-acquired commercial property worth Rs. 50,00,000 into the property of his Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) on 1st July 2025 without receiving any consideration. The HUF lets out this property and earns a rental income of Rs. 3,00,000 during the financial year 2025-26. On 1st January 2026, a total partition of the HUF takes place, and the commercial property is distributed equally among Kuber, his wife, and his major son.

subject: Taxation
prompt: How is the rental income of Rs. 3,00,000 earned by the HUF up to the date of partition taxed?
optionA: Taxed in the hands of the HUF.
optionB: Deemed to be the income of Mr. Kuber and clubbed in his total income under section 64(2).
optionC: Divided among all family members equally.
optionD: Exempt from tax.
answerText: Deemed to be the income of Mr. Kuber and clubbed in his total income under section 64(2).
explanation: Under section 64(2), when an individual converts their separate property into HUF property without adequate consideration, the income derived from such property is deemed to be the income of the individual member (Mr. Kuber), not the HUF.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Following the total partition on 1st January 2026, how will the rental income attributable to the share received by Mr. Kuber's wife be taxed?
optionA: Taxed in the hands of the wife.
optionB: Deemed to be the income of Mr. Kuber and included in his total income.
optionC: Taxed in the hands of the HUF post-partition.
optionD: Exempt from tax.
answerText: Deemed to be the income of Mr. Kuber and included in his total income.
explanation: Section 64(2) specifically provides that upon partition of an HUF, income derived by the spouse of the individual from the converted property received on partition is deemed to arise to the individual and is clubbed in their total income.

subject: Taxation
prompt: How will the rental income attributable to the share received by the major son upon partition be taxed?
optionA: Clubbed in Mr. Kuber's total income.
optionB: Taxed directly in the hands of the major son.
optionC: Taxed in the hands of the HUF.
optionD: Exempt from tax.
answerText: Taxed directly in the hands of the major son.
explanation: Section 64(2) clubbing on partition applies to the portion received by the spouse of the individual, not to the portion received by children (especially major children). Thus, the major son is taxed directly on his share.
conceptTags: Major Son | HUF Partition | Tax Assessment

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the legal fiction created under section 64(2) when a member converts separate property into HUF property?
optionA: The property is treated as sold, attracting capital gains.
optionB: The property is treated as remaining the individual property of the member for income-tax assessment of its yield.
optionC: The HUF is treated as a corporate entity.
optionD: The income is treated as agricultural income.
answerText: The property is treated as remaining the individual property of the member for income-tax assessment of its yield.
explanation: Section 64(2) creates a statutory fiction whereby income from property converted by a member to HUF property without adequate consideration is treated as income of the individual member rather than the HUF.

subject: Taxation
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Mr. and Mrs. Sharma have a minor son, Master Kunal, aged 10 years. Mr. Sharma's total income before any clubbing is Rs. 18,00,000, and Mrs. Sharma's total income before any clubbing is Rs. 22,00,000. Mr. Sharma gifts Rs. 10,00,000 to Kunal out of his personal savings. Kunal deposits this money in a corporate fixed deposit on 1st April 2025 at an interest rate of 10% per annum, earning Rs. 1,00,000 as interest during the financial year 2025-26. Additionally, Kunal wins a prize of Rs. 50,000 in a state-level chess championship.

subject: Taxation
prompt: In whose total income shall the interest income of Rs. 1,00,000 earned by minor Kunal be included?
optionA: Mr. Sharma, being the donor of the asset.
optionB: Mrs. Sharma, because her total income is higher than Mr. Sharma's.
optionC: Master Kunal, in his individual return.
optionD: Divided equally between Mr. and Mrs. Sharma.
answerText: Mrs. Sharma, because her total income is higher than Mr. Sharma's.
explanation: Section 64(1A) mandates that the income of a minor child is included in the total income of the parent whose total income (excluding the minor's income) is higher. Since Mrs. Sharma's income (Rs. 22L) exceeds Mr. Sharma's (Rs. 18L), it is clubbed with Mrs. Sharma.
conceptTags: Minor Income | Higher Income Parent | Section 64(1A)

subject: Taxation
prompt: What amount of exemption under section 10(32) is available against the clubbed interest income of Rs. 1,00,000?
optionD: Nil
explanation: Section 10(32) grants an exemption of up to Rs. 1,500 per minor child whose income is clubbed under section 64(1A), or the actual income clubbed, whichever is less.

subject: Taxation
prompt: How will the prize of Rs. 50,000 won by Kunal in the chess championship be taxed?
optionA: Clubbed in Mrs. Sharma's total income.
optionB: Clubbed in Mr. Sharma's total income.
optionC: Assessed directly in the hands of minor Kunal and not clubbed.
optionD: Exempt from tax under section 10.
answerText: Assessed directly in the hands of minor Kunal and not clubbed.
explanation: Income earned by a minor child from any activity involving application of specialized skill, talent, or specialized knowledge (such as competitive chess) is excluded from clubbing under section 64(1A) and taxed in the minor's hands.
conceptTags: Talent Exception | Minor Child | Chess Prize

subject: Taxation
prompt: If Master Kunal had a physical disability of the nature specified under section 80U, how would his total income be treated?
optionA: Clubbed with the higher-earning parent after 80U deduction.
optionB: Assessed entirely in the hands of Master Kunal without clubbing.
optionC: Split between the parents equally.
optionD: Exempt from all income taxes.
answerText: Assessed entirely in the hands of Master Kunal without clubbing.
explanation: The proviso to section 64(1A) explicitly states that the income of a minor child suffering from any disability specified under section 80U shall not be clubbed in the parent's income and is taxed directly in the hands of the minor.

subject: Taxation
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Mr. Rohan and Mr. Sohan are brothers-in-law. On 1st June 2025, Mr. Rohan gifts Rs. 5,00,000 to Mr. Sohan’s wife, Mrs. Meena. Simultaneously, on the same date, Mr. Sohan gifts Rs. 5,00,000 to Mr. Rohan’s wife, Mrs. Shweta. Mrs. Meena invests the gifted amount in debentures earning interest of Rs. 60,000 during the previous year 2025-26. Mrs. Shweta also invests her gifted amount in shares earning dividend income of Rs. 60,000 during the same period.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What legal principle governs the taxability of income earned by Mrs. Meena and Mrs. Shweta in this scenario?
optionA: The doctrine of independent gifts.
optionB: The doctrine of cross-transfers (indirect transfers).
optionC: The principle of mutual benefit trusts.
optionD: The rule of corporate tax avoidance.
answerText: The doctrine of cross-transfers (indirect transfers).
explanation: This is a classic case of cross-transfers where interconnected gifts are made to each other's spouses to bypass direct clubbing provisions. The courts treat the transferors as indirect transferors.

subject: Taxation
prompt: In whose total income will the interest income of Rs. 60,000 earned by Mrs. Meena be clubbed?
optionA: Mr. Sohan, her husband.
optionB: Mr. Rohan, the actual indirect transferor.
optionC: Mrs. Meena herself.
optionD: Equally between Rohan and Sohan.
answerText: Mr. Rohan, the actual indirect transferor.
explanation: Due to the cross-transfer arrangement, Mr. Rohan is considered the indirect transferor of the assets held by Mrs. Meena. Hence, the income is clubbed in Mr. Rohan's total income under section 64(1)(iv).

subject: Taxation
prompt: In whose total income will the dividend income of Rs. 60,000 earned by Mrs. Shweta be clubbed?
optionA: Mr. Rohan, her husband.
optionB: Mr. Sohan, the indirect transferor.
optionC: Mrs. Shweta herself.
optionD: Exempt from tax.
answerText: Mr. Sohan, the indirect transferor.
explanation: Applying the cross-transfer rule, Mr. Sohan is treated as the indirect transferor of the assets held by Mrs. Shweta, and consequently, the dividend income is clubbed in Mr. Sohan's total income.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Would the clubbing apply if the gifts made by Rohan and Sohan were made in different financial years with no connection or prior agreement between them?
optionA: Yes, cross-transfer applies regardless of timing.
optionB: No, if the transfers are independent, genuine, and not part of an interconnected arrangement or quid pro quo, cross-transfers do not apply.
optionC: Yes, because both are related parties.
optionD: No, gifts between brothers-in-law are always exempt.
answerText: No, if the transfers are independent, genuine, and not part of an interconnected arrangement or quid pro quo, cross-transfers do not apply.
explanation: Judicial rulings establish that cross-transfers apply only when the transfers are inter-dependent and form part of a synchronized arrangement. If they are independent and lack a quid pro quo, direct clubbing rules apply only to direct spouse transfers.
conceptTags: Independent Transfers | Cross-Transfer Limits | Case Law

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following losses cannot be set off against any other head of income in the same assessment year under the Income-tax Act, 1961?
optionA: Business loss of a specified business referred to in section 35AD
optionB: Loss from house property
optionC: Loss from a speculative business
optionD: Loss from an ordinary non-speculative business
answerText: Business loss of a specified business referred to in section 35AD
explanation: As per section 73A, any loss computed in respect of any specified business referred to in section 35AD can be set off only against profits and gains, if any, of any other specified business. It cannot be set off against income under any other head.
conceptTags: Set-off of losses | Specified business | Section 35AD

subject: Taxation
prompt: Under section 70, inter-source adjustment is generally permissible. Which of the following inter-source adjustments is NOT allowed?
optionA: Loss from house property A set off against income from house property B
optionB: Loss from a speculative business set off against profit from an ordinary business
optionC: Loss from an ordinary business set off against income from a speculative business
optionD: Loss from a non-speculative business set off against income from house property
answerText: Loss from a speculative business set off against profit from an ordinary business
explanation: Under section 73(1), any loss computed in respect of a speculative business carried on by the assessee cannot be set off except against profits and gains of another speculative business. Thus, it cannot be set off against ordinary business profits.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the maximum period for which business loss (other than speculation loss and specified business loss) can be carried forward and set off under section 72?
optionA: 4 assessment years
optionB: 8 assessment years
optionC: Indefinitely
optionD: 10 assessment years
answerText: 8 assessment years
explanation: Under section 72(3), business loss can be carried forward for a maximum of 8 assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment year for which the loss was first computed.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Can a loss from an activity of owning and maintaining race horses be set off against income from salary in the same assessment year?
optionA: Yes, without any restriction
optionB: No, it cannot be set off against income under any other head, nor can it be set off against any other source under the head Income from Other Sources
optionC: Yes, subject to a limit of Rs. 2,00,000
optionD: Yes, if the assessee maintains regular books of accounts
answerText: No, it cannot be set off against income under any other head, nor can it be set off against any other source under the head Income from Other Sources
explanation: Under section 74A(3), the loss incurred in the activity of owning and maintaining race horses can be set off only against income from the same activity i.e., owning and maintaining race horses. It cannot be set off against any other head or source.

subject: Taxation
prompt: In the case of a company (other than a company in which public are substantially interested), unabsorbed depreciation can be carried forward:
optionA: For 8 assessment years only
optionB: For 4 assessment years only
optionC: Indefinitely, even if there is a change in shareholding
optionD: Indefinitely, subject to the provisions of section 79
answerText: Indefinitely, even if there is a change in shareholding
explanation: As per section 32(2), unabsorbed depreciation can be carried forward indefinitely and has no time limit. Unlike business losses, unabsorbed depreciation is not subject to the change in shareholding restrictions under section 79.

subject: Taxation
prompt: For carrying forward and setting off of accumulated business losses in case of closely held companies, what percentage of voting power must remain continuously beneficially held under section 79?
optionA: Not less than 51%
optionB: Not less than 49%
optionC: Not less than 75%
optionD: Not less than 26%
answerText: Not less than 51%
explanation: Section 79 provides that in case of a company in which public are not substantially interested, loss incurred in any year prior to the previous year can be carried forward only if not less than 51% of the voting power is beneficially held by the same persons on the last day of the previous year.
conceptTags: Section 79 | Change in shareholding | Business loss

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following losses can be carried forward even if the return of income is filed after the due date specified under section 139(1)?
optionA: Business loss
optionB: Speculation loss
optionC: Loss from house property
optionD: Capital loss
answerText: Loss from house property
explanation: As per section 80 read with section 139(3), filing the return of income within the due date under section 139(1) is mandatory for carrying forward business loss, speculation loss, specified business loss, and capital loss. However, loss under the head 'Income from house property' and unabsorbed depreciation can be carried forward even if the return is filed late.
conceptTags: Section 80 | Due date of return | House property loss

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the maximum period for carrying forward capital losses (both short-term and long-term) under section 74?
optionA: 4 assessment years
optionB: 8 assessment years
optionC: Indefinitely
optionD: 12 assessment years
answerText: 8 assessment years
explanation: Under section 74(1) and 74(2), both short-term capital losses and long-term capital losses can be carried forward for a maximum of 8 assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment year in which the loss was first computed.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Can a long-term capital loss be set off against short-term capital gains in the same assessment year?
optionA: No, long-term capital loss can only be set off against long-term capital gains
optionB: Yes, long-term capital loss can be set off against both short-term and long-term capital gains
optionC: No, capital losses cannot be set off against capital gains at all
optionD: Yes, but only up to Rs. 1,00,000
answerText: Yes, long-term capital loss can be set off against both short-term and long-term capital gains
explanation: Under section 70(3), a long-term capital loss can be set off against any capital gain, whether short-term or long-term. However, a short-term capital loss can be set off against both short-term and long-term capital gains as well.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the order of priority for setting off unabsorbed depreciation, current year business loss, and brought forward business loss?
optionA: Current year business loss -> Brought forward business loss -> Unabsorbed depreciation
optionB: Current year business loss -> Unabsorbed depreciation -> Brought forward business loss
optionC: Unabsorbed depreciation -> Current year business loss -> Brought forward business loss
optionD: Brought forward business loss -> Current year business loss -> Unabsorbed depreciation
answerText: Current year business loss -> Brought forward business loss -> Unabsorbed depreciation
explanation: The order of set-off under the Act is: (1) Current year deductions like depreciation, capital expenditure on scientific research, etc.; (2) Current year business loss; (3) Brought forward business loss under section 72; (4) Unabsorbed depreciation under section 32(2).
conceptTags: Order of set-off | Unabsorbed depreciation | Business loss

subject: Taxation
prompt: Under section 71(3A), loss from house property can be set off against any other head of income in any assessment year up to a maximum of:
optionD: No limit
explanation: As per section 71(3A), where the net result of computation under the head 'Income from house property' is a loss, the assessee can set off such loss against income under any other head to the extent of Rs. 2,00,000 in any assessment year.
conceptTags: House property loss | Section 71 | Inter-head adjustment

subject: Taxation
prompt: Can a loss under the head 'Income from Salaries' be set off against income under any other head of income?
optionA: Yes, up to Rs. 2,00,000
optionB: Yes, without any limit
optionC: No, loss under the head 'Salaries' cannot be set off against income under any other head
optionD: Yes, only against income from house property
answerText: No, loss under the head 'Salaries' cannot be set off against income under any other head
explanation: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, there cannot be a negative income from salary under normal circumstances, but even if a computational loss arises under the head 'Salaries' (e.g., allowances exceeding income), it cannot be set off against income under any other head under section 71.

subject: Taxation
prompt: For how many assessment years can a speculation loss be carried forward under section 73?
optionA: 4 assessment years
optionB: 8 assessment years
optionC: Indefinitely
optionD: 6 assessment years
answerText: 4 assessment years
explanation: Under section 73(4), speculation loss can be carried forward for a maximum of 4 assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment year for which the loss was first computed.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following incomes can be reduced by setting off brought forward business loss under section 72?
optionA: Income from salary
optionB: Profits and gains of business or profession
optionC: Capital gains
optionD: Winning from lotteries
answerText: Profits and gains of business or profession
explanation: Brought forward business loss under section 72 can be set off only against profits and gains of business or profession.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Can a registered firm (partnership firm) carry forward and set off its business losses?
optionA: No, partnership firms cannot carry forward losses
optionB: Yes, the firm itself carries forward and sets off the loss against its own future business income
optionC: No, the loss must be allocated to partners for carry forward
optionD: Yes, but only unabsorbed depreciation can be carried forward by the firm
answerText: Yes, the firm itself carries forward and sets off the loss against its own future business income
explanation: A partnership firm (whether registered or not) is a separate assessable entity. Business losses are carried forward by the firm itself to be set off against its future business profits, and not by the partners (except in case of dissolution/discontinuation where specific rules apply).
conceptTags: Partnership firm | Business loss | Assessment entity

subject: Taxation
prompt: What happens to the unabsorbed depreciation when there is no business income in the current year, but the assessee has income from capital gains and other sources?
optionA: It lapses permanently
optionB: It can be set off against capital gains and other sources
optionC: It can be set off against salary income only
optionD: It can be carried forward indefinitely, but first must be set off against any other head of income in the current year
answerText: It can be carried forward indefinitely, but first must be set off against any other head of income in the current year
explanation: Under section 32(2), if unabsorbed depreciation cannot be fully set off against business income in the current year, it is added to the depreciation of the next year. However, in the current year, it can be set off against any other head of income (except salary) after inter-head adjustments are exhausted.
conceptTags: Unabsorbed depreciation | Section 32 | Priority of set-off

subject: Taxation
prompt: Can a loss from an exempt source of income be set off against taxable income?
optionA: Yes, up to Rs. 2,00,000
optionB: No, since the income itself is exempt, any related loss cannot be set off against taxable income
optionC: Yes, under section 71
optionD: Yes, provided books of accounts are audited
answerText: No, since the income itself is exempt, any related loss cannot be set off against taxable income
explanation: Since the income from an exempt source does not form part of total income, any loss incurred from such exempt source cannot be set off against taxable income.

subject: Taxation
prompt: In the event of the death of an assessee, can the legal representative carry forward and set off the business losses of the deceased assessee?
optionA: Yes, the legal representative can carry forward and set off the deceased's business losses
optionB: No, business losses lapse upon the death of the assessee
optionC: Yes, but only for a maximum of 1 year
optionD: No, only unabsorbed depreciation can be carried forward by the legal representative
answerText: No, business losses lapse upon the death of the assessee
explanation: Under the Income-tax Act, business losses of the deceased assessee cannot be carried forward and set off by the legal representative, because the legal representative is not the same assessee who incurred the loss. (Note: This is an exception compared to inheritance of businesses where succession rules apply differently, but personal business loss under Sec 72 lapses upon death).
conceptTags: Death of assessee | Legal representative | Business loss

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which section of the Income-tax Act, 1961 deals with the carry forward and set-off of losses from house property?
optionA: Section 71
optionB: Section 71B
optionC: Section 72
optionD: Section 74
answerText: Section 71B
explanation: Section 71B specifically deals with the carry forward and set-off of loss from house property for up to 8 assessment years against income from house property.
conceptTags: Section 71B | House property loss | Carry forward

subject: Taxation
prompt: Can a loss from an ordinary business be set off against salary income in the same assessment year?
optionA: Yes, without any restrictions
optionB: Yes, up to Rs. 2,00,000
optionC: No, business loss cannot be set off against salary income under section 71
optionD: Yes, if the business is a proprietary concern
answerText: No, business loss cannot be set off against salary income under section 71
explanation: Under section 71(2), business loss cannot be set off against income under the head 'Salaries'.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Can a short-term capital loss be carried forward if the return of income is filed after the due date under section 139(1)?
optionA: Yes, always
optionB: No, section 80 bars the carry forward if the return is filed belatedly
optionC: Yes, up to 4 years
optionD: Yes, with the permission of the Principal Commissioner
answerText: No, section 80 bars the carry forward if the return is filed belatedly
explanation: Section 80 mandates that returns for losses under section 72(1) (business loss), section 73(2) (speculation loss), section 73A(2) (specified business loss), section 74(1) (capital loss), and section 74A(3) (race horse loss) must be filed within the due date specified under section 139(1) in order to carry them forward.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the treatment of losses under the head 'Income from Other Sources' (other than race horses and lotteries)?
optionA: They cannot be set off against any income
optionB: They can be set off against any other income under the same head or any other head under inter-source and inter-head rules
optionC: They can only be carried forward for 8 years
optionD: They lapse immediately and cannot be set off even within the same head
answerText: They can be set off against any other income under the same head or any other head under inter-source and inter-head rules
explanation: Losses under the head 'Income from Other Sources' (general sources, e.g., loss on maintenance of machinery let out) can be set off against any other income under the same head (inter-source) and against any other head of income (inter-head) under sections 70 and 71, and cannot be carried forward.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Can a loss from an activity of owning and maintaining race horses be carried forward?
optionA: No, it lapses in the same year
optionB: Yes, for a maximum of 4 assessment years
optionC: Yes, for a maximum of 8 assessment years
optionD: Yes, indefinitely
answerText: Yes, for a maximum of 4 assessment years
explanation: Under section 74A(3), loss from the activity of owning and maintaining race horses can be carried forward for a maximum of 4 assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment year for which the loss was first computed.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following losses can be set off against winning from lotteries, crossword puzzles, or game shows?
optionA: Business loss
optionB: Capital loss
optionC: Loss from house property
optionD: None of the above
answerText: None of the above
explanation: As per section 58(4), no deduction in respect of any expenditure or allowance or set-off of any loss can be allowed against winnings from lotteries, crossword puzzles, card games, races, gambling, betting, etc.
conceptTags: Lottery winnings | Section 58 | Restrictions on set-off

subject: Taxation
prompt: In case of amalgamation of companies, can the accumulated loss and unabsorbed depreciation of the amalgamating company be carried forward by the amalgamated company?
optionA: Never
optionB: Yes, under section 72A, subject to fulfillment of specified conditions
optionC: Yes, automatically without any conditions
optionD: Only unabsorbed depreciation can be carried forward, not business loss
answerText: Yes, under section 72A, subject to fulfillment of specified conditions
explanation: Section 72A allows the accumulated loss and unabsorbed depreciation of an amalgamating company to be carried forward and set off by the amalgamated company, provided prescribed conditions relating to industrial undertakings, continuity of business, and level of production are met.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Can a speculation business loss be set off against the income of an ordinary non-speculative business in the same assessment year?
optionA: Yes, under inter-source adjustment
optionB: Yes, up to Rs. 2,00,000
optionC: No, speculation loss can only be set off against speculation profits
optionD: Yes, if both businesses are carried on by the same company
answerText: No, speculation loss can only be set off against speculation profits
explanation: Section 73(1) explicitly prohibits setting off speculation loss against any income other than profits and gains of another speculation business.

subject: Taxation
prompt: If an assessee incurs a loss in a business that was discontinued in an earlier year, can such business loss be carried forward and set off against current business income?
optionA: No, discontinued business losses cannot be carried forward
optionB: Yes, provided the loss was computed and returned when the business was active, and the 8-year time limit has not expired
optionC: Yes, indefinitely
optionD: No, unless the business is restarted in the current year
answerText: Yes, provided the loss was computed and returned when the business was active, and the 8-year time limit has not expired
explanation: Under section 72, the discontinuation of a business does not prevent the carry forward and set-off of its business loss, provided the loss was duly determined in earlier years and the 8-year time limit has not expired.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the maximum period for carrying forward and setting off loss from house property under section 71B?
optionA: 4 assessment years
optionB: 8 assessment years
optionC: 10 assessment years
optionD: Indefinitely
answerText: 8 assessment years
explanation: Under section 71B, loss under the head 'Income from house property' can be carried forward for a maximum of 8 assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment year in which the loss was first computed.
conceptTags: Section 71B | House property | Carry forward limit

subject: Taxation
prompt: Can an individual set off business loss against capital gains in the same assessment year under inter-head adjustment?
optionA: Yes, business loss can be set off against capital gains
optionB: No, business loss cannot be set off against capital gains under section 71
optionC: Yes, up to Rs. 2,00,000
optionD: Yes, if capital gains are short-term only
answerText: No, business loss cannot be set off against capital gains under section 71
explanation: Under section 71, business loss can be set off against income under any other head EXCEPT 'Salaries'. However, capital gains are not restricted; wait, let's check section 71: business loss CAN be set off against capital gains. Let's verify: section 71 permits business loss to be set off against capital gains (both STCG and LTCG) and other heads except salary. Ah, let's look at the options. Option 1 says 'No, business loss cannot be set off against capital gains'. That is incorrect because business loss CAN be set off against capital gains. Thus, Option 1 ('Yes, business loss can be set off against capital gains') is correct.

subject: Taxation
prompt: In which of the following scenarios does the restriction under section 79 (change in shareholding) NOT apply regarding carry forward of business losses?
optionA: A closely held company where there is a change in shareholding due to death or gift by a shareholder to relative
optionB: A public company where shares are traded on a recognized stock exchange
optionC: A closely held company where 60% shares change hands due to a public offer
optionD: Both (a) and (b)
answerText: Both (a) and (b)
explanation: Section 79 specifically states that its restrictions regarding change in shareholding do not apply to a company in which public are substantially interested (public companies). Furthermore, specific exemptions are provided for closely held companies in cases of death, gifts, start-ups, etc.

subject: Taxation
prompt:
CASE SCENARIO: Mr. Raghav, an individual resident in India, furnishes the following details of his income and losses for the Financial Year 2025-26 (A.Y. 2026-27): 
1. Loss from speculative business A: Rs. 60,000
2. Profit from speculative business B: Rs. 90,000
3. Loss from non-speculative textile business: Rs. 1,50,000
4. Profit from non-speculative readymade garments business: Rs. 80,000
5. Loss from self-occupied house property: Rs. 2,50,000
6. Income from other sources (interest on fixed deposits): Rs. 3,00,000
He files his return of income on 28th July 2026.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the net taxable income or loss from speculative businesses after inter-source adjustment for Mr. Raghav for A.Y. 2026-27?
optionA: Loss of Rs. 60,000
optionB: Profit of Rs. 30,000
optionC: Profit of Rs. 90,000
optionD: Nil, as they cancel out
answerText: Profit of Rs. 30,000
explanation: Under section 70(1), loss from speculative business A (Rs. 60,000) can be set off against profit from speculative business B (Rs. 90,000). The net result is a profit of Rs. 30,000 from speculative businesses.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the treatment of the loss from the non-speculative textile business (Rs. 1,50,000) after inter-source adjustment with readymade garments business?
optionA: Entire loss of Rs. 1,50,000 is set off against garments profit, leaving a net business loss of Rs. 70,000
optionB: Textile business loss of Rs. 1,50,000 is set off against garments business profit of Rs. 80,000, leaving a business loss of Rs. 70,000 to be carried forward or set off against other heads
optionC: Textile business loss cannot be set off against garments business profit
optionD: Textile business loss lapses entirely
answerText: Textile business loss of Rs. 1,50,000 is set off against garments business profit of Rs. 80,000, leaving a business loss of Rs. 70,000 to be carried forward or set off against other heads
explanation: Under section 70, loss from non-speculative textile business (Rs. 1,50,000) can be set off against profit from readymade garments business (Rs. 80,000), leaving a net business loss of Rs. 70,000.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the maximum amount of loss from house property that Mr. Raghav can set off against his interest income under other heads in A.Y. 2026-27?
optionD: Nil
explanation: Under section 71(3A), the loss from house property that can be set off against income under any other head in any assessment year is restricted to a maximum of Rs. 2,00,000. The remaining Rs. 50,000 must be carried forward under section 71B.
conceptTags: House property loss | Section 71(3A) | Inter-head adjustment

subject: Taxation
prompt: Considering that Mr. Raghav filed his return on 28th July 2026, can he carry forward the unabsorbed house property loss of Rs. 50,000?
optionA: No, because the return was filed after 31st July
optionB: Yes, because filing return within due date is not mandatory for carrying forward house property loss
optionC: No, house property loss cannot be carried forward under any circumstance
optionD: Yes, but only for 1 year
answerText: Yes, because filing return within due date is not mandatory for carrying forward house property loss
explanation: Section 80 mandates timely filing under section 139(1) for carrying forward business losses, capital losses, etc., but house property loss under section 71B and unabsorbed depreciation can be carried forward even if the return of income is filed belatedly.
conceptTags: Section 80 | House property loss | Due date

subject: Taxation
prompt:
CASE SCENARIO: M/s. Apex Enterprises (a partnership firm) has two manufacturing units (Unit 1 and Unit 2) and a speculative trading division. For the P.Y. 2025-26, the financial results are as under:
- Profit from Unit 1 (manufacturing): Rs. 4,00,000
- Loss from Unit 2 (manufacturing): Rs. 6,50,000
- Loss from speculative trading division: Rs. 1,20,000
- Brought forward business loss of Unit 1 from P.Y. 2022-23: Rs. 1,00,000
- Unabsorbed depreciation pertaining to Unit 2 from P.Y. 2024-25: Rs. 80,000.
The firm filed its return of income on time.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the business income of M/s. Apex Enterprises after inter-source set-off of current year manufacturing losses and profits?
optionA: Profit of Rs. 4,00,000
optionB: Loss of Rs. 2,50,000
optionC: Loss of Rs. 6,50,000
optionD: Nil
answerText: Loss of Rs. 2,50,000
explanation: Under section 70, current year loss from Unit 2 (Rs. 6,50,000) is set off against current year profit of Unit 1 (Rs. 4,00,000), resulting in a net current business loss of Rs. 2,50,000.

subject: Taxation
prompt: How should the brought forward business loss of Rs. 1,00,000 from P.Y. 2022-23 be treated in P.Y. 2025-26?
optionA: It can be set off against current year business profits, but since there is a net current business loss, it is carried forward further
optionB: It lapses because current year has a loss
optionC: It can be set off against speculative trading profit
optionD: It can be set off against partner's salary
answerText: It can be set off against current year business profits, but since there is a net current business loss, it is carried forward further
explanation: Brought forward business loss under section 72 can only be set off against business profits. Since the current year results in a net business loss, brought forward business loss cannot be set off and must be carried forward for the remaining years.
conceptTags: Section 72 | Brought forward loss | Partnership firm

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the treatment of the speculative trading loss of Rs. 1,20,000 incurred by the firm?
optionA: It can be set off against Unit 1's manufacturing profit
optionB: It can be set off against the net business loss
optionC: It cannot be set off against manufacturing profits and must be carried forward for up to 4 assessment years
optionD: It lapses immediately
answerText: It cannot be set off against manufacturing profits and must be carried forward for up to 4 assessment years
explanation: Under section 73, speculation loss cannot be set off against non-speculation business income (manufacturing profit). It must be carried forward to be set off against speculation profits in subsequent years for a maximum of 4 assessment years.

subject: Taxation
prompt: How is the unabsorbed depreciation of Rs. 80,000 treated?
optionA: It lapses due to lack of business profit
optionB: It can be added to current year unabsorbed depreciation and carried forward indefinitely, or set off against any other head of income (except salary) if available
optionC: It can only be carried forward for 8 years
optionD: It must be allocated to partners
answerText: It can be added to current year unabsorbed depreciation and carried forward indefinitely, or set off against any other head of income (except salary) if available
explanation: Unabsorbed depreciation under section 32(2) can be carried forward indefinitely. In the current year, after inter-source and inter-head adjustments, it can be absorbed against other heads of income (except salary) or carried forward.

subject: Taxation
prompt:
CASE SCENARIO: Mr. Karan furnishes the following particulars of capital gains and losses for the Assessment Year 2026-27:
- Short-term capital gain (STCG) on sale of shares: Rs. 1,50,000
- Short-term capital loss (STCL) on sale of land: Rs. 2,40,000
- Long-term capital gain (LTCG) on sale of building: Rs. 90,000
- Long-term capital loss (LTCL) on sale of gold: Rs. 60,000
- Brought forward short-term capital loss from A.Y. 2023-24: Rs. 50,000.
He has no income under any other head and filed his return within the due date under section 139(1).

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the net short-term capital loss/gain after inter-source set-off for A.Y. 2026-27 (excluding brought forward losses)?
optionA: STCG of Rs. 1,50,000
optionB: STCL of Rs. 90,000
optionC: STCL of Rs. 2,40,000
optionD: Nil
answerText: STCL of Rs. 90,000
explanation: Under section 70(2), short-term capital loss on sale of land (Rs. 2,40,000) can be set off against short-term capital gain on sale of shares (Rs. 1,50,000), resulting in a net short-term capital loss of Rs. 90,000.
conceptTags: Short-term capital loss | Inter-source adjustment | Section 70

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the net long-term capital gain/loss after inter-source set-off for A.Y. 2026-27?
optionA: LTCG of Rs. 90,000
optionB: LTCL of Rs. 60,000
optionC: LTCG of Rs. 30,000
optionD: Nil
answerText: LTCG of Rs. 30,000
explanation: Under section 70(3), long-term capital loss on sale of gold (Rs. 60,000) can be set off against long-term capital gain on sale of building (Rs. 90,000), resulting in a net long-term capital gain of Rs. 30,000.
conceptTags: Long-term capital gain | Inter-source adjustment | Section 70

subject: Taxation
prompt: Can the net short-term capital loss of Rs. 90,000 be set off against the net long-term capital gain of Rs. 30,000 in the same assessment year?
optionA: No, short-term capital loss cannot be set off against long-term capital gain
optionB: Yes, short-term capital loss can be set off against both short-term and long-term capital gains
optionC: Yes, but only up to Rs. 10,000
optionD: No, capital losses cannot be set off against capital gains at all
answerText: Yes, short-term capital loss can be set off against both short-term and long-term capital gains
explanation: Under section 70, a short-term capital loss can be set off against any capital gain, whether short-term or long-term. Thus, STCL of Rs. 90,000 can be set off against LTCG of Rs. 30,000, leaving a net short-term capital loss of Rs. 60,000 for the year.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the total capital loss to be carried forward by Mr. Karan to A.Y. 2027-28 (including brought forward STCL)?
optionA: Rs. 60,000 current STCL only
optionB: Rs. 50,000 brought forward STCL only
optionC: Rs. 1,10,000 (Current net STCL of Rs. 60,000 + Brought forward STCL of Rs. 50,000)
optionD: Nil, as capital losses cannot be carried forward
answerText: Rs. 1,10,000 (Current net STCL of Rs. 60,000 + Brought forward STCL of Rs. 50,000)
explanation: Current year net STCL is Rs. 60,000. Brought forward STCL from A.Y. 2023-24 is Rs. 50,000 (which can be carried forward for 8 years under section 74). Both are carried forward under section 74, totaling Rs. 1,10,000.

subject: Taxation
prompt:
CASE SCENARIO: XYZ Ltd., a closely held domestic company, has the following income/loss details for A.Y. 2026-27:
- Business loss (computed) for P.Y. 2025-26: Rs. 8,00,000
- Brought forward business loss from P.Y. 2021-22: Rs. 3,00,000
- Brought forward unabsorbed depreciation from P.Y. 2023-24: Rs. 2,50,000
- Income from house property: Rs. 5,00,000
- Dividend income: Rs. 1,00,000
During P.Y. 2025-26, there was a change in shareholding, and shareholders holding 60% of voting power on 31-3-2021 were not the same persons holding 60% of voting power on 31-3-2026 (none of the statutory exemptions apply).

subject: Taxation
prompt: Is the brought forward business loss of Rs. 3,00,000 from P.Y. 2021-22 allowed to be carried forward and set off in view of the change in shareholding?
optionA: Yes, because business losses are never restricted by shareholding changes
optionB: No, because more than 51% of voting power has changed hands, violating section 79
optionC: Yes, up to 50%
optionD: Yes, because unabsorbed depreciation and business losses follow identical rules
answerText: No, because more than 51% of voting power has changed hands, violating section 79
explanation: Section 79 provides that loss incurred in any year prior to the previous year cannot be carried forward and set off if there is a change in shareholding exceeding 49% (i.e., less than 51% voting power held by same persons). Hence, the brought forward business loss of Rs. 3,00,000 lapses.
conceptTags: Section 79 | Change in shareholding | Company taxation

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the status of the brought forward unabsorbed depreciation of Rs. 2,50,000 in light of the change in shareholding under section 79?
optionA: It lapses entirely along with the business loss
optionB: It is not affected by section 79 and can be carried forward / set off
optionC: It can only be set off against house property income
optionD: It can be carried forward for only 8 years
answerText: It is not affected by section 79 and can be carried forward / set off
explanation: Section 79 restricts the carry forward and set off of business losses due to changes in shareholding, but it does NOT apply to unabsorbed depreciation under section 32(2). Unabsorbed depreciation remains fully eligible.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Can XYZ Ltd. set off its current year business loss of Rs. 8,00,000 against its house property income of Rs. 5,00,000 under inter-head adjustment?
optionA: Yes, business loss can be set off against house property income
optionB: No, business loss cannot be set off against house property income under section 71
optionC: Yes, up to Rs. 2,00,000 only
optionD: No, because business losses cannot be set off against any other head
answerText: Yes, business loss can be set off against house property income
