explanation: Under Section 80, the requirement of filing a return within the due date under Section 139(1) applies to business losses (Sec 72), speculative losses (Sec 73), specified business losses (Sec 73A), capital losses (Sec 74), and losses from horse races (Sec 74A). House property loss (Sec 71B) and unabsorbed depreciation (Sec 32(2)) can be carried forward even if the return is filed belatedly.
conceptTags: House Property Loss | Section 80 | Carry Forward

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the penalty for failure to comply with the requirement of quoting PAN or Aadhaar under Section 272B?
optionB: Rs. 10,000 for each default
optionC: Rs. 1,000 per day
optionD: Rs. 50,000 flat penalty
answerText: Rs. 10,000 for each default
explanation: Under Section 272B, if a person fails to comply with the provisions of Section 139A (quoting PAN/Aadhaar), the Assessing Officer may direct that such person shall pay a penalty of Rs. 10,000 for each default.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Who is authorized to sign and verify the return of income of a Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) when the designated partner is incapacitated or unable to sign?
optionA: Any designated partner
optionB: Any partner of the LLP
optionC: The auditor of the LLP
optionD: The designated partner holding majority profit sharing ratio
answerText: Any designated partner
explanation: Under Section 140(cd), the return of income of an LLP must be signed and verified by the designated partner, or where there is no such designated partner or where for any unavoidable reason such designated partner is unable to sign, by any partner thereof.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Under Section 139(4), a belated return for Assessment Year 2026-27 can be filed up to:
optionA: 31st March 2027
optionB: 31st December 2027
optionC: 3 months prior to the end of the assessment year
optionD: 30th June 2027
answerText: 31st March 2027
explanation: As per Section 139(4), any person who has not furnished a return within the time allowed under Section 139(1) may furnish the return for any previous year at any time before 31st March of the relevant assessment year or before the completion of the assessment, whichever is earlier.

subject: Taxation
prompt: When is an advance tax installment due for the period ending 15th September for a non-corporate assessee?
optionA: 15% of advance tax payable
optionB: 45% of advance tax payable
optionC: 75% of advance tax payable
optionD: 100% of advance tax payable
answerText: 45% of advance tax payable
explanation: For advance tax installments, the cumulative percentages due are: By 15th June: not less than 15%; By 15th September: not less than 45%; By 15th December: not less than 75%; By 15th March: 100%. Thus, by 15th September, cumulative is 45%.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Is advance tax liability attracted if the tax payable by an assessee during the financial year is Rs. 8,000?
optionA: Yes, advance tax is payable if tax liability is Rs. 5,000 or more.
optionB: No, advance tax is payable only if the tax liability is Rs. 10,000 or more.
optionC: Yes, advance tax is payable for any positive tax liability.
optionD: No, advance tax applies only to companies.
answerText: No, advance tax is payable only if the tax liability is Rs. 10,000 or more.
explanation: Under Section 208, advance tax is payable during any financial year in every case where the amount of such tax payable by the assessee is Rs. 10,000 or more.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the consequence of failing to pay advance tax or paying less than 90% of the assessed tax as advance tax, attracting interest under Section 234B?
optionA: Interest is charged at 1% per month from 1st April of the assessment year till the date of determination of tax under Section 143(1) or regular assessment.
optionB: Interest is charged at 1% per month from 15th September of the financial year.
optionC: Interest is charged at 1.5% per month from the end of the financial year.
optionD: No interest is charged if the return is filed within the due date under Section 139(1).
answerText: Interest is charged at 1% per month from 1st April of the assessment year till the date of determination of tax under Section 143(1) or regular assessment.
explanation: Interest under Section 234B is calculated at 1% per month or part of a month from 1st April of the assessment year up to the date of determination under Section 143(1) (or regular assessment).

subject: Taxation
prompt: Can a resident senior citizen (aged 80 years or more) file their return of income in paper form, or is electronic filing mandatory?
optionA: Electronic filing is mandatory for all individuals without exception.
optionB: Senior citizens aged 60 or more can opt for paper filing.
optionC: An individual whose total income exceeds Rs. 5 lakhs or who is a resident and ordinary resident having foreign assets must file electronically, but super senior citizens having no business income may file in paper form under specific CBDT exemptions.
optionD: Paper filing is universally permitted for individuals.
answerText: An individual whose total income exceeds Rs. 5 lakhs or who is a resident and ordinary resident having foreign assets must file electronically, but super senior citizens having no business income may file in paper form under specific CBDT exemptions.
explanation: CBDT rules require electronic filing for most assessees, but individual super senior citizens (80+ years) filing ITR-1 or ITR-4 in paper form have traditionally been permitted under specific exemptions, though digital compliance has expanded. However, standard rule states individuals with business income or specific conditions must file electronically.
conceptTags: Electronic Filing | Senior Citizen | Return of Income

subject: Taxation
prompt: Under Section 139(3), what must be done to ensure that a loss from capital gains under Section 74 can be carried forward?
optionA: The return must be filed within the due date specified under Section 139(1).
optionB: The return can be filed at any time before 31st March of the assessment year.
optionC: The loss must be intimated to the Assessing Officer in writing separately.
optionD: Capital loss does not require filing a return for carry forward.
answerText: The return must be filed within the due date specified under Section 139(1).
explanation: Section 80 mandates that losses specified under Section 139(3) (which includes capital losses under Section 74) cannot be carried forward unless the return of income is furnished within the due date specified under Section 139(1).
conceptTags: Carry Forward of Losses | Capital Loss | Section 139(3)

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following bodies is required to furnish a return of income under Section 139(4C)?
optionA: Scientific research association
optionB: Political party
optionC: University, college, or other institution referred to in Section 10(23C)
optionD: Both (a) and (c)
answerText: Both (a) and (c)
explanation: Section 139(4C) mandates return filing for specific institutions such as scientific research associations, news agencies, educational institutions, and medical institutions referred to in Section 10(23C). Political parties are covered under Section 139(4B).
conceptTags: Exempt Institutions | Section 139(4C) | Return of Income

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the time limit for filing an updated return under Section 139(8A) if the assessee wishes to file it for Assessment Year 2026-27?
optionA: Up to 31st March 2028
optionB: Up to 31st March 2029
optionC: Up to 31st December 2028
optionD: Up to 30th June 2028
answerText: Up to 31st March 2029
explanation: An updated return under Section 139(8A) can be furnished within 24 months from the end of the relevant assessment year. For AY 2026-27, the relevant assessment year ends on 31st March 2027; adding 24 months gives 31st March 2029.

subject: Taxation
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: M/s. Apex Technologies LLP is a partnership firm engaged in software development. For the financial year 2025-26 (AY 2026-27), its accounts are audited under the Income-tax Act, 1961. The designated partner, Mr. Rohan, prepared the return of income. The firm incurred a net business loss of Rs. 4,50,000 and total income under other heads is nil. Due to administrative delays, the firm filed its return of income on 15th December 2026.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What was the statutory due date under Section 139(1) for M/s. Apex Technologies LLP to file its return of income for AY 2026-27?
optionA: 31st July 2026
optionB: 31st October 2026
optionC: 30th November 2026
optionD: 31st March 2027
answerText: 31st October 2026
explanation: Since the LLP's accounts are required to be audited under the Income-tax Act, the due date for filing the return of income under Section 139(1) is 31st October of the assessment year.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Can M/s. Apex Technologies LLP carry forward its business loss of Rs. 4,50,000 given the date on which the return was filed?
optionA: Yes, because the return was filed before 31st March 2027.
optionB: No, because the return was filed after the due date under Section 139(1), violating Section 80 read with Section 139(3).
optionC: Yes, business losses can be carried forward irrespective of the return filing date.
optionD: No, because LLPs are not permitted to carry forward business losses.
answerText: No, because the return was filed after the due date under Section 139(1), violating Section 80 read with Section 139(3).
explanation: Under Section 80, carry forward and set-off of business losses is contingent upon filing the return of income within the due date specified under Section 139(1). Since the return was filed on 15th December 2026 (after 31st October 2026), the loss cannot be carried forward.
conceptTags: Carry Forward of Losses | Section 80 | LLP

subject: Taxation
prompt: Who is authorized to sign and verify the return of income of M/s. Apex Technologies LLP under Section 140?
optionA: Any employee authorized by the Board
optionB: The designated partner, or any partner if the designated partner is unable to sign
optionC: The statutory auditor of the LLP
optionD: The Chief Financial Officer of the LLP
answerText: The designated partner, or any partner if the designated partner is unable to sign
explanation: Section 140(cd) states that the return of income of an LLP must be signed and verified by the designated partner or, if unavailable, by any partner thereof.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Is M/s. Apex Technologies LLP liable to pay any late fee under Section 234F for filing the return on 15th December 2026?
optionA: No, because the firm incurred a loss and has no taxable income.
optionB: Yes, a late fee of Rs. 5,000 is payable as the return was furnished after the due date.
optionC: Yes, a late fee of Rs. 1,000 is payable.
optionD: No late fee is attracted for partnership firms.
answerText: Yes, a late fee of Rs. 5,000 is payable as the return was furnished after the due date.
explanation: Section 234F imposes a late fee of Rs. 5,000 for failure to furnish a return within the due date under Section 139(1), regardless of whether the assessee has taxable income or a loss, provided the total income exceeds Rs. 5 lakhs (Wait, Section 234F fee applies to any person required to file under 139(1). If total income is nil/loss, is it Rs. 5,000 or Rs. 1,000? For firms, income is computed; if total income is nil/loss, fee is Rs. 5,000 if income exceeds basic exemption limit, but wait—let's check standard rule: Rs. 5,000 if total income exceeds Rs. 5 lakhs, otherwise Rs. 1,000. Since total income is nil (loss), total income does not exceed Rs. 5 lakhs, so late fee is Rs. 1,000). Let's verify option: Rs. 1,000 is correct for total income not exceeding Rs. 5,00,000.

subject: Taxation
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Mr. Vikram, a resident individual aged 45 years, earns a salary income of Rs. 8,00,000 and capital gains of Rs. 1,50,000 during the financial year 2025-26. He did not pay any advance tax during the year. He missed the due date of 31st July 2026 and eventually furnished his belated return of income on 10th January 2027, paying all due taxes along with the belated return.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the late fee payable by Mr. Vikram under Section 234F for filing his belated return on 10th January 2027?
optionD: Nil, since he paid all taxes voluntarily
explanation: Since Mr. Vikram's total income exceeds Rs. 5,00,000 (Salary Rs. 8L + Capital Gains Rs. 1.5L = Rs. 9.5L), the late fee under Section 234F for late filing is Rs. 5,000.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Can Mr. Vikram revise the belated return filed on 10th January 2027 under Section 139(5) if he discovers an error?
optionA: No, because a belated return cannot be revised.
optionB: Yes, a belated return furnished under Section 139(4) can be revised under Section 139(5).
optionC: Yes, but only with the approval of the Principal Commissioner.
optionD: No, because the original due date of 31st July 2026 has passed.
answerText: Yes, a belated return furnished under Section 139(4) can be revised under Section 139(5).
explanation: Section 139(5) explicitly permits any person who has furnished a return under sub-section (1) or sub-section (4) to file a revised return before 31st March of the assessment year.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Is Mr. Vikram liable to interest under Section 234B for default in payment of advance tax?
optionA: No, because salary income is subject to TDS and advance tax does not apply to salaried individuals.
optionB: Yes, if his advance tax shortfall is 90% or more of the assessed tax, interest under Section 234B is attracted.
optionC: No, because he paid all taxes before filing the belated return.
optionD: Yes, a flat interest of 12% is charged.
answerText: Yes, if his advance tax shortfall is 90% or more of the assessed tax, interest under Section 234B is attracted.
explanation: Advance tax applies to all assessees including salaried individuals if tax liability is Rs. 10,000 or more and TDS does not cover it entirely. If advance tax paid is less than 90% of assessed tax, Section 234B interest is attracted.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the last date up to which Mr. Vikram could have filed his belated return under Section 139(4) for AY 2026-27?
optionA: 31st December 2026
optionB: 31st March 2027
optionC: 30th June 2027
optionD: 31st July 2027
answerText: 31st March 2027
explanation: Under Section 139(4), a belated return for AY 2026-27 can be filed up to 31st March 2027 or before completion of assessment, whichever is earlier.

prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Aethelgard Public Ltd., an Indian company, is required to get its accounts audited under the Companies Act, 2013. For the financial year 2025-26, the company filed its original return of income on 20th September 2026. During March 2027, the company's internal audit reveals that certain foreign dividend income of Rs. 10,00,000 was inadvertently omitted from the return filed.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What was the due date under Section 139(1) for Aethelgard Public Ltd. to file its original return of income for AY 2026-27?
optionA: 31st July 2026
optionB: 31st October 2026
optionC: 30th November 2026
optionD: 31st March 2027
answerText: 31st October 2026
explanation: For a company whose accounts are audited under the Companies Act (and not required to furnish a transfer pricing report), the due date under Section 139(1) is 31st October of the assessment year.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Can Aethelgard Public Ltd. furnish a revised return under Section 139(5) to include the omitted foreign dividend income?
optionA: No, because the original return was filed before the due date.
optionB: Yes, a revised return can be filed before 31st March 2027 or before completion of assessment, whichever is earlier.
optionC: No, foreign income can only be declared through an updated return under Section 139(8A).
optionD: Yes, but it requires prior approval of the Assessing Officer.
answerText: Yes, a revised return can be filed before 31st March 2027 or before completion of assessment, whichever is earlier.
explanation: Section 139(5) allows any person who has furnished a return under Section 139(1) to file a revised return anytime before 31st March of the relevant assessment year.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Who is authorized to sign and verify the return of income of Aethelgard Public Ltd. under Section 140?
optionA: Any shareholder holding more than 10% shares
optionB: The Managing Director of the company, or any director if the MD is absent or unable to sign
optionC: The Company Secretary alone
optionD: The Chief Accountant
answerText: The Managing Director of the company, or any director if the MD is absent or unable to sign
explanation: Under Section 140(c), the return of a company must be signed and verified by the Managing Director, or where there is no Managing Director or he is unable to sign, by any director of the company.

subject: Taxation
prompt: If Aethelgard Public Ltd. fails to file any return and the Assessing Officer issues a notice, or if the company wishes to update its income after the expiry of the revised return period, which provision applies?
optionA: Section 139(4) belated return
optionB: Section 139(8A) updated return
optionC: Section 142(1) inquiry notice
optionD: Section 148 reassessment notice
answerText: Section 139(8A) updated return
explanation: Section 139(8A) provides the mechanism for furnishing an updated return within 24 months from the end of the relevant assessment year, even after the expiry of the time limit for filing a revised return.

subject: Taxation
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Dr. Meera is a practicing surgeon whose gross receipts from her profession exceed Rs. 50 lakhs during the financial year 2025-26. Her books of account are maintained and audited as required under Section 44AB. She deposited Rs. 1,50,000 in cash into a current account maintained with a scheduled bank during the year. She filed her return of income on 10th November 2026.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the due date under Section 139(1) for Dr. Meera to file her return of income for AY 2026-27?
optionA: 31st July 2026
optionB: 31st October 2026
optionC: 30th November 2026
optionD: 31st December 2026
answerText: 31st October 2026
explanation: Since Dr. Meera is an assessee (working as a professional) whose accounts are required to be audited under Section 44AB of the Income-tax Act, her due date under Section 139(1) is 31st October of the assessment year.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Was Dr. Meera mandatorily required to file a return of income under Section 139(1) even if her total income was below the basic exemption limit, based on the cash deposit mentioned in the facts?
optionA: No, because the cash deposit was below Rs. 1 crore.
optionB: Yes, because cash deposits in current accounts exceeding Rs. 50,000 trigger mandatory filing.
optionC: Yes, because current account cash deposits exceeding Rs. 1 crore trigger mandatory filing under the seventh proviso to Section 139(1).
optionD: No, professionals are exempt from the seventh proviso.
answerText: Yes, because current account cash deposits exceeding Rs. 1 crore trigger mandatory filing under the seventh proviso to Section 139(1).
explanation: The seventh proviso to Section 139(1) mandates return filing if aggregate cash deposits in one or more current accounts exceed Rs. 1 crore. Since Dr. Meera deposited Rs. 1,50,000, which is well below Rs. 1 crore, this specific proviso does not trigger mandatory filing (though she is required to file anyway due to audit requirements and income levels).

subject: Taxation
prompt: Is Dr. Meera liable to pay any late fee under Section 234F for filing her return on 10th November 2026, given that her due date was 31st October 2026?
optionA: No late fee is payable since she is a professional.
optionB: Yes, a late fee of Rs. 5,000 is payable because the return was filed after the due date and her total income exceeds Rs. 5,00,000.
optionC: Yes, a late fee of Rs. 1,000 is payable.
optionD: No late fee is payable if tax audit report is uploaded on time.
answerText: Yes, a late fee of Rs. 5,000 is payable because the return was filed after the due date and her total income exceeds Rs. 5,00,000.
explanation: Section 234F prescribes a late fee of Rs. 5,000 if the return is furnished after the due date under Section 139(1) and total income exceeds Rs. 5,00,000.

subject: Taxation
prompt: If Dr. Meera's tax audit report under Section 44AB is required to be furnished electronically, by what date must it be uploaded?
optionA: 31st October 2026
optionB: 30th September 2026
optionC: 31st July 2026
optionD: 30th November 2026
answerText: 30th September 2026
explanation: As per Rule 6G, the tax audit report under Section 44AB must be furnished electronically at least one month prior to the due date for filing the return of income under Section 139(1). Since the due date is 31st October 2026, the audit report must be uploaded by 30th September 2026.
conceptTags: Tax Audit Report | Section 44AB | Due Date

subject: Taxation
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Mr. & Mrs. Kapoor are resident individuals. Mr. Kapoor holds financial interest in an entity located in London, United Kingdom. During the financial year 2025-26, Mr. Kapoor's total income computed under the provisions of the Act is Rs. 3,80,000, which is below the basic exemption limit of Rs. 3,00,000 (under the new tax regime, or assume Rs. 2,50,000 under old regime, in either case below basic exemption limit). Mrs. Kapoor's total income is Rs. 6,50,000. Neither of them incurred any high-value electricity expenditure or bank deposits exceeding threshold limits.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Is Mr. Kapoor mandatorily required to file a return of income under Section 139(1) for AY 2026-27?
optionA: No, because his total income is below the basic exemption limit.
optionB: Yes, because he is a resident and ordinary resident individual having a financial interest in an entity located outside India.
optionC: No, unless the foreign entity distributed dividend during the year.
optionD: Yes, because all married individuals must file joint returns.
answerText: Yes, because he is a resident and ordinary resident individual having a financial interest in an entity located outside India.
explanation: Under the fourth proviso to Section 139(1), a resident and ordinary resident individual who is a beneficial owner of any asset (including financial interest in any entity) located outside India must mandatorily file a return of income, regardless of their income level.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the due date under Section 139(1) for Mr. Kapoor to file his return of income for AY 2026-27, assuming he is not subject to tax audit?
optionA: 31st July 2026
optionB: 31st October 2026
optionC: 30th November 2026
optionD: 31st March 2027
answerText: 31st October 2026
explanation: As per the explanation to Section 139(1), the due date for filing return of income for an assessee who is required to furnish a report under the fourth proviso (foreign assets) or whose accounts are audited is 31st October of the assessment year.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the due date under Section 139(1) for Mrs. Kapoor to file her return of income for AY 2026-27, assuming she has no foreign assets and is not subject to audit?
optionA: 31st July 2026
optionB: 31st October 2026
optionC: 30th November 2026
optionD: 31st March 2027
answerText: 31st July 2026
explanation: For an individual whose accounts are not required to be audited and who does not have foreign assets, the due date for filing the return of income under Section 139(1) is 31st July of the assessment year.

subject: Taxation
prompt: If Mr. Kapoor fails to report his foreign financial interest in his return of income, what penal consequence under the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015 or Income-tax Act may apply?
optionA: A flat penalty of Rs. 1,000 under Section 234F.
optionB: A penalty of Rs. 10,000 under the Black Money Act / Income-tax Act provisions for non-disclosure.
optionC: No penalty if tax on foreign income is nil.
optionD: Imprisonment for 7 years without option of fine.
answerText: A penalty of Rs. 10,000 under the Black Money Act / Income-tax Act provisions for non-disclosure.
explanation: Failure to disclose foreign assets or furnishing inaccurate particulars in the return of income attracts strict penalties, including a penalty of Rs. 10,000 under Section 43 of the Black Money Act (or relevant provisions under Income-tax Act for non-reporting of foreign assets).

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the basic exemption limit for an individual resident in India aged 82 years for the Assessment Year corresponding to the previous year, assuming the individual opts for the default tax regime under section 115BAC?
explanation: Under the default tax regime of section 115BAC for individuals, the basic exemption limit is universally Rs. 3,00,000 irrespective of the age of the assessee. The higher exemption limits for senior and super senior citizens are not available under section 115BAC.
conceptTags: Section 115BAC | Basic Exemption Limit | Default Tax Regime

subject: Taxation
prompt: Mr. A, a resident individual, has a total income of Rs. 7,05,000 comprising solely of salary income. He exercises the option to shift out of the default tax regime. What is the marginal relief available under section 87A?
optionD: Nil
explanation: Under section 87A for the old regime, rebate is available up to Rs. 12,500 if total income does not exceed Rs. 5,00,000. Here, total income is Rs. 7,05,000, exceeding Rs. 5,00,000, hence no direct rebate. Marginal relief is computed on the excess of total income over Rs. 5,00,000 (i.e., Rs. 2,05,000) compared to the tax on Rs. 5,00,000 (which is zero). Tax on Rs. 7,05,000 at old rates is Rs. 56,000. Excess income over Rs. 5,00,000 is Rs. 2,05,000. Marginal relief = Tax payable (Rs. 56,000) - Excess income (Rs. 2,05,000)? Wait, marginal relief = tax on total income minus tax on Rs. 5,00,000 + (Total Income - 5,00,000). Tax on Rs. 7,05,000 = 56,000. Excess over 5L = 2,05,000. Relief = 56,000 - 0 = 56,000... actually, tax payable cannot exceed income in excess of 5L. Here tax is 56,000, excess is 2,05,000, so no relief. Let's re-verify standard rule: if total income exceeds 5L under old regime, marginal relief is not applicable since rebate under 87A is strictly for income up to 5L. Therefore, marginal relief is Nil.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Under the default tax regime pursuant to section 115BAC, which of the following deductions under Chapter VI-A is allowed to an individual employee?
optionA: Section 80C
optionB: Section 80CCD(2)
optionC: Section 80D
optionD: Section 80TTA
answerText: Section 80CCD(2)
explanation: Section 115BAC disallows most deductions under Chapter VI-A, including 80C, 80D, and 80TTA. However, employer's contribution to notified pension scheme under section 80CCD(2) is expressly allowed as a deduction under the default tax regime.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the surcharge rate applicable to an individual having a total income of Rs. 5.5 crores under the default tax regime of section 115BAC?
explanation: Under section 115BAC, the maximum rate of surcharge is capped at 25% for total income exceeding Rs. 2 crores, unlike the old regime where the maximum surcharge rate can go up to 37% for income exceeding Rs. 5 crores.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Mr. X has a total income of Rs. 51,00,000 (inclusive of capital gains taxable under section 111A and 112A). What is the maximum marginal relief available in respect of surcharge?
optionD: The excess of tax payable including surcharge on total income of Rs. 51,00,000 over the tax payable on Rs. 50,00,000 plus the amount of income exceeding Rs. 50,00,000
answerText: The excess of tax payable including surcharge on total income of Rs. 51,00,000 over the tax payable on Rs. 50,00,000 plus the amount of income exceeding Rs. 50,00,000
explanation: Marginal relief ensures that the incremental tax and surcharge liability on income exceeding a threshold (like Rs. 50 lakhs) does not exceed the incremental income itself. The correct formula and conceptual definition is the excess of tax plus surcharge on total income over the tax on the threshold plus the incremental income.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following incomes is subject to special rate of tax and is NOT eligible for basic exemption limit absorption against it in the case of a resident individual?
optionA: Long-term capital gains under section 112A exceeding Rs. 1,00,000
optionB: Casual income like winning from lotteries under section 115BB
optionC: Short-term capital gains under section 111A
optionD: Both (A) and (B)
answerText: Both (A) and (B)
explanation: For a resident individual, short-fall in basic exemption can be adjusted against normal income and STCG under 111A (if resident), but casual incomes under section 115BB and LTCG under section 112A/112 do not permit unexhausted basic exemption to be offset against them.
conceptTags: Special Rates | Basic Exemption | Capital Gains

subject: Taxation
prompt: Health and Education Cess is computed at what percentage on the income-tax inclusive of surcharge?
explanation: Health and Education Cess is levied at the rate of 4% on the aggregate of income-tax and applicable surcharge for all assessees.
conceptTags: Health and Education Cess | Tax Computation

subject: Taxation
prompt: Under section 115BAC, can an individual assessee having income from business or profession withdraw from the default regime and opt for the old tax regime?
optionA: Yes, every year at the time of filing the return of income.
optionB: Yes, once in a lifetime.
optionC: Yes, but once they opt out, they can never opt back into section 115BAC except when they cease to have business income.
optionD: No, once opted out, they cannot choose the default regime ever again under any circumstance.
answerText: Yes, but once they opt out, they can never opt back into section 115BAC except when they cease to have business income.
explanation: An assessee having business or profession income who opts out of section 115BAC is allowed to enter back into the default regime only once. Once they opt out again, they cannot choose the default regime unless they cease to have income from business or profession.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the tax rate on short-term capital gains covered under section 111A?
explanation: Short-term capital gains on transfer of equity shares or units of equity oriented fund or business trust on a recognized stock exchange where STT is paid is taxable at a special rate of 15% under section 111A.

subject: Taxation
prompt: In computing total income under the Income-tax Act, 1961, losses from house property can be set off against salary income up to a maximum amount of:
optionD: Nil
explanation: Under section 71(3A), loss from house property can be set off against any other head of income up to a maximum limit of Rs. 2,00,000 in any assessment year.
conceptTags: Set-off of Losses | House Property | Head of Income

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following deductions is NOT disallowed under section 115BAC for an individual/HUF?
optionA: Standard deduction from salary under section 16(ia)
optionB: Entertainment allowance deduction under section 16(ii)
optionC: Professional tax deduction under section 16(iii)
optionD: Interest on housing loan for self-occupied property under section 24(b)
answerText: Standard deduction from salary under section 16(ia)
explanation: Standard deduction of Rs. 50,000 (and family pension deduction) is explicitly allowed under section 115BAC(ia) for salaried individuals and pensioners. Entertainment allowance and professional tax under section 16 and housing loan interest for self-occupied property are disallowed.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the rebate under section 87A available under the default tax regime of section 115BAC for an individual whose total income does not exceed Rs. 7,00,000?
optionC: Actual tax liability or Rs. 25,000, whichever is lower
optionD: Actual tax liability or Rs. 12,500, whichever is lower
answerText: Actual tax liability or Rs. 25,000, whichever is lower
explanation: Under section 87A for the default tax regime (section 115BAC), a resident individual with total income up to Rs. 7,00,000 is entitled to a rebate equal to 100% of income-tax or Rs. 25,000, whichever is lower.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Mr. B has long-term capital gains on land of Rs. 4,00,000 (taxable under section 112) and other normal income of Rs. 1,50,000. His total income is Rs. 5,50,000. Assuming he is a resident individual under the old regime, how is his tax calculated?
optionA: LTCG taxed at 20% and normal income taxed at slab rates
optionB: LTCG and normal income clubbed and taxed at slab rates after basic exemption
optionC: Basic exemption is first exhausted against normal income, and unexhausted basic exemption is allowed against LTCG under section 112
optionD: LTCG is exempt up to Rs. 5,50,000
answerText: Basic exemption is first exhausted against normal income, and unexhausted basic exemption is allowed against LTCG under section 112
explanation: For a resident individual, if total income (excluding special rate incomes) is less than the basic exemption limit, the unexhausted basic exemption limit can be set off against long-term capital gains taxable under section 112.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following entities is subject to Alternate Minimum Tax (AMT) under section 115JC?
optionA: Company
optionB: Co-operative society
optionC: Partnership firm
optionD: Both Partnership firm and Co-operative society (subject to conditions)
answerText: Both Partnership firm and Co-operative society (subject to conditions)
explanation: AMT under section 115JC applies to non-corporate taxpayers (including partnership firms, LLPs, and co-operative societies) who claim deductions under specific sections like 10AA or Chapter VI-A (C). Companies are subject to MAT under section 115JB.
conceptTags: Alternate Minimum Tax | Section 115JC | Non-corporate Assessee

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the rate of Alternate Minimum Tax (AMT) under section 115JC (excluding co-operative societies opting for specific concessional rates)?
explanation: The AMT rate under section 115JC for non-corporate assessees (other than co-operative societies specified under sections 115BAD/115BAE) is 15% (plus applicable surcharge and cess).

subject: Taxation
prompt: Can tax credit for AMT paid under section 115JD be carried forward? If yes, for how many assessment years?
optionA: No, AMT credit cannot be carried forward.
optionB: Yes, up to 10 assessment years.
optionC: Yes, up to 15 assessment years.
optionD: Yes, indefinitely.
answerText: Yes, up to 15 assessment years.
explanation: Tax credit under section 115JD for AMT paid can be carried forward for up to 15 successive assessment years to be set off when normal tax exceeds AMT.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the surcharge rate for an individual with total income of Rs. 3 crores under the old tax regime?
explanation: Under the old tax regime, the surcharge rate is 25% if the total income exceeds Rs. 2 crores but does not exceed Rs. 5 crores.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following deductions/exemptions is NOT available under section 115BAC?
optionA: Leave Travel Concession (LTC) exemption under section 10(5)
optionB: Standard deduction under section 16(ia)
optionC: Conveyance allowance granted to meet official duties
optionD: Transport allowance granted to a blind employee
answerText: Leave Travel Concession (LTC) exemption under section 10(5)
explanation: LTC exemption under section 10(5) is specifically disallowed under section 115BAC. Conveyance allowance for official duties and transport allowance for handicapped employees remain exempt.

subject: Taxation
prompt: In case of a domestic company, what is the Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) rate under section 115JB?
explanation: The MAT rate under section 115JB for domestic companies is 15% of book profit (plus applicable surcharge and cess).

subject: Taxation
prompt: How is agricultural income treated while computing income tax liability for a resident individual in India when non-agricultural income exceeds the basic exemption limit?
optionA: Agricultural income is fully taxed at normal slab rates.
optionB: Agricultural income is added to non-agricultural income for rate purposes (partial integration).
optionC: Agricultural income is exempt and ignored for all purposes.
optionD: Agricultural income is taxed at a flat rate of 30%.
answerText: Agricultural income is added to non-agricultural income for rate purposes (partial integration).
explanation: Agricultural income is exempt under section 10(1), but for tax calculation of resident individuals/HUFs, it is subject to partial integration if non-agricultural income exceeds the basic exemption limit and agricultural income exceeds Rs. 5,000.
conceptTags: Agricultural Income | Partial Integration | Tax Computation

subject: Taxation
prompt: Under partial integration of agricultural income, what is the first step in tax computation?
optionA: Tax on agricultural income plus non-agricultural income minus tax on agricultural income alone.
optionB: Tax on agricultural income plus non-agricultural income minus tax on basic exemption limit plus agricultural income.
optionC: Tax on agricultural income alone.
optionD: Tax on non-agricultural income alone.
answerText: Tax on agricultural income plus non-agricultural income minus tax on basic exemption limit plus agricultural income.
explanation: Step 1 of partial integration is computing tax on (Non-agricultural income + Agricultural income). Step 2 is computing tax on (Basic exemption limit + Agricultural income). Step 1 minus Step 2 gives the tax on non-agricultural income.
conceptTags: Partial Integration | Agricultural Income | Step-by-step Computation

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following incomes is chargeable to tax at special rates under Chapter XII?
optionA: Winnings from lotteries, crossword puzzles, races (Section 115BB)
optionB: Long-term capital gains on equity shares (Section 112A)
optionC: Short-term capital gains on securities (Section 111A)
optionD: All of the above
answerText: All of the above
explanation: All listed incomes are subject to special tax rates under Chapter XII of the Income-tax Act, 1961.
conceptTags: Special Rates | Chapter XII | Capital Gains | Casual Income

subject: Taxation
prompt: Mr. Y has long-term capital gains under section 112 of Rs. 3,50,000 and total income of Rs. 4,50,000 under the old tax regime. What is the tax liability before cess?
optionA: Nil, because total income is below Rs. 5,00,000 and rebate under 87A applies.
optionB: Tax computed on LTCG at 20% after basic exemption adjustment.
optionC: Tax computed at flat 20% on entire LTCG without basic exemption.
optionD: Nil, because capital gains are exempt.
answerText: Nil, because total income is below Rs. 5,00,000 and rebate under 87A applies.
explanation: Since total income is Rs. 4,50,000 (which is less than Rs. 5,00,000), resident individual is eligible for rebate under section 87A up to Rs. 12,500. Tax before rebate will be fully rebated, resulting in nil tax liability.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the tax rate on dividend income received by a domestic company from another domestic company under section 115BAA, assuming no special deductions are claimed?
optionD: Normal corporate tax rate of 22%
answerText: Normal corporate tax rate of 22%
explanation: Under section 115BAA, domestic companies are taxed at a concessional rate of 22% (plus surcharge and cess) on their total income, which includes dividend income.
conceptTags: Section 115BAA | Domestic Company | Concessional Tax Rate

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following losses cannot be carried forward if the return of income is filed after the due date specified under section 139(1)?
optionA: Loss from house property
optionB: Loss from business and profession (speculative or non-speculative) and Capital losses
optionC: Unabsorbed depreciation
optionD: Only speculative business loss
answerText: Loss from business and profession (speculative or non-speculative) and Capital losses
explanation: Under section 80 read with section 139(3), business losses (speculative, non-speculative, specified business) and capital losses cannot be carried forward if the return of income is not filed within the due date under section 139(1). House property loss and unabsorbed depreciation are exceptions.
conceptTags: Carry Forward of Losses | Section 139(3) | Due Date

subject: Taxation
prompt: Under the optional/old tax regime, what is the surcharge rate for an individual having total income of Rs. 52 lakhs?
explanation: For total income exceeding Rs. 50 lakhs up to Rs. 1 crore, the surcharge rate is 10% under both the old tax regime and the default tax regime.

subject: Taxation
prompt: When is marginal relief calculated for an individual whose total income exceeds Rs. 50 lakhs?
optionA: When the tax payable on total income exceeds the tax payable on Rs. 50,00,000 by an amount greater than the income earned over Rs. 50,00,000.
optionB: Whenever income exceeds Rs. 50 lakhs.
optionC: Only when capital gains are included in total income.
optionD: When surcharge is 15%.
answerText: When the tax payable on total income exceeds the tax payable on Rs. 50,00,000 by an amount greater than the income earned over Rs. 50,00,000.
explanation: Marginal relief is designed to eliminate the anomaly where the additional tax and surcharge on incremental income exceeding a threshold exceeds the incremental income itself.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following allowances is fully taxable under both the old and default tax regimes (section 115BAC)?
optionA: Uniform allowance
optionB: City compensatory allowance
optionC: Hostel allowance for children
optionD: Transport allowance for blind employees
answerText: City compensatory allowance
explanation: City Compensatory Allowance (CCA) is fully taxable under both tax regimes. Uniform allowance and transport allowance for blind employees have exemptions under section 10(14). Hostel allowance is exempt up to Rs. 300 p.m. per child under old regime but disallowed under 115BAC.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the maximum deduction allowed under section 80CCD(1) for an employee contributing to the National Pension System (NPS) under the old tax regime?
optionA: 10% of salary
optionB: 10% of salary or Rs. 1,50,000, whichever is less
optionC: 20% of gross total income
answerText: 10% of salary or Rs. 1,50,000, whichever is less
explanation: Employee's contribution to NPS under section 80CCD(1) is deductible up to 10% of salary (basic + DA forming part), subject to the overall ceiling of Rs. 1,50,000 under section 80CCE.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which section provides for an additional deduction of up to Rs. 50,000 for employee/self-employed person's contribution to NPS, over and above the Rs. 1,50,000 limit under section 80CCE?
optionA: Section 80CCD(1)
optionB: Section 80CCD(1B)
optionC: Section 80CCD(2)
optionD: Section 80C
answerText: Section 80CCD(1B)
explanation: Section 80CCD(1B) allows an additional deduction up to Rs. 50,000 for contributions to NPS, which is exempt from the overall Rs. 1,50,000 limit of section 80CCE.

subject: Taxation
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Mr. Rajesh (aged 45 years), a resident individual, derives income from salary and capital gains. For the Previous Year 2025-26, his salary (computed) is Rs. 12,00,000 after standard deduction. He also has long-term capital gains on sale of listed equity shares (STT paid) amounting to Rs. 2,50,000 and short-term capital gains under section 111A amounting to Rs. 1,50,000. He makes a donation of Rs. 20,000 to Prime National Relief Fund (eligible for 100% deduction without qualifying limit under section 80G) and pays Rs. 30,000 towards medical insurance premium for his parents (senior citizens) via cheque. He evaluates computing his tax liability under the default tax regime (section 115BAC).

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is Mr. Rajesh's total income for the Assessment Year corresponding to P.Y. 2025-26 under the default tax regime?
explanation: Total income is computed by aggregating salary (Rs. 12,00,000), LTCG under 112A (Rs. 2,50,000), and STCG under 111A (Rs. 1,50,000) = Rs. 16,00,000. Deductions under Chapter VI-A (80G and 80D) are not available under section 115BAC.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Under the default tax regime of section 115BAC, are the deductions under section 80G and section 80D available to Mr. Rajesh?
optionA: Yes, both are fully available.
optionB: Only section 80G is available.
optionC: Only section 80D is available.
optionD: Neither deduction is available.
answerText: Neither deduction is available.
explanation: Section 115BAC explicitly disallows most deductions under Chapter VI-A, including deductions under section 80G (donations) and section 80D (medical insurance).

subject: Taxation
prompt: How is the long-term capital gain under section 112A of Rs. 2,50,000 taxed for Mr. Rajesh under section 115BAC?
optionA: Fully exempt from tax.
optionB: Exempt up to Rs. 1,00,000 and the balance Rs. 1,50,000 taxable at 10% (plus applicable surcharge and cess).
optionC: Taxable at flat 20% on the entire Rs. 2,50,000.
optionD: Taxable at slab rates.
answerText: Exempt up to Rs. 1,00,000 and the balance Rs. 1,50,000 taxable at 10% (plus applicable surcharge and cess).
explanation: Under section 112A, long-term capital gains on transfer of equity shares are exempt up to Rs. 1,00,000, and the excess is taxable at 10% without indexation, which applies identically under section 115BAC.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the tax rate applicable on the short-term capital gains under section 111A of Rs. 1,50,000?
optionD: At normal slab rates
explanation: STCG on equity shares/units on which STT is paid is taxable at a special rate of 15% under section 111A, regardless of whether the assessee opts for section 115BAC.

subject: Taxation
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: M/s. Zenith Associates, a partnership firm, has a net profit of Rs. 40,00,000 as per its Profit and Loss Account for P.Y. 2025-26. During computation of business income under the normal provisions, it claims a weighted deduction of Rs. 5,00,000 under section 35(1)(ii) for scientific research. Consequently, its business income under normal provisions is computed at Rs. 32,00,000. It has no other income. The firm is subject to Alternate Minimum Tax (AMT) under section 115JC.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the adjusted total income of M/s. Zenith Associates for the purpose of computing Alternate Minimum Tax under section 115JC?
explanation: Adjusted total income under section 115JC is computed by taking total income under normal provisions (Rs. 32,00,000) and adding back deductions claimed under Chapter VI-A (C) or section 35AD/35(1)(ii) etc. Here, the deduction under 35(1)(ii) of Rs. 5,00,000 added back makes adjusted total income Rs. 37,00,000.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the AMT rate applicable to M/s. Zenith Associates under section 115JC?
explanation: The AMT rate for non-corporate assessees like partnership firms is 15% (plus applicable surcharge and health and education cess) under section 115JC.

subject: Taxation
prompt: If the tax payable under normal provisions is Rs. 9,98,400 (inclusive of surcharge and cess) and AMT payable is Rs. 11,58,300, what is the AMT credit eligible to be carried forward under section 115JD?
optionA: Nil
explanation: AMT credit under section 115JD is the excess of AMT liability over the tax payable under normal provisions (Rs. 11,58,300 - Rs. 9,98,400 = Rs. 1,59,900).

subject: Taxation
prompt: For how many assessment years can the excess AMT credit calculated under section 115JD be carried forward by M/s. Zenith Associates?
optionA: 5 assessment years
optionB: 10 assessment years
optionC: 15 assessment years
optionD: Indefinitely
answerText: 15 assessment years
explanation: AMT credit can be carried forward for up to 15 successive assessment years to be set off in the year when normal tax exceeds AMT.

subject: Taxation
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Mr. Suresh, aged 58 years, has total non-agricultural income of Rs. 8,50,000 and net agricultural income of Rs. 3,50,000 for P.Y. 2025-26. He evaluates his tax liability under the old tax regime (slab rates: upto Rs. 2.5L nil, 2.5L-5L @ 5%, 5L-10L @ 20%, above 10L @ 30%).

subject: Taxation
prompt: Does the rule of partial integration of agricultural income apply to Mr. Suresh for P.Y. 2025-26 under the old tax regime?
optionA: No, because his non-agricultural income is less than Rs. 10,00,000.
optionB: Yes, because his non-agricultural income exceeds the basic exemption limit (Rs. 2,50,000) and agricultural income exceeds Rs. 5,000.
optionC: No, because agricultural income is less than non-agricultural income.
optionD: Yes, but only if he opts for section 115BAC.
answerText: Yes, because his non-agricultural income exceeds the basic exemption limit (Rs. 2,50,000) and agricultural income exceeds Rs. 5,000.
explanation: Partial integration applies if two conditions are met: (1) net agricultural income exceeds Rs. 5,000, and (2) non-agricultural income exceeds the basic exemption limit. Here, Rs. 8,50,000 > Rs. 2,50,000 and Rs. 3,50,000 > Rs. 5,000.

subject: Taxation
prompt: In Step 1 of the partial integration method, what income is taken to compute income tax?
optionC: Rs. 12,00,000 (Non-agricultural income + Agricultural income)
answerText: Rs. 12,00,000 (Non-agricultural income + Agricultural income)
explanation: Step 1 of partial integration computes tax on the aggregate of non-agricultural income and net agricultural income (Rs. 8,50,000 + Rs. 3,50,000 = Rs. 12,00,000).

subject: Taxation
prompt: In Step 2 of the partial integration method for Mr. Suresh, what income amount is used for computing tax?
optionB: Rs. 6,00,000 (Basic exemption limit Rs. 2,50,000 + Agricultural income Rs. 3,50,000)
answerText: Rs. 6,00,000 (Basic exemption limit Rs. 2,50,000 + Agricultural income Rs. 3,50,000)
explanation: Step 2 computes tax on the aggregate of the basic exemption limit (Rs. 2,50,000) and net agricultural income (Rs. 3,50,000), totaling Rs. 6,00,000.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Is Mr. Suresh eligible for rebate under section 87A under the old tax regime given his total non-agricultural income of Rs. 8,50,000?
optionA: Yes, rebate of Rs. 12,500 is available.
optionB: Yes, rebate of Rs. 25,000 is available.
optionC: No, because his total non-agricultural income exceeds Rs. 5,00,000.
optionD: No, because he has agricultural income.
answerText: No, because his total non-agricultural income exceeds Rs. 5,00,000.
explanation: Under the old tax regime, rebate under section 87A is available only if total non-agricultural income does not exceed Rs. 5,00,000. Since Mr. Suresh's non-agricultural income is Rs. 8,50,000, he is not eligible.

subject: Taxation
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: XYZ Ltd., a domestic company, reports a total income of Rs. 45,00,000 under the normal provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961 for P.Y. 2025-26. However, its book profit computed under section 115JB is Rs. 70,00,000. The company does not opt for concessional tax regimes under section 115BAA or 115BAB. The applicable corporate tax rate under normal provisions is 25% (since turnover in P.Y. 2023-24 did not exceed Rs. 400 crores). The MAT rate under section 115JB is 15%.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the tax liability of XYZ Ltd. under normal provisions (ignoring surcharge and cess)?
explanation: Tax under normal provisions is 25% of total income of Rs. 45,00,000, which equals Rs. 11,25,000.
conceptTags: Corporate Tax | Normal Provisions | XYZ Ltd

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the tax liability under MAT pursuant to section 115JB (ignoring surcharge and cess)?
explanation: MAT liability under section 115JB is 15% of book profit of Rs. 70,00,000, which equals Rs. 10,50,000.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which tax liability will be applicable to XYZ Ltd. for P.Y. 2025-26?
optionA: Rs. 10,50,000, being tax under MAT
optionB: Rs. 11,25,000, being tax under normal provisions
optionC: Average of both
optionD: Higher of normal tax and MAT
answerText: Rs. 11,25,000, being tax under normal provisions
explanation: If the tax payable under normal provisions (Rs. 11,25,000) is higher than the MAT liability (Rs. 10,50,000), the regular tax under normal provisions is payable.
conceptTags: Tax Liability | MAT vs Normal Tax

subject: Taxation
prompt: Can XYZ Ltd. generate MAT credit under section 115JAA for P.Y. 2025-26?
optionA: Yes, equal to Rs. 75,000.
optionB: Yes, equal to Rs. 10,50,000.
optionC: No, because normal tax exceeds MAT liability.
optionD: Yes, equal to normal tax minus MAT.
answerText: No, because normal tax exceeds MAT liability.
explanation: MAT credit is generated only when the tax payable under MAT exceeds the tax payable under normal provisions. Here, normal tax exceeds MAT, so no MAT credit is generated.

subject: Taxation
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: Mr. Vikram, a resident individual aged 52 years, has a total income of Rs. 51,50,000 for P.Y. 2025-26 under the default tax regime of section 115BAC, consisting entirely of salary and bank interest. He wishes to compute his income tax liability including surcharge and marginal relief.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the surcharge rate applicable to Mr. Vikram whose total income is Rs. 51,50,000 under section 115BAC?
optionA: Nil
explanation: For an individual with total income exceeding Rs. 50 lakhs up to Rs. 1 crore, the surcharge rate is 10% under section 115BAC (as well as under the old regime).

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the primary purpose of computing marginal relief for Mr. Vikram?
optionA: To reduce his basic tax rate.
optionB: To ensure that the incremental tax and surcharge on income above Rs. 50,00,000 does not exceed the incremental income of Rs. 1,50,000.
optionC: To exempt capital gains from tax.
optionD: To claim deductions under Chapter VI-A.
answerText: To exempt capital gains from tax.
explanation: Marginal relief ensures that the additional tax payable due to imposition of surcharge on crossing Rs. 50 lakhs does not exceed the extra income earned over Rs. 50 lakhs.

subject: Taxation
prompt: How is the marginal relief calculated in Mr. Vikram's case?
optionA: Tax and surcharge on Rs. 51,50,000 minus tax on Rs. 50,00,000 plus excess income over Rs. 50,00,000
optionB: Tax on Rs. 51,50,000 minus tax on Rs. 50,00,000
optionC: Surcharge on Rs. 51,50,000
answerText: Tax and surcharge on Rs. 51,50,000 minus tax on Rs. 50,00,000 plus excess income over Rs. 50,00,000
explanation: Marginal relief is computed as: (Tax + Surcharge on Total Income) minus [Tax on Rs. 50,00,000 + (Total Income - Rs. 50,00,000)].

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the final step in computing Mr. Vikram's total tax liability after determining tax, surcharge, and marginal relief?
optionA: Add 2% Health and Education Cess
optionB: Add 4% Health and Education Cess
optionC: Add 3% Education Cess
optionD: No cess is added
answerText: Add 4% Health and Education Cess
explanation: Health and Education Cess at the rate of 4% is added to the income tax liability after adjusting for surcharge and marginal relief.
conceptTags: Health and Education Cess | Final Tax Liability

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following constitutional amendments paved the way for the introduction of Goods and Services Tax (GST) in India?
optionA: 101st Constitution Amendment Act, 2016
optionB: 103rd Constitution Amendment Act, 2019
optionC: 99th Constitution Amendment Act, 2014
optionD: 105th Constitution Amendment Act, 2021
answerText: 101st Constitution Amendment Act, 2016
explanation: The 101st Constitution Amendment Act, 2016 inserted Article 246A, empowering the Parliament and State Legislatures to make laws with respect to GST. This landmark amendment fundamentally restructured India's indirect tax framework.
conceptTags: Constitutional Amendment | Article 246A | Introduction of GST

subject: Taxation
prompt: Under Article 279A of the Constitution of India, who is the Chairperson of the Goods and Services Tax Council?
optionA: Prime Minister of India
optionB: Union Minister of State for Finance
optionC: Union Finance Minister
optionD: Governor of the Reserve Bank of India
answerText: Union Finance Minister
explanation: Article 279A mandates the constitution of the GST Council by the President. The Union Finance Minister acts as the Chairperson of the GST Council, while the Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue or Finance is a member.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following items is currently NOT subsumed under GST and continues to be taxed under the pre-GST central excise and state VAT regime?
optionA: Medicinal formulations containing alcohol
optionB: Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF)
optionC: High Speed Diesel (HSD)
optionD: Toothpaste and soaps
answerText: High Speed Diesel (HSD)
explanation: Petroleum crude, high speed diesel, motor spirit (petrol), natural gas, and aviation turbine fuel (ATF) have been temporarily excluded from GST. The GST Council will decide the date from which GST will be levied on these petroleum products.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the primary voting weight allocated to the Central Government and the State Governments combined in the decisions of the GST Council?
optionA: Center has 1/3rd weight and States have 2/3rd weight combined
optionB: Center has 1/2 weight and States have 1/2 weight combined
optionC: Center has 2/3rd weight and States have 1/3rd weight combined
optionD: Center has 3/4th weight and States have 1/4th weight combined
answerText: Center has 1/3rd weight and States have 2/3rd weight combined
explanation: According to Article 279A, the vote of the Central Government has a weight of one-third of the total votes cast, and the votes of all the State Governments taken together have a weight of two-thirds of the total votes cast in that meeting.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following taxes levied by the Central Government was NOT subsumed into GST?
optionA: Central Excise Duty
optionB: Service Tax
optionC: Basic Customs Duty
optionD: Additional Excise Duty (Goods of Special Importance)
answerText: Basic Customs Duty
explanation: Basic Customs Duty (BCD) is levied on goods imported into India under the Customs Act, 1962, and has not been subsumed under GST. Central Excise, Service Tax, and Additional Excise Duties were subsumed.
conceptTags: Subsumed Taxes | Customs Duty | Central Levies

subject: Taxation
prompt: GST is a destination-based consumption tax. What does this fundamentally imply regarding tax revenue collection?
optionA: Tax revenue accrues to the state where the manufacturing unit is located
optionB: Tax revenue accrues to the state where the goods or services are consumed
optionC: Tax revenue is retained entirely by the Central Government
optionD: Tax revenue is distributed equally among all states regardless of consumption
answerText: Tax revenue accrues to the state where the goods or services are consumed
explanation: GST is a destination-based tax, meaning the tax revenue goes to the state where the final consumption takes place, unlike origin-based taxes which favoured manufacturing states.
conceptTags: Destination-Based Tax | Consumption Tax | Revenue Distribution

subject: Taxation
prompt: Under the dual GST model implemented in India, intra-state supplies attract which of the following combinations of taxes?
optionA: Only IGST
optionB: CGST and SGST/UTGST
optionC: CGST and IGST
optionD: VAT and Central Excise
answerText: CGST and SGST/UTGST
explanation: In an intra-state supply of goods or services, both Central GST (CGST) and State GST (SGST) or Union Territory GST (UTGST) are levied concurrently on the same taxable value.
conceptTags: Dual GST Model | CGST | SGST | Intra-state Supply

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which article of the Constitution of India defines 'Goods and Services Tax' as any tax on supply of goods, or services or both except taxes on the supply of the alcoholic liquor for human consumption?
optionA: Article 366(12A)
optionB: Article 246A
optionC: Article 279A
optionD: Article 265
answerText: Article 366(12A)
explanation: Article 366(12A) of the Constitution of India defines GST as 'any tax on supply of goods, or services or both except taxes on the supply of the alcoholic liquor for human consumption'.
conceptTags: Constitutional Definitions | Article 366(12A) | Scope of GST

subject: Taxation
prompt: What majority is required for taking any decision in the GST Council?
optionA: Simple majority of members present and voting
optionB: Not less than three-fourths of the weighted votes of the members present and voting
optionC: Two-thirds majority of all members of the council
optionD: Unanimous consent of all members
answerText: Not less than three-fourths of the weighted votes of the members present and voting
explanation: Every decision of the GST Council must be taken at a meeting by a majority of not less than three-fourths of the weighted votes of the members present and voting.
conceptTags: GST Council | Decision Making | Three-fourths Majority

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following authorities administers the Integrated Goods and Services Tax (IGST) on inter-state supplies and imports?
optionA: State Government exclusively
optionB: Central Government exclusively
optionC: Both Central and State Governments in a 50:50 ratio
optionD: GST Council directly
answerText: Central Government exclusively
explanation: IGST is levied and collected by the Central Government under the IGST Act, and the tax is subsequently apportioned between the Centre and the consuming State as per the recommendations of the GST Council.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Why was the 'additional tax of up to 1% on inter-state supply of goods' proposed during the conceptual stages of GST ultimately dropped?
optionA: It violated the fundamental destination-based nature of GST and caused cascading effects
optionB: It generated too much revenue for the Centre
optionC: It was declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court prior to enactment
optionD: States requested higher compensation instead
answerText: It violated the fundamental destination-based nature of GST and caused cascading effects
explanation: The proposed 1% additional tax on inter-state supplies was dropped because it violated the fundamental destination-based principle of GST, acted as a cascading tax (origin-based), and created economic distortions.
conceptTags: Inter-state Supply | Additional Tax | Economic Distortions

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which Constitutional provision prohibits any tax to be levied or collected except by authority of law?
optionA: Article 246
optionB: Article 265
optionC: Article 279A
optionD: Article 300A
answerText: Article 265
explanation: Article 265 of the Constitution of India lays down that 'No tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law', which forms the foundational bedrock for all tax legislation, including GST.
conceptTags: Article 265 | Authority of Law | Constitutional Safeguard

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following taxes levied by State Governments was NOT subsumed into GST?
optionA: State VAT / Sales Tax
optionB: Entertainment Tax (levied by states)
optionC: Stamp Duty
optionD: Luxury Tax
answerText: Stamp Duty
explanation: Stamp duty levied on immovable property transactions has not been subsumed under GST. State VAT, entertainment tax, and luxury tax levied by states were successfully subsumed.
conceptTags: Subsumed Taxes | State Levies | Stamp Duty

subject: Taxation
prompt: In the context of GST, what does the acronym SGST stand for?
optionA: Standard Goods and Services Tax
optionB: State Goods and Services Tax
optionC: Special Goods and Services Tariff
optionD: Seamless Goods and Services Transaction
answerText: Standard Goods and Services Tax
explanation: SGST stands for State Goods and Services Tax, levied by individual state governments on intra-state supplies under respective State GST Acts.

subject: Taxation
prompt: How does GST eliminate the cascading effect of taxes (tax on tax)?
optionA: By offering exemptions to all small businesses
optionB: By providing seamless Input Tax Credit (ITC) across the supply chain
optionC: By fixing a uniform tax rate of 18% on all goods and services
optionD: By collecting tax only at the retail level
answerText: By providing seamless Input Tax Credit (ITC) across the supply chain
explanation: GST eliminates the cascading effect by allowing registered taxable persons to claim Input Tax Credit (ITC) for taxes paid on inputs at each stage of the supply chain, ensuring tax is paid only on the value added.
conceptTags: Cascading Effect | Input Tax Credit | Value Addition

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which specific constitutional article empowers Parliament to make laws with respect to GST while granting concurrent powers to State Legislatures?
optionA: Article 246A
optionB: Article 248
optionC: Article 254
optionD: Article 286
answerText: Article 246A
explanation: Article 246A (introduced by the 101st Amendment) gives both Parliament and State Legislatures the power to make laws with respect to GST imposed by the Union or by the State respectively.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the status of 'alcoholic liquor for human consumption' under the GST framework?
optionA: Taxable at the highest GST slab of 28% plus cess
optionB: Completely outside the purview of GST; continues to be taxed by states
optionC: Taxable under CGST only
optionD: Exempted from all forms of taxation
answerText: Completely outside the purview of GST; continues to be taxed by states
explanation: Alcoholic liquor for human consumption is completely kept outside the constitutional definition and purview of GST. States retain the exclusive power to levy excise duty and sales tax/VAT on it.
conceptTags: Alcoholic Liquor | Constitutional Exclusions | State Taxation

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following lists in the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution was amended to accommodate GST?
optionA: List I (Union List) only
optionB: List II (State List) only
optionC: Both List I (Union List) and List II (State List)
optionD: List III (Concurrent List) only
answerText: Both List I (Union List) and List II (State List)
explanation: The Seventh Schedule was amended: entries in List I (Union List) and List II (State List) were modified (e.g., Entry 92 and 92C of Union List deleted; Entry 54 of State List modified) to enable dual GST.
conceptTags: Seventh Schedule | Union List | State List | Constitutional Amendments

subject: Taxation
prompt: Under GST law, what is the nomenclature used for supplies made within the same Union Territory without a legislature?
optionA: CGST and SGST
optionB: CGST and UTGST
optionC: IGST only
optionD: UGST and IGST
answerText: CGST and UTGST
explanation: For intra-UT supplies in Union Territories without a legislature (like Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep), CGST and UTGST (Union Territory Goods and Services Tax) are levied concurrently.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following taxes levied by local bodies (such as municipalities) was subsumed into GST?
optionA: Property tax
optionB: Octroi and Entry Tax
optionC: Professional tax
optionD: Vehicle parking tax
answerText: Octroi and Entry Tax
explanation: Octroi and Entry Tax levied by local bodies were subsumed into GST. Property tax, professional tax, and local parking taxes remain outside GST and continue to be levied by local authorities.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What was the primary legislative objective behind enacting the Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Act, 2017?
optionA: To provide permanent financial grants to underdeveloped states
optionB: To compensate states for any revenue loss arising due to the implementation of GST for a transition period
optionC: To fund infrastructure projects in union territories
optionD: To compensate central government for losses incurred in inter-state trade
answerText: To compensate states for any revenue loss arising due to the implementation of GST for a transition period
explanation: The GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 was enacted to provide compensation to states for loss of revenue arising on account of implementation of GST for a transition period (originally 5 years) funded via a cess on luxury and demerit goods.
conceptTags: GST Compensation | Compensation Cess | Transition Period

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which constitutional article places restrictions on the imposition of tax on the sale or purchase of goods in the course of inter-state trade or commerce?
optionA: Article 269
optionB: Article 286
optionC: Article 301
optionD: Article 304
answerText: Article 286
explanation: Article 286 of the Constitution imposes restrictions on imposition of tax on the sale or purchase of goods in the course of inter-state trade or commerce, which led to the formulation of IGST.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What is the role of the Goods and Services Tax Network (GSTN)?
optionA: To adjudicate tax disputes between taxpayers and the department
optionB: To provide the IT infrastructure and services to central and state governments, taxpayers, and other stakeholders
optionC: To formulate tax rates and exemption policies
optionD: To audit all registered taxpayers annually
answerText: To provide the IT infrastructure and services to central and state governments, taxpayers, and other stakeholders
explanation: GSTN is a non-profit, non-government company providing the robust IT backbone and shared IT infrastructure for registration, return filing, tax payments, and matching of invoices under GST.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following best describes the tax structure of GST regarding multiple rate slabs?
optionA: Single flat rate across all goods and services
optionB: Multiple rate slabs (e.g., 0%, 5%, 12%, 18%, 28%) along with a compensation cess on specified goods
optionC: Regressive rate structure decreasing with higher transaction value
optionD: Discretionary rates decided by individual states
answerText: Multiple rate slabs (e.g., 0%, 5%, 12%, 18%, 28%) along with a compensation cess on specified goods
explanation: India has adopted a multi-rate GST structure with standard slabs of 0%, 5%, 12%, 18%, and 28%, supplemented by a compensation cess on luxury, sin, and demerit goods.
conceptTags: Rate Slabs | Multi-rate GST | Compensation Cess

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which authority is empowered to make recommendations on GST rates, exemption lists, and threshold limits under Article 279A?
optionA: Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC)
optionB: Goods and Services Tax Council (GST Council)
optionC: NITI Aayog
optionD: Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
answerText: Goods and Services Tax Council (GST Council)
explanation: Article 279A empowers the GST Council to make recommendations to the Union and States on GST rates, exemptions, threshold limits, model GST laws, etc.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Can a supplier registered in Maharashtra charge IGST on the supply of goods to a buyer located within Maharashtra?
optionA: Yes, if the buyer requests an inter-state invoice
optionB: No, because a supply within the same state is an intra-state supply attracting CGST and SGST
optionC: Yes, if the goods originated outside Maharashtra
optionD: Yes, at the discretion of the supplier
answerText: No, because a supply within the same state is an intra-state supply attracting CGST and SGST
explanation: When both the location of the supplier and the place of supply are in the same state, it constitutes an intra-state supply, which mandatorily attracts CGST and SGST/UTGST, not IGST.
conceptTags: Intra-state Supply | CGST and SGST | Place of Supply

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following constitutional provisions guarantees freedom of trade, commerce, and intercourse throughout the territory of India, subject to public interest restrictions?
optionA: Article 14
optionB: Article 19(1)(g)
optionC: Article 301
optionD: Article 32
answerText: Article 301
explanation: Article 301 of the Constitution states that trade, commerce, and intercourse throughout the territory of India shall be free, which necessitated careful structuring of IGST to prevent trade barriers between states.
conceptTags: Article 301 | Freedom of Trade | Inter-state Commerce

subject: Taxation
prompt: Under the pre-GST indirect tax regime, what was the primary cause of the 'cascading effect'?
optionA: Non-availability of cross-credit between Central taxes (like Excise) and State taxes (like VAT)
optionB: Excessive use of electronic invoicing
optionC: Uniform tax rates across all states
optionD: Exemption of small traders from taxation
answerText: Non-availability of cross-credit between Central taxes (like Excise) and State taxes (like VAT)
explanation: The cascading effect occurred because Central taxes paid on inputs could not be set off against State taxes output liabilities (and vice versa), leading to tax being levied on tax.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which of the following entities functions as the apex operational body for administering central indirect tax laws including GST at the national level?
optionA: Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT)
optionB: Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC)
optionC: Goods and Services Tax Network (GSTN)
optionD: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
answerText: Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC)
explanation: The Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) under the Ministry of Finance administers central indirect tax laws, including CGST, IGST, and Customs.

subject: Taxation
prompt: In the context of petroleum and natural gas, when can the GST Council notify the levy of GST on crude oil and high-speed diesel?
optionA: Automatically after 10 years from GST rollout
optionB: Only upon the recommendation of the GST Council
optionC: By a direct executive order of the Prime Minister
optionD: After ratification by all 28 states unconditionally
answerText: Only upon the recommendation of the GST Council
explanation: As per Article 246A and related constitutional provisions, GST on petroleum crude, HSD, petrol, natural gas, and ATF will be levied from a date to be recommended by the GST Council.
conceptTags: Petroleum Products | GST Council | Constitutional Provisions

subject: Taxation
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: M/s Apex Manufacturing Ltd., located in the State of Gujarat, procures raw materials worth Rs. 10,00,000 from local suppliers within Gujarat and pays CGST and SGST. It also imports specialized machinery from Germany, paying Basic Customs Duty and IGST. The company manufactures finished goods and sells 60% of its production to buyers in Maharashtra and 40% to buyers within Gujarat.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What type of tax will M/s Apex Manufacturing Ltd. charge on the sale of goods made to buyers located in Maharashtra?
optionA: CGST and SGST
optionB: IGST
optionC: UTGST and CGST
optionD: State VAT
answerText: IGST
explanation: Since the location of the supplier is in Gujarat and the place of supply (buyer) is in Maharashtra, it is an inter-state supply, which attracts Integrated Goods and Services Tax (IGST).
conceptTags: Inter-state Supply | IGST | Place of Supply

subject: Taxation
prompt: What type of tax will M/s Apex Manufacturing Ltd. charge on the sale of goods made to buyers located within Gujarat?
optionA: IGST only
optionB: CGST and SGST
optionC: CGST and UTGST
optionD: Basic Customs Duty
answerText: CGST and SGST
explanation: When both the supplier and the buyer are located within the same state (Gujarat), it is an intra-state supply, attracting CGST and SGST concurrently.

subject: Taxation
prompt: Can M/s Apex Manufacturing Ltd. utilize the IGST paid on the import of machinery against the CGST/SGST liability arising on intra-state sales?
optionA: No, import IGST cannot be utilized for domestic supplies
optionB: Yes, IGST credit can be utilized against CGST and SGST liability in the prescribed order
optionC: Yes, but only against SGST and never against CGST
optionD: No, import duties cannot be set off under GST
answerText: Yes, IGST credit can be utilized against CGST and SGST liability in the prescribed order
explanation: Input Tax Credit (ITC) of IGST paid on imports is seamlessly integrated into the GST credit pool and can be utilized against CGST and SGST liabilities after utilizing available IGST liability first.
conceptTags: Input Tax Credit | IGST Utilization | Import of Machinery

subject: Taxation
prompt: Which constitutional principle ensures that the revenue from the IGST charged on sales to Maharashtra eventually benefits the consuming state?
optionA: Origin-based taxation principle
optionB: Destination-based consumption tax principle
optionC: Central revenue pooling principle
optionD: State equalization grant principle
answerText: Destination-based consumption tax principle
explanation: GST is a destination-based consumption tax; hence, the IGST collected on inter-state sales is apportioned to the consuming state where the goods are finally consumed.
conceptTags: Destination-Based Tax | IGST Apportionment | Consumption Principle

subject: Taxation
prompt: CASE SCENARIO: The State of Zeta has recently witnessed a sharp decline in its state tax revenues following the nationwide rollout of GST. The state finance minister raises concerns in a GST Council meeting regarding budgetary shortfalls. Simultaneously, the Council discusses whether to bring electricity and alcoholic liquor for human consumption under the GST net, and whether to revise the compensation cess rates on luxury vehicles.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What constitutional mechanism was originally established to protect states like Zeta from revenue shortfalls during the initial years of GST?
optionA: Permanent special grants from the RBI
optionB: GST Compensation to States Act providing guaranteed revenue growth backed by a compensation cess
optionC: Automatic borrowing rights from international banks
optionD: Exemption from paying Central taxes
answerText: GST Compensation to States Act providing guaranteed revenue growth backed by a compensation cess
explanation: The GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 guaranteed states a 14% protected revenue growth for a transition period, funded through a compensation cess levied on luxury and demerit goods.
conceptTags: GST Compensation | Protected Revenue | Compensation Cess

subject: Taxation
prompt: Can the GST Council unilaterally bring 'alcoholic liquor for human consumption' under GST without a constitutional amendment?
optionA: Yes, by a three-fourths majority vote in the GST Council
optionB: No, because the Constitution explicitly excludes alcoholic liquor from the definition of GST under Article 366(12A)
optionC: Yes, if all Union Territories agree
optionD: Yes, through an executive notification issued by the Ministry of Finance
answerText: No, because the Constitution explicitly excludes alcoholic liquor from the definition of GST under Article 366(12A)
explanation: Alcoholic liquor for human consumption is excluded by definition in Article 366(12A). Bringing it under GST requires a formal constitutional amendment passed by Parliament and ratified by states.

subject: Taxation
prompt: What voting majority is required in the GST Council for decisions regarding changes in compensation cess or tax rates?
optionA: Simple majority (more than 50%)
